faq.q: How many calories in Soya (Soy Milk)?
faq.a: A 250ml cup of sweetened hawker soya has 130 calories. Order it kosong (no sugar) and it drops to about 85 calories. The soya cincau (Michael Jackson) version with grass jelly comes in at around 150 calories for a slightly larger 300ml serve.

faq.q: Is soya milk a good drink choice when you're trying to lose weight?
faq.a: Honestly, yes, especially compared to teh tarik or Milo ais. At 85 to 130 calories per cup, it gives you 8g of protein, which is decent for a drink. The kosong version is particularly solid because you get real satiety from the protein without the sugar hit.

faq.q: What is the difference between soya kosong and soya manis calories?
faq.a: About 45 calories. Kosong is roughly 85 kcal per 250ml, while the sweetened version is around 130 kcal. That 45-calorie gap is almost entirely from the sugar syrup. If you drink soya every day, switching to kosong saves you over 300 calories a week without giving up anything.

foods.name: Air Tebu
foods.metaDescription: Air Tebu has 220 calories per glass, all from natural sugarcane sugar. Here's what adds up and how to enjoy it without wrecking your calorie count.
foods.summary: Fresh-pressed sugarcane juice that tastes innocent but packs 57g of pure sugar into a single cold glass.
foods.answer: Air Tebu comes in at 220 calories per glass (around 300ml with ice). That's all from sugar, because sugarcane juice is basically liquid sucrose with zero fat and zero protein. The number is honest and it's not small. A plain glass with ice sits at 220 cal, add lime and you're at 230, and if you go with asam boi it creeps up to 250 because of the sugar and salt coating on the plum.
realTalk: So Air Tebu is 220 calories and every single one of those calories comes from sugar. No fat, no protein, just 57g of pure sucrose, glucose, and fructose pressed straight out of the sugarcane. The thing is, it doesn't feel like 220 calories because it's cold, it's refreshing, and it goes down in about 90 seconds. That's the trap lah. Your brain barely registers it as food, but your calorie count absolutely does. If you're someone who grabs one of these every time you're at the pasar malam or waiting for your food at the mamak, that habit alone could be adding 1,500 calories a week to your total.

The math shifts a bit depending on what you add. Plain with ice is your baseline at 220 cal. Throw in a squeeze of lime and you're at 230, basically no difference. But asam boi pushes it to 250 because that preserved plum has a proper sugar and salt coating on it. Also worth knowing: the portion size matters a lot here. A small cup is maybe 200ml, a big roadside plastic bag can easily be 400 to 500ml, which means you could be looking at 300 to 370 calories for one drink. If you're serious about tracking, eyeball the portion or ask for a standard size, bro. Don't let the uncle upsell you a jumbo bag without knowing what you're signing up for.
lighter: Order one glass, not two. It sounds obvious but at the roadside stall the uncle will pour you a second without asking and suddenly you've had 440 calories of juice before your meal even arrives.
Plain with ice only. Skipping asam boi saves you 30 calories and quite a bit of sodium from the salt coating on that plum.
Pair it with a low-calorie meal, not nasi kandar. Air Tebu as a drink with something like grilled fish or a light soup makes more sense than drinking it alongside a 700-calorie rice plate.
Ask for less ice if you want more juice per glass, but don't ask for a bigger glass thinking it's 'just juice'. Bigger glass means more sugar, full stop.
Treat it as an occasional drink, not your daily default. If you switch your daily Air Tebu habit to plain water or cincau, you save over 1,500 calories a week without changing anything else you eat.

faq.q: How many calories in Air Tebu?
faq.a: One standard glass of fresh-pressed Air Tebu with ice is 220 calories. That goes up to 230 if you add lime, and around 250 with asam boi.

faq.q: Is Air Tebu healthy or just sugar water?
faq.a: Honest answer: it's mostly sugar. Sugarcane does have trace minerals but the main thing you're drinking is about 57g of carbs in one glass. It's not poison, but if you're watching your calories it adds up fast, especially if you have two glasses without thinking about it.

faq.q: Can I drink Air Tebu if I'm trying to lose weight?
faq.a: You can, just count it. At 220 calories a glass it's not terrible compared to a large Teh Tarik or a Sirap Bandung, but it's also not a free drink. Stick to one glass, skip the asam boi, and make sure the rest of your meal is on track.

foods.name: Air Kelapa
foods.metaDescription: Air kelapa (young coconut water + flesh) is about 100 calories per whole coconut. One of the best low-cal drinks at the hawker stall, honestly.
foods.summary: Fresh young coconut water with soft jelly flesh, one of the lightest things you can drink at a Malaysian hawker stall.
foods.answer: One whole young coconut (water plus flesh) comes in at 100 calories for roughly 390g of drink and snack combined. The coconut water alone is about 66 calories for 300ml, and the soft jelly flesh adds another 34 calories on top. So yeah, air kelapa is genuinely one of the lowest-calorie things you can order at a hawker stall.
realTalk: Bro, 100 calories for a whole coconut. The water is 66 calories for 300ml and the isi adds 34 calories, so we are talking about a legit low-calorie option that actually fills you up a bit. The 21g of carbs here is a mix of natural sugars from the water and flesh, and at that total it is not going to wreck your deficit if you are eating one a day. This is the drink you want to be ordering at the pasar malam instead of that teh tarik with three teaspoons of condensed milk.

The thing that changes the maths here is whether you eat the flesh or skip it. Air sahaja, just the water, is only 65 calories. Add the isi kelapa muda and you get 34 extra calories for 90g of soft jelly, which is honestly worth it because the flesh keeps you more satisfied. What you want to avoid is the blended versions some stalls sell with added sugar or syrup, because suddenly your 100-calorie coconut turns into a 200-calorie dessert drink. Stick to the plain, chop it open in front of you version and you are fine lah.
lighter: Order air sahaja without the flesh to drop from 100 calories down to 65 calories, a small but real saving.
Skip any stall that adds sugar syrup or flavouring to the coconut water, that doubles the calories for no reason.
Drink it plain and cold, no ice blending, blending sometimes means added ingredients you did not ask for.
Use it as a swap for teh tarik or Milo ais, both of which are 150 to 250 calories, and you save a decent chunk across the week.
If you want the flesh, eat it slowly, it is actually quite filling for 34 calories and will stop you snacking right after.

faq.q: How many calories in Air Kelapa?
faq.a: A whole young coconut with water and flesh is about 100 calories (390g total). The water alone is 66 calories for 300ml, and the soft jelly flesh adds 34 calories. If you skip the flesh, you are looking at 65 calories.

faq.q: Is air kelapa good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, yes. At 65 to 100 calories depending on whether you eat the flesh, it is one of the best drink options at a hawker stall. It hydrates you, has a bit of natural sugar to settle a craving, and keeps the calorie count low. Just make sure nobody is adding syrup to it.

faq.q: How much sugar is in coconut water?
faq.a: The whole coconut order here has 21g of carbs, most of which is a mix of natural sugars from the water and flesh. That is comparable to a small banana. It is not zero sugar, but it is a far better choice than teh tarik or any syrup-based drink at the stall.

foods.name: Cincau
foods.metaDescription: Plain cincau (grass jelly drink) is about 80 calories a glass, and almost all of it comes from the syrup. Here's how to make the most of it.
foods.summary: A classic Malaysian grass jelly drink where the jelly is basically free calories and the syrup does all the damage.
foods.answer: Plain cincau (air cincau) comes in at around 80 calories per glass. The grass jelly itself is basically free at 20 calories for 100g, so almost all the calories come from the sugar syrup. Ask for kurang manis and you drop it to around 50 calories. Get the soya version (Michael Jackson) and you are looking at 140 calories, though you do get some protein out of it.
realTalk: Cincau is genuinely one of the better drink options you can order at the mamak or the roadside stall. 80 calories for a full glass, and the grass jelly has practically nothing in it, around 20 calories for 100g. The jelly is basically a free food. The entire calorie count comes from 45g of sugar syrup which adds 55 calories. So if you are cutting, this is a solid choice compared to teh tarik or Milo ais which can hit 150 to 200 calories easily.

The real thing that changes the number is how heavy-handed the uncle is with the syrup. Some stalls just dump it in. Always ask for kurang manis lah, it is not a weird request and it drops you from 80 to about 50 calories. The soya cincau version (what people call Michael Jackson) replaces the water with soya milk, so you get a bit of protein out of it but also about 60 to 70 extra calories, landing around 140 total. Still not bad for a drink. The versions to avoid are anything with condensed milk drizzled over it.
lighter: Ask for kurang manis every single time. You cut from 80 calories down to about 50 without touching anything else.
Stick to air cincau instead of soya cincau if you are purely watching calories. Saves you about 60 calories per glass.
Skip any version that comes with condensed milk or evaporated milk. Those can push the drink past 150 to 200 calories fast.
Order it without extra syrup drizzled on top. Some stalls do this for sweetness, it is optional.
Eat the jelly. Seriously, it is filling and basically zero calories. Do not leave it behind.

variants.note: Grass jelly, sugar syrup, water and ice only

faq.q: How many calories in Cincau?
faq.a: A standard glass of plain cincau with syrup is about 80 calories. The grass jelly itself contributes almost nothing (around 20 cal per 100g). The syrup is where the calories come from. Ask for kurang manis and you drop it to roughly 50 calories.

faq.q: Is cincau good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, plain cincau is one of the better drink choices at the mamak. 80 calories for a full glass is pretty reasonable. The jelly is filling too, so it does not feel like you are drinking air. Just watch the syrup, and avoid the condensed milk version.

faq.q: What is the difference between air cincau and soya cincau?
faq.a: Air cincau is just grass jelly, syrup and water, around 80 calories. Soya cincau (the Michael Jackson drink) swaps the water for soya milk, which adds about 60 to 70 extra calories and some protein. It comes in at roughly 140 calories total.

foods.name: Ais Kacang (ABC)
foods.metaDescription: Ais Kacang (ABC) has about 350 calories a bowl. Most of it is syrup and condensed milk, not the ice. Here's what actually changes the count.
foods.summary: Malaysia's favourite shaved ice dessert, loaded with red beans, jelly, corn, and enough syrup to make your dentist cry.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of Ais Kacang (ABC) at your local hawker comes in at around 350 calories for a 350g serving. That's not terrible for a dessert, but it's almost entirely sugar from the syrups and condensed milk. The shaved ice itself is basically nothing, only 5 calories. All the damage comes from those generous pours of rose syrup and gula melaka, plus the condensed milk drizzled on top. Add a scoop of ice cream and you're looking at 430 calories. Add durian? 480. It adds up fast for something that feels so light going down.
realTalk: So 350 calories for a bowl of ABC, is that good or bad? Honestly, for a dessert it's not the worst thing in the world, but you need to understand where those calories come from because the breakdown is wild. The shaved ice, which is like 250g of the bowl, contributes maybe 5 calories. Basically nothing. The entire calorie count sits in the 70g of syrups at 140 calories and the 35g of condensed milk at 100 calories. That's 240 calories of pure sugar before you even count the red beans and toppings. Fair warning though, these numbers are a genuine ballpark estimate because solid nutritional data for Malaysian hawker desserts is thin. The actual count depends entirely on how heavy-handed your uncle with the syrup bottle is.

Here's what really moves the needle: the syrup pour and whether they use condensed or evaporated milk. Ask for kurang manis and you can probably knock it down to around 220 calories, that's not a small saving. Swap condensed for evaporated milk and you cut another chunk of fat and sugar. The toppings like attap chee, corn, and agar jelly together are only about 45 calories for 100g, so those are not your enemy here. Red beans at 55 calories for 60g are actually decent, a bit of fibre and protein in there. Where people really go off the rails is adding ice cream (430 cal total) or durian (480 cal for 2 small pieces). If you're dieting, ABC is fine as an occasional thing, just skip the ice cream scoop and say kurang manis like you mean it.
lighter: Say kurang manis when you order. That one request can drop it from 350 to around 220 calories.
Ask the stall to use evaporated milk instead of condensed milk. Less sugar, less fat, still creamy.
Skip the ice cream scoop. That single addition adds 80 to 100 calories for what is basically a garnish.
Go easy on the durian add-on. Two small pieces put you at 480 calories total, which is starting to look like a full meal.
Share a bowl lah. Half a bowl is 175 calories and you still get the full taste experience.

faq.q: How many calories in Ais Kacang (ABC)?
faq.a: A standard hawker bowl of Ais Kacang is around 350 calories for a 350g serving. The syrups and condensed milk account for most of it (about 240 calories between them). The shaved ice itself is only 5 calories.

faq.q: Is ABC a healthy dessert choice when dieting?
faq.a: Compared to cakes or fried desserts it's on the lighter end, but 350 calories is still 350 calories. The upside is you can control it. Order kurang manis and swap condensed for evaporated milk and you're down to roughly 220 calories, which is pretty reasonable for a dessert.

faq.q: Does adding durian to ABC make a big difference?
faq.a: Yes, noticeably. Two small pieces of durian (about 80g) add roughly 120 to 130 calories, pushing the total to around 480 calories. Durian is about 150 calories per 100g so it adds up quickly even in small amounts.

foods.name: Bubur Cha Cha
foods.metaDescription: Bubur Cha Cha has around 360 calories per bowl. Here's what's actually driving that number and how to enjoy it without wrecking your day.
foods.summary: Sweet potato and yam cubes with sago bobbing around in pandan-scented coconut milk, served warm or cold. One of those desserts that tastes like your grandma made it.
foods.answer: One bowl of Bubur Cha Cha (around 300g) comes in at roughly 360 calories. That's not outrageous for a dessert, but it's not light either. The coconut milk broth alone contributes about 120 calories, and then gula melaka adds another 95. So nearly 60% of your calories are just from the liquid before you even get to the sweet potato and yam. Still, 360 calories for a full bowl that genuinely satisfies a sweet craving is pretty decent compared to, say, a slice of cake or a bubble tea.
realTalk: 360 calories per bowl is honestly fair for a dessert, but know what you're paying for. The gula melaka and santan together are about 215 calories before the solid stuff even touches your lips. The sweet potato (52 cal), yam (55 cal), and sago (38 cal) are the innocent bystanders here. Carbs are high at 62g, fat is moderate at 12g, and protein is basically nothing at 3g. Worth flagging that these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard nutrition data for hawker Bubur Cha Cha is genuinely thin. Different stalls vary a lot in how heavy-handed they are with the coconut milk and sugar. Take the 360 as a reasonable middle-ground figure, not gospel.

What actually swings the number is how much santan they pour. A kopitiam version that's thick and creamy can push you to 430 calories no problem, while a lighter street stall version might land closer to 300. If you're served extra gravy (the broth part), you're adding roughly 10 to 15 calories per extra 10g of that liquid. The sago and tapioca jelly are basically pure carbs but they're not the main offender. Cold versus warm makes zero difference to your calorie count, so don't kid yourself that ais version is the diet option, bro. If you want to actually reduce it, the only real lever is asking for less gravy.
lighter: Ask for less broth. The coconut milk gravy is 120 calories for 130g. Getting half a ladle less saves you 40 to 50 calories immediately.
Share a bowl. At 360 calories it is not tragic, but half a bowl as a dessert after a meal is a smarter call than a full one on top of nasi kandar.
Eat the warm version slowly. It cools down, you eat less fast, you feel full sooner. Cold iced versions go down way too quick.
Skip the extra gula melaka drizzle that some stalls offer on top. That's another 30 to 40 calories you don't need.
Count it as your dessert for the day, not a snack between meals. It's sweet enough to genuinely satisfy a craving so treat it like that and move on.

faq.a: A standard bowl of Bubur Cha Cha (about 300g) has around 360 calories. The coconut milk and gula melaka account for most of it, roughly 215 calories combined.

faq.q: Is Bubur Cha Cha fattening?
faq.a: It is not the worst dessert choice at 360 calories a bowl, but it has very little protein and about 62g of carbs, so it does not keep you full for long. If you are counting calories, one bowl is fine as your dessert for the day. Two bowls lah, that's when it becomes a problem.

faq.q: Is the cold or warm version of Bubur Cha Cha lower in calories?

foods.name: Sang Nyuk Mian
foods.metaDescription: Sang Nyuk Mian (KK fresh pork noodle soup) has around 460 calories per bowl. Here's what's actually in it and how to order smarter.
foods.summary: Sabah's favourite Hakka fresh pork noodle soup, a clear peppery broth loaded with thin pork slices, liver, and your choice of noodle.
foods.answer: One bowl of Sang Nyuk Mian with yellow mee in soup comes in at around 460 calories, with 30g of protein, 45g of carbs, and 14g of fat. That's a decent, filling meal that won't wreck your day if you're watching your intake. The protein count is solid, mostly from the pork slices and liver, which makes this one of the more diet-friendly noodle soups you can order in Kota Kinabalu.
realTalk: Sang Nyuk Mian is a KK staple, a Hakka-style fresh pork noodle soup that you'll find at old-school coffee shops around the city. The broth is clear and peppery, nothing like the heavy curry or coconut milk bases you get elsewhere. It's non-halal, pork all the way. A standard bowl comes with thin slices of fresh pork (mixed lean cuts), a bit of pork liver, some greens, and your choice of noodle swimming in that clean bone broth. At around 460 calories per bowl, it's genuinely one of the more reasonable noodle options out there. The calorie count is honest but do note these are ballpark estimates since hard nutritional data for this dish is basically nonexistent. The broth itself is only about 35 calories. What adds up is the noodles (195 calories for 150g of yellow mee) and the pork lard and fried shallot garnish that goes on top, which chips in about 60 calories from just 12g.

What actually moves the numbers here is the garnish and the noodle choice. That lard and shallot topping sounds small but it's adding 60 calories of mostly fat. If you ask them to go easy on the lard, you can shave maybe 30 to 40 calories off without losing much. Swap yellow mee for bee hoon and you drop to around 430 calories. The kon lou (dry) version sounds like it should be the same but it's not. The dry toss uses extra pork lard oil and dark soy, which pushes it to about 560 calories, so if you're counting, stick to the soup version. The liver adds protein for almost no extra calories, so actually don't skip it.
lighter: Order soup version, not kon lou. The dry version adds roughly 100 calories from the extra oil toss.
Ask for less lard garnish. The fried shallot and pork lard on top accounts for 60 calories from just 12g, and most shops will reduce it if you ask.
Choose bee hoon over yellow mee. You save about 30 calories and the lighter noodle still soaks up the broth well.
Don't add extra pork belly or fatty cuts as side toppings. The lean sliced pork in a standard bowl is already pretty clean.
Skip the refill on broth if it comes with a lot of lard oil floating on top. The base broth is low calorie but some shops add more oil than others.

faq.q: What is Sang Nyuk Mian?
faq.a: Sang Nyuk Mian is a Hakka fresh pork noodle soup popular in Kota Kinabalu, Sabah. Sang nyuk literally means fresh pork in Hakka. The soup is a clear, peppery bone broth served with thin slices of fresh pork, pork liver, greens, and your choice of noodle. It is a non-halal dish.

faq.q: Is Sang Nyuk Mian a healthy choice for weight loss?
faq.a: It's one of the better noodle options if you're watching calories. At 460 calories with 30g of protein, the soup version gives you a filling, high-protein meal without a crazy calorie load. The broth itself is very low in calories. The main things to watch are the pork lard garnish and whether you order the dry (kon lou) version, which adds about 100 extra calories.

foods.name: Beaufort Mee
foods.metaDescription: Beaufort Mee has around 620 calories per plate. Here's what's driving those numbers and how the dry konlon version changes the math.
foods.summary: A smoky charcoal wok-fried yellow noodle dish from Beaufort, Sabah, topped with pork slices, char siu, choy sum, and a thick savoury gravy.
foods.answer: Beaufort Mee comes in at around 620 calories for a standard hawker plate (about 420g). That gets you 37g of protein, 53g of carbs, and 26g of fat. The bulk of those calories come from the wok-fried yellow noodles cooked with lard (320 cal) and the pork slices plus char siu on top. It's a genuinely filling plate and not outrageously high for a full noodle meal, but the lard and starchy gravy are doing real work on that calorie count.
realTalk: Beaufort Mee is a Sabah thing, so if you're from KL or peninsular Malaysia, you might not have heard of it. Basically: yellow egg noodles, tossed hard in a charcoal-fired wok until you get that proper smoky wok hei, then served with slices of lean pork, char siu (BBQ roast pork), a starchy soy-oyster sauce gravy poured on top, and blanched choy sum on the side. It's non-halal, pork-based, and absolutely worth going out of your way for if you're in Sabah. At 620 calories for a standard plate, it's not a diet food, but it's also not crazy. The protein is solid at 37g, which is better than a lot of noodle dishes this size. The main calorie drivers are the lard used to fry the noodles (big one) and the char siu, which is sweet-glazed and fatty by nature. Fair warning though: this is a ballpark estimate. Hard nutrition data on Beaufort Mee specifically is basically nonexistent, so treat these numbers as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually shifts the calorie count is the gravy and the fat used in the wok. That starchy gravy adds about 80 calories on its own but it's also where a lot of the sodium hides. The dry version (konlon style, tossed in just soy and lard) comes in around 560 calories because you lose the gravy entirely. If the stall lets you add extra char siu or prawns, you're probably looking at 730 calories or more. The choy sum is basically free at 20 calories for 80g, so don't skip it. If you're watching your intake, go konlon, skip the extra meat, and ask if they can go lighter on the oil in the wok, though at a proper Beaufort Mee stall good luck with that last one.
lighter: Order the konlon (dry) version instead of wet, saves you roughly 60 calories by cutting the starchy gravy.
Skip the char siu upsell or added seafood, going from standard to extra meat jumps the plate by about 110 calories.
Ask for extra choy sum instead of extra meat. More greens at basically zero calories, and it fills the plate up properly.
Eat half the noodles and double the greens if they let you customise. The noodles are where most of the calories are sitting.
Share a plate if you're just trying a taste, then eat something lighter alongside. Beaufort Mee is a once-in-a-while dish, not a daily staple.

faq.q: What actually is Beaufort Mee?
faq.a: It's a wok-fried yellow noodle dish from Beaufort town in Sabah, Borneo. What makes it different from regular fried noodles is the charcoal wok hei (that smoky flavour from the intense heat) and the thick starchy pork gravy poured over the top. It's a non-halal dish with lean pork slices and char siu.

faq.q: Is Beaufort Mee healthy?
faq.a: Compared to a lot of noodle dishes, it holds up okay. You get 37g of protein from the pork slices and char siu, which is solid. The issue is the lard in the wok and the starchy gravy adding up. It's a fine meal if you're eating it once in a while, less ideal if you're tracking your intake carefully every day.

foods.name: Tamparuli Mee
foods.metaDescription: Tamparuli Mee has around 630 calories per plate. Springy handmade egg noodles with siew yoke, char siew and chun kien. Here's what drives the numbers.
foods.summary: Sabah's handmade springy yellow noodles fried in dark soy sauce, topped with roasted pork belly, BBQ pork, egg roll and scrambled egg, a kedai kopi classic from Tamparuli town.
foods.answer: A plate of Tamparuli Mee comes in at around 630 calories for a standard 340g serve. That is for the classic dry version with handmade egg noodles, siew yoke (roasted pork belly), char siew, chun kien (egg roll), and scrambled egg. It is a solid, filling plate and not something you would eat on a deficit without thinking about it, but it is also not some obscene blowout. The 630 figure is a ballpark estimate since hard nutrition data for this dish is basically nonexistent, so take it as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.
realTalk: Tamparuli Mee is a fried noodle dish from Tamparuli, a small town about an hour from Kota Kinabalu in Sabah. For anyone not from Sabah: the noodles here are handmade, thick, springy egg noodles, closer in texture to a good wantan mee noodle but chewier, and they hold the dark soy sauce coating really well. The full plate comes with siew yoke (roasted pork belly), char siew (BBQ pork), and chun kien (a Sabah-style egg roll), all sitting on top. It is not halal. The 630 calorie estimate for a standard plate is exactly that, an estimate, because nobody has actually lab-tested this dish and we are working backwards from the components. The real number could sit anywhere from 580 to 700 depending on how heavy-handed the cook is with oil and how thick they slice the siew yoke. Take it as a reasonable ballpark, not a precise count.

The biggest calorie drivers on this plate are the noodles themselves at around 255 calories and the siew yoke at about 145 calories for just 50g. Pork belly is fatty by nature, so if you get a generous stall that loads it up, you can easily push past 700 calories. The scrambled egg and stir-fry oil together add another 90 calories, which sounds low but oil accumulates fast in a wok. If you are watching the numbers, the practical moves are: eat the standard portion rather than upsizing (saves you roughly 120 calories right there), ask for less oil if the stall allows it, and load up on the veg portion since that whole 70g of greens is only contributing about 40 calories. Swapping siew yoke for a leaner protein like steamed chicken, if the stall offers it, would also knock off 50 to 80 calories without making the plate feel empty.
lighter: Stick to the standard portion and skip the upsized plate, which saves around 120 calories
Ask for less oil when ordering, wok frying adds significant calories and some stalls are more generous than others
Go easy on or skip the siew yoke topping if you want the biggest single calorie reduction, pork belly at 145 calories per 50g is the heaviest item on the plate
Eat the vegetables first so you fill up on the lowest-calorie part before reaching for more noodles
Skip sugary drinks on the side, a kopi susu or teh tarik adds another 100 to 150 calories to what is already a substantial meal

faq.q: What is Tamparuli Mee?
faq.a: Tamparuli Mee is a fried noodle dish from Tamparuli town in Sabah, Malaysia. faq.a: It is not a low-calorie dish at 630 calories a plate, but it is not a disaster either. You get 26g of protein which is decent, and the portion is filling. The fat count of 28g is the part to watch, driven mainly by the pork belly and wok oil. If you are on a calorie deficit, it fits fine as a main meal as long as you keep the rest of the day lighter.

foods.name: Tenom Mee
foods.metaDescription: Tenom Mee dry tossed runs about 670 calories a bowl. Here's what's driving that number and how to eat it without blowing your day.
foods.summary: Springy fresh egg noodles from Sabah's Tenom town, tossed in pork lard sauce and served with char siew, eaten dry or in a clear pork broth.
foods.answer: A bowl of Tenom Mee dry tossed comes in at around 670 calories for a 330g serving. That's a solid number, and it's mostly coming from two places: the fresh egg noodles (280 cal) and the char siew with that pork lard toss sauce (another 375 cal combined). Not a light meal, but not outrageous either for something this filling. Fair warning though, these are ballpark estimates since hard nutrition data on Tenom Mee specifically is basically nonexistent.
realTalk: Tenom Mee is a Sabah thing, specifically from the town of Tenom in the interior. If you've never been to Sabah, think of it as that region's answer to wantan mee: springy fresh egg noodles (sang mee) served dry tossed in a pork lard and soy-based sauce, topped with char siew and a handful of blanched veg. It's non-halal. The dry version sits at around 670 calories for a standard bowl, and honestly that's reasonable for what you're getting, but be clear about what's pushing the number up. The pork lard toss and sauce alone is about 175 calories in a small 25g portion. Add in 80g of char siew at 200 calories and you've already spent 375 cal on the fat and protein before the noodles even show up. These are estimates, bah, because proper nutrition lab data for Tenom Mee basically doesn't exist anywhere. Take the numbers as a solid ballpark, not gospel.

The soup version drops to around 480 calories because you swap the lard toss for a lighter clear pork broth, so that's your easiest win if you're watching calories. The noodle portion itself is the other big lever: 170g of fresh egg noodles is 280 calories, and hawker bowls can easily go heavier than that. If you pile on roasted pork belly and Hakka egg rolls on top of your char siew, you're looking at closer to 820 calories for the mixed toppings version. The veg (choy sum, blanched) is basically free at 15 calories for 60g, so don't skip it. Order extra vegetables if you can, it adds volume without touching the total much.
lighter: Order the soup version instead of dry tossed: you save roughly 190 calories just by switching from lard toss to clear broth.
Ask for less char siew or replace some of it with extra blanched vegetables, the veg runs about 15 calories per 60g versus 200 for the pork.
Skip the mixed toppings upgrade (char siew plus siu yuk plus chun kien) and stick to char siew only, saves you around 150 calories.
Share a bowl if the hawker gives you a big portion, Tenom Mee served at kopitiam sometimes runs larger than the standard 330g estimate.
Don't add extra sauce or ask for less lard drizzle when ordering dry; that pork lard component is where a big chunk of the fat calories hide.

foods.name: Hinava
foods.metaDescription: Hinava is about 200 cal per plate (150g) with 23g protein and zero oil. The Sabah raw fish dish that quietly wins on calories.
foods.summary: Kadazan-Dusun raw tenggiri cured in lime juice with shallots, ginger, chilli, and bambangan seed. One of the lowest-calorie high-protein dishes in Sabah.
foods.answer: A small plate of Hinava comes in at around 200 calories for 150g, which is genuinely impressive for something this satisfying. You're getting 23g of protein from the cured tenggiri, with only 5g carbs and 8g fat. The lime juice does the heavy lifting on "cooking" the fish, so there's no oil involved at all. That's the whole reason the numbers are this low.
realTalk: Hinava is a Kadazan-Dusun raw fish dish from Sabah. Thin slices of tenggiri cured in lime juice, mixed with shallots, ginger, chilli, and grated bambangan seed. If you've never had it, think ceviche but with Bornean flavour. The acid firms the fish up so it doesn't taste raw, and there is absolutely no oil involved. That's why the calorie count is so low. At around 200 calories for a 150g plate you're getting 23g of protein for basically nothing. To be straight with you though, the numbers here are a ballpark estimate because solid nutritional data on Hinava is basically nonexistent, so treat this as a reasonable guide, not gospel.

What actually moves the numbers is the fish-to-condiment ratio. The tenggiri carries almost all of it at 167 calories for 120g. The bambangan seed adds maybe 15 calories, the shallots and ginger another 16. Swap the whole thing to hinava udang (prawn) and you're looking at about 130 calories per plate, which is genuinely ridiculous value for the protein you get. Double the tenggiri to 240g and your calorie count jumps close to 300. So portion size is the one lever here, not the recipe itself.
lighter: Go for hinava udang instead of tenggiri to cut down to around 130 calories while keeping the protein close.
Skip or reduce the bambangan seed if you want to shave a few extra carbs off.
Eat it as a side and pair with sayur manis or ulam instead of rice to keep the whole meal under 400 calories.
Watch your serving size at a buffet spread. A small plate is 150g and 200 calories. A heaped plate can easily double that.
Ask for extra chilli and lime on the side instead of more fish to bulk up the flavour without adding calories.

faq.a: A standard small plate of Hinava (about 150g) is roughly 200 calories, with 23g protein, 5g carbs, and 8g fat. The numbers are low because there is no cooking oil involved. Lime juice cures the raw tenggiri, so you get a high-protein dish without any frying.

faq.q: What is Hinava?
faq.a: Hinava is a traditional Kadazan-Dusun dish from Sabah, Borneo. It is raw Spanish mackerel (ikan tenggiri) sliced thin and cured in lime or calamansi juice until the acid firms up the fish. It gets mixed with sliced shallots, ginger, bird's eye chilli, and often grated bambangan seed, which adds a subtle tangy bitterness. Think of it as the Sabah answer to ceviche.

faq.q: Is Hinava good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, yes. 200 calories for 23g of protein is a solid deal. There is no oil, no heavy sauce, no rice mixed in. The main thing to watch is portion size at a buffet or feast, because it is easy to stack a bigger plate than you think. Swap to the prawn version (hinava udang) and you drop to about 130 calories with similar protein.

foods.name: Bosou
foods.metaDescription: Bosou is around 35 calories per 2-tbsp serving. Sabah fermented raw fish condiment, pungent and eaten in tiny amounts with rice.
foods.summary: Bosou is a traditional Kadazan-Dusun fermented condiment made from raw fish or meat, cooked rice, and pangi seed, eaten in small spoonfuls alongside plain rice.
foods.answer: Two tablespoons of bosou (about 30g) comes in at roughly 35 calories, with 3g protein, 4g carbs, and 1g fat. It is a condiment, not a main dish, so you are realistically eating a tiny spoonful or two with your rice, which means the calorie hit is almost nothing. The fermented fish and lacto-fermented rice do most of the nutritional work here, with pangi seed and salt adding almost zilch in calories.
realTalk: Bosou is a Kadazan-Dusun preserved food from Sabah, and if you have never heard of it, think of it as the Borneo answer to budu or belacan, except way more intense. Raw freshwater fish (or wild boar meat) gets mixed with cooked rice and pangi seed, then left to ferment for days or weeks until it turns sour and pungent. You eat it in small amounts with plain white rice, not as a main dish. The calories are almost laughably low at around 35 per 2-tablespoon serving, and that is honestly the right way to eat it anyway because the flavour is strong enough that nobody is piling on three ladles. Worth flagging: the wild boar and pork variants (bosou daging) are non-halal. These numbers are a ballpark estimate since hard nutritional data for bosou is basically nonexistent, so treat the figures as a reasonable educated guess rather than lab-tested gospel.

What actually changes the calories here is mostly the protein source and how much you eat. Bosou ikan (fish version) sits at about 35 calories per 30g serving because freshwater fish is lean. Swap to bosou daging with wild boar or pork, and you are looking at closer to 50 calories for the same 30g because red meat carries more fat. The bambangan variant (wild mango added to the fish bosou) lands around 40 calories, just slightly higher from the fruit sugars. None of these numbers are scary for a dieter, honestly. The real calorie impact comes from whatever rice you eat bosou with, not the bosou itself. A 200g bowl of white rice is 260 calories. Your two tablespoons of bosou next to it is 35 calories. You do the maths lah.
lighter: Stick to the fish version (bosou ikan) over the meat version to keep it at 35 calories instead of 50 per serving.
Treat it as a condiment, not a side dish. Two tablespoons is the traditional portion and more than enough given how strong the flavour is.
Pair it with cauliflower rice or a smaller rice portion if you are actively cutting, since the bosou itself is not the calorie problem.
Go heavy on plain blanched vegetables alongside it. Sayur manis or kangkung with bosou and rice is a genuinely filling, low-calorie plate.
Avoid versions where extra oil or coconut milk has been stirred in during preparation, which some modern takes do to mellow the sourness.

faq.q: What exactly is bosou and how is it eaten?
faq.a: Bosou is a traditional Kadazan-Dusun fermented food from Sabah made by mixing raw freshwater fish or meat with cooked rice and pangi seed, then fermenting the mixture for several days to weeks. It develops a sour, funky flavour similar to very strong budu. You eat it in small spoonfuls alongside plain white rice, not as a standalone dish. The wild boar and pork versions are non-halal.

faq.q: Is bosou healthy or good for weight loss?
faq.a: For a dieter, bosou is basically a non-issue calorie-wise at 35 calories per serving. It also delivers 3g of protein from the fermented fish. Fermented foods carry probiotic benefits from the lacto-fermentation process. The main thing to watch is sodium since it is preserved with salt, but if you are counting calories, the bosou is not your problem. Your rice portion is.

foods.name: Pinasakan
foods.metaDescription: Pinasakan is around 240 calories per serving with 34g protein. Sabah turmeric-simmered fish is one of the lightest lauk you can eat.
foods.summary: A traditional Kadazandusun fish dish from Sabah, small oily fish simmered with turmeric and a souring agent until tangy and broth-y, with barely any oil in sight.
foods.answer: Pinasakan comes in at around 240 calories per serving (2 small fish plus broth, about 230g total). That's for the classic basung or mackerel scad version, simmered in turmeric and a souring agent like takob-akob or tamarind, no frying involved. Almost all of those 240 calories are coming from the fish itself, which is why this dish punches way above its weight for protein, 34g of it.
realTalk: Pinasakan is a Kadazandusun staple from Sabah that most peninsular Malaysians have never heard of, and honestly that's their loss. The dish is simple: small fish (usually basung, which is mackerel scad) simmered with turmeric, lemongrass, ginger, and a souring agent, the traditional choice being takob-akob, a wild fruit that grows in Sabah, though bambangan or tamarind works too. No coconut milk, no frying, no heavy rempah. The result is a tangy, lightly brothy fish dish that tastes way more interesting than it sounds. At 240 calories for two fish plus broth, the calorie count is genuinely low, and 34g of protein from one lauk is better than most things on a nasi campur spread. Fair warning though: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data on Pinasakan is basically nonexistent. The figures here are built from the fish species and cooking method, treat them as a reasonable guide rather than a lab result.

What actually moves the numbers is the fish size and whether anyone decided to fry the fish first before simmering, which some cooks do. If you get a larger serving or bigger fish (say tenggiri instead of basung), you're looking at closer to 280 calories. The broth itself contributes almost nothing calorie-wise, maybe 10 to 15 calories, so drinking the broth is fine. Where people wreck the maths is on the rice side: most Sabahans eat this with a generous plate of rice, so add 200 to 350 calories depending on your portion lah. Pinasakan as a lauk is one of the easiest high-protein, low-fat choices you can make at a Sabah spread. The rice is where you have to use your head.
lighter: Eat it with less rice. The fish itself is already low cal, so don't undermine it with three scoops of nasi.
Ask for less broth if you're eating out and the cook adds salt generously.
Stick to the sada version with basung rather than upgrading to tenggiri, which adds another 40 calories per serving.
Pair it with sayur manis or tuhau on the side instead of a fried lauk so your whole plate stays reasonable.
If cooking at home, use fresh takob-akob or tamarind rather than packaged paste, which sometimes has added sugar.

faq.a: A standard serving of Pinasakan (2 small basung fish plus broth, around 230g) comes to about 240 calories, with 34g protein and only 9g fat. It's one of the lighter fish dishes you'll find in Sabah cooking.

faq.q: What is Pinasakan exactly?
faq.a: Pinasakan is a traditional Kadazandusun dish from Sabah. Small fish, usually basung (mackerel scad), are simmered with turmeric, lemongrass, ginger, and a sour ingredient like takob-akob (a wild fruit) or bambangan (a Sabah wild mango). No deep frying, no thick coconut gravy. It's broth-y, tangy, and very simple. If you've only eaten peninsular fish dishes, think of it as the Sabah answer to asam pedas but much lighter.

faq.q: Is Pinasakan good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, yes. For 240 calories you get 34g of protein, which is solid. The cooking method uses no added oil to speak of, and the souring agent keeps the broth light instead of rich. The main thing to watch is your rice portion on the side, because nobody's eating Pinasakan without rice.

foods.name: Sinalau Bakas
foods.serving: 1 portion sliced smoked wild boar (hawker stall, ~200g)
foods.metaDescription: Sinalau bakas (Sabah smoked wild boar) packs around 560 cal for a 200g hawker portion. Here's what's driving the number and how to eat it smarter.
foods.summary: Sabah's famous smoked wild boar, slow-cooked over fire until the fat renders and the skin gets that deep, smoky bark that you will be thinking about for days.
foods.answer: Sinalau bakas comes in at around 560 calories for a standard 200g hawker portion of fatty shoulder or rib cuts. That is all from protein and fat, zero carbs, so if you are tracking macros it is 44g protein and 40g fat in one sitting. The number jumps to 820 calories once you add rice, which is how most people actually eat it at a kedai kopi. For leaner cuts like leg meat, you are looking at closer to 320 calories for the same 200g weight. Bear in mind this is a ballpark figure since hard nutritional data on smoked wild boar is basically nonexistent, so treat it as a solid estimate rather than a lab result.
realTalk: Sinalau bakas is a Kadazan-Dusun dish from Sabah where wild boar is rubbed with garlic, lemongrass, turmeric and salt, then slow-smoked over a wood fire. If you are from the peninsula, think of it as the Sabah version of babi panggang but wilder, smokier, and more rustic. A typical hawker portion of 200g of fatty shoulder or rib cuts sits at around 560 calories, and bro, it earns every single one of them. The lean muscle itself is only about 210 calories for 130g, but the 50g of rendered fat on the bone brings in another 315 calories on its own. That fat is also exactly why this thing tastes so good, so there is no mystery here. It is non-halal, by the way, so plan accordingly. Hard numbers on smoked wild boar are genuinely scarce, so these figures are a careful estimate based on USDA wild boar data and the actual fat content of typical cuts. Treat it as a solid ballpark, not a lab-certified figure.

What actually moves the number is which cut you get. Lean leg cuts at 200g drop all the way to around 320 calories, basically a different meal lah. Fatty shoulder or rib with the fat cap intact is the standard hawker serve and that is where you hit 560. Add a plate of rice (200g cooked, roughly 260 calories) and the whole meal is about 820 calories, which is fine if that is your one big meal of the day. The sinalau-in-a-bun version at Kota Kinabalu restaurants is actually more calorie-controlled at 480 calories total because you only get about 100g of meat in the bun. If you are watching your intake, ask for the lean cuts specifically or split a portion with someone. There is no gravy, no sauce, no oil added after smoking, so what you see is what you get.
lighter: Ask specifically for leg or loin cuts instead of shoulder or rib. Same 200g portion drops from 560 to around 320 calories.
Split the portion. A 100g serving of the standard fatty cuts is about 280 calories and honestly still very satisfying because the flavour is so intense.
Skip the rice or go half portion (100g cooked rice instead of 200g) to save about 130 calories if you are having it as a rice set.
Eat it as the protein anchor of your meal and fill the rest of your plate with sayur manis or tuhau. Both are near-zero calories and pair well with the smoky flavour.
If you are at a restaurant doing the sinalau bun, that is your best calorie value at 480 calories for a full meal.

faq.a: A standard 200g hawker portion of sinalau bakas (fatty shoulder or rib cuts) has around 560 calories, with 44g protein and 40g fat and zero carbs. Leaner leg cuts at the same weight come in closer to 320 calories. Add 200g of white rice for the full set and you are at about 820 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is sinalau bakas?
faq.a: Sinalau bakas is a traditional Kadazan-Dusun dish from Sabah, East Malaysia. Wild boar (bakas) is rubbed with garlic, lemongrass, turmeric and salt, then slow-smoked over a wood fire. The result is deeply smoky, rich meat with a bark on the outside and tender, fatty flesh inside. It is non-halal.

faq.q: Is sinalau bakas high in fat?
faq.a: Yes, the typical hawker portion with shoulder or rib cuts is about 40g of fat per 200g serving, which is high. The fat is all from the animal itself, mostly saturated fat from the rendered pork fat layer. If you want a lower-fat version, ask for leg cuts specifically and the fat content drops significantly, bringing calories down to around 320 for the same portion size.

foods.name: Tuhau
foods.metaDescription: Tuhau (Sabah wild ginger sambal) has around 35 calories per 50g serving raw. Here's what changes the count and why it's basically a free condiment.
foods.summary: A pungent wild ginger sambal from Sabah, eaten raw with lime and chilli, pickled, or stir-fried, and one of the lowest-calorie condiments you will find on any Malaysian table.
foods.answer: Tuhau as a raw sambal condiment comes in at about 35 calories per 50g serving, which is basically nothing. The tuhau stems themselves (around 40g) account for 28 of those calories, with bird's eye chilli, lime juice, and a trace of salt or shrimp paste making up the rest. You are essentially getting a punchy, flavour-bomb condiment for free from a calorie standpoint.
realTalk: Tuhau is one of those Sabah things that people from outside Borneo have genuinely never heard of, which is a shame because it deserves more attention. It comes from the stem of a wild ginger plant called Etlingera, sliced paper-thin and eaten raw as a sambal with lime, bird's eye chilli, and salt, or pickled (jeruk), or stir-fried. The flavour is aggressively pungent, sharper than regular ginger, a bit funky, and completely addictive once you get used to it. From a calorie standpoint it is basically a free food. Raw sambal tuhau sits at around 35 calories for a 50g condiment serving, with most of that coming from the stems themselves at 28 calories. Worth flagging that hard nutritional data on tuhau is basically nonexistent, so this is a ballpark estimate based on comparable wild ginger plants. The actual number could be slightly off, but we are clearly talking about something in the 30 to 40 calorie range regardless.

The only thing that meaningfully changes the maths with tuhau is cooking method. Raw or pickled, you are staying in the 30 to 35 calorie zone per serving. The moment you stir-fry it, even just one to two teaspoons of oil adds around 40 calories, pushing tuhau goreng up to roughly 75 calories per 60g serving. That is still low for a cooked veg dish, but it is more than double the raw version. The other variable to watch is portion creep. A proper condiment scoop is about 50g. If you are at a Sabah family makan and you start heaping it on like a side salad, the calories scale with you, lah. As a condiment eaten the normal way alongside rice and a main, tuhau is about as diet-friendly as it gets.
lighter: Stick with raw sambal tuhau or jeruk over goreng. Stir-frying adds around 40 extra calories from oil alone, which more than doubles the count.
Watch the shrimp paste amount. Belacan is low calorie but high sodium, so if you are watching water retention keep it to a trace.
Eat it as a condiment, not a side dish. A proper 50g condiment scoop is 35 calories. If you pile on 150g like a salad, those numbers scale up accordingly.
Pair it with lean proteins like steamed fish or grilled chicken. The punch of tuhau means you need less sauce overall, which saves calories elsewhere.
If having jeruk tuhau, check if sugar was added during pickling. Traditional recipes use minimal sugar but some commercial versions add a fair bit.

faq.a: A standard 50g condiment serving of raw sambal tuhau is around 35 calories. Stir-fried tuhau goreng jumps to about 75 calories per 60g serving once you add oil, while pickled jeruk tuhau sits at roughly 30 calories for a similar portion.

faq.q: What exactly is tuhau?
faq.a: Tuhau is a wild ginger plant (Etlingera) native to Sabah and parts of Borneo. The stem is sliced very finely and eaten raw as a sambal with lime and chilli, pickled in vinegar and salt (jeruk), or stir-fried. It has a sharp, pungent aroma that is somewhere between ginger and galangal but with its own character. Think of it as Sabah's answer to a fiery herb condiment.

faq.q: Is tuhau healthy?
faq.a: For a condiment, yes, very much so. It is near-zero calorie, has no added fat in its raw form, and contains the same beneficial compounds found in ginger and galangal family plants. The main thing to watch is sodium if it is heavily salted or made with fermented shrimp paste, but you are typically eating such a small amount that it barely registers.

foods.name: Bambangan
foods.metaDescription: Jeruk bambangan is just 35 calories per serving. Sabah wild sour mango, pickled with its own seed paste. Full breakdown here.
foods.summary: Bambangan is a wild Sabah mango eaten pickled, in coconut gulai, or raw in salads like hinava, and the pickled version is one of the lightest condiments on any Sabah spread.
foods.answer: Jeruk bambangan comes in at just 35 calories for an 85g condiment serving. That's the pickled version you'd get on the side with your rice, made from sour unripe bambangan flesh with grated seed paste and a bit of salt and chili. Basically zero fat, 8g of carbs, basically nothing protein-wise. It's one of the lowest-calorie condiments you'll find on a Sabah table, so go ahead and pile it on.
realTalk: If you're not from Sabah, you've probably never heard of bambangan, and that's a tragedy. It's a wild mango species (Mangifera pajang) that grows in Borneo, and it does not taste like the sweet Harum Manis you buy at the pasar malam. This thing is aggressively sour and fibrous, and when they pickle it as jeruk, they grate the seed kernel into the mix too, which gives it this funky, slightly bitter edge. At 35 calories for an 85g serving, the pickled version is essentially a free food. The carbs are all coming from the fruit flesh itself, there's no added sugar in the traditional preparation, and the fat is literally zero. It's mostly just fruit, salt, and chili. If you're eating this as a condiment alongside plain rice and some grilled fish, you're doing great.

What changes the maths is the cooking method. The jeruk version at 35 calories is not the same as bambangan gulai. Once you cook bambangan in coconut milk curry, a 150g serving jumps to around 140 calories because coconut milk is adding 80 to 100 calories of saturated fat on its own. The bambangan flesh isn't the problem there, the santan is. The hinava version sits in the middle at around 60 calories because the raw bambangan is mixed into a lime-cured seafood salad with no oil, just the fruit contribution of about 30 to 40 calories to the dish. So if you want bambangan at its lightest, eat it jeruk style as a condiment, not as the star of a coconut gravy.
lighter: Stick to the jeruk version as a condiment, not as a main dish, and you're keeping it at 35 calories per serving.
Skip the bambangan gulai if you're watching calories. The coconut milk alone adds 80 to 100 calories that have nothing to do with the fruit.
If you're having bambangan in hinava, keep the portion small since the salad is low-cal but the total dish calories depend on what fish goes in.
Don't add sugar to your jeruk. Traditional versions have none. If you're buying pre-made pickled bambangan, check the label because some commercial ones add sugar.
Use bambangan jeruk as a replacement for heavier condiments like sambal with oil or peanut sauce. Same flavour punch, fraction of the calories.

faq.q: How many calories in Bambangan?
faq.a: A standard condiment serving of jeruk bambangan (85g, pickled) has 35 calories, with 8g carbs, 1g protein and essentially no fat. If it's cooked in coconut milk as gulai, a 150g serving jumps to around 140 calories because of the santan.

faq.q: What exactly is bambangan?
faq.a: Bambangan is a wild mango species (Mangifera pajang) native to Borneo, particularly Sabah. It's not sweet like regular mango. It's sour and fibrous, and the seed kernel is also edible and gets grated into the pickle. You'll find it at Kadazan-Dusun tables and in Sabah markets, usually as jeruk (pickled condiment), in coconut gulai, or raw in hinava salad.

faq.q: Is bambangan healthy?
faq.a: The pickled version is genuinely low-calorie at 35 calories per serving, with no fat and no added sugar in traditional preparation. The fibre from the fruit flesh is a bonus. The gulai version is higher in calories due to coconut milk, not the fruit itself. As a condiment to replace heavier sauces, jeruk bambangan is a solid choice if you're watching your intake.

foods.name: Sayur Manis (Cangkuk Manis / Sabah Veg)
foods.metaDescription: Sayur manis goreng telur is around 185 calories per plate. The veg is barely 40 kcal, the oil is what does the damage. Full breakdown here.
foods.summary: Sabah famous sweet-leaf vegetable, stir-fried with egg at the hawker stall, one of the cheapest and most genuinely low-calorie sides you can order if you watch the oil.
foods.answer: A plate of sayur manis goreng telur comes in at around 185 calories for a 150g hawker serving. That number sounds almost too good to be true for a stir-fry, and honestly it kind of is, because the veg itself is only about 40 calories. The egg adds roughly 65 kcal and the cooking oil contributes around 75 kcal for a standard tablespoon. If you order it without egg (just garlic or dried shrimp), you're looking at closer to 120 calories per plate. This is a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for sayur manis specifically is thin, but the numbers are grounded in the known calorie values of each component.
realTalk: Sayur manis, or cangkuk manis, is a leafy green vegetable (Sauropus androgynus) that is pretty much Sabah's signature veg. If you grew up outside Borneo you might not have seen it before, but walk into any Sabah hawker centre and it's on every single table. The leaves are tender, slightly sweet, and cook down fast. Calorie-wise it is genuinely one of the best things you can eat at a hawker stall. The veg itself clocks in at around 40 kcal per plate. The goreng telur version sits at about 185 kcal total, which is really not bad at all for a cooked side dish. Where things go sideways is the oil, which at about 1 to 1.5 tablespoons contributes roughly 75 to 120 kcal on its own. So yeah, technically this is an oily dish that happens to contain a very low-calorie vegetable. Keep that in mind. These numbers are an honest estimate, not lab-verified figures, because published data on sayur manis is scarce, so treat the 185 as a solid ballpark rather than gospel.

The thing that actually changes the maths here is how much oil the uncle uses. A generous wok toss at a hawker stall can easily push past 1.5 tablespoons of oil, which adds another 30 to 45 kcal on top of what is already counted here. At home you can do this with half the oil and barely notice the difference in taste. The egg is optional but adds a proper 65 kcal and 6g of protein, which honestly makes the dish more worth it as a meal component. The no-egg version at around 120 calories is basically free food in calorie terms. If you see a masak lemak version on the menu, that coconut milk base will push it up to around 260 calories, still not terrible but a different animal from the simple stir-fry. Order the plain garlic or dried shrimp version when you're cutting, add the egg when you want more staying power.
lighter: Order goreng bawang (no egg) instead of goreng telur to drop from 185 to around 120 calories per plate.
At home, use one teaspoon of oil instead of a tablespoon and a half. You save roughly 80 to 100 calories and the veg still tastes good because the leaves themselves are flavourful.
Ask the hawker to go light on oil (kurang minyak) if you order it out. Some will, some won't, but worth asking.
Pair it with a plain protein like steamed fish or grilled chicken instead of fatty lauk to keep the whole meal in check.
Avoid the masak lemak version if you are counting, the coconut milk bumps it up by about 75 calories compared to a simple stir-fry.

faq.a: A standard hawker plate of sayur manis goreng telur (stir-fried with egg) is around 185 calories per 150g serving. The no-egg version with just garlic or dried shrimp is closer to 120 calories. These are estimates as hard published data for this specific vegetable is limited.

faq.q: What exactly is sayur manis and is it healthy?
faq.a: Sayur manis, also called cangkuk manis or Sabah veg, is a leafy green vegetable (Sauropus androgynus) widely eaten in Sabah, Sarawak, and Brunei. The leaves are soft, mildly sweet, and cook very quickly. The vegetable itself is genuinely low in calories at roughly 40 kcal per cooked plate. It is also a decent source of protein for a leaf vegetable. The main calorie driver when you order it at a stall is the cooking oil, not the veg.

faq.q: How does sayur manis compare to kangkung belacan calorie-wise?
faq.a: Sayur manis goreng telur at around 185 calories is fairly similar to kangkung belacan in the same weight range. Both are leafy stir-fries where the oil does most of the calorie work. If you order both without extra protein additions, the calorie difference is modest. Sayur manis without egg at 120 calories is one of the lighter veg options you can order at a hawker stall.

foods.name: Latok (Sea Grapes)
foods.metaDescription: Latok (sea grapes) is about 30 calories per plate. One of the lowest-calorie things you can eat in Sabah. Here's what actually changes that number.
foods.summary: A fresh, briny Sabah seaweed eaten raw with chilli-lime or sambal belacan, and one of the lightest things you'll find on any table.
foods.answer: A small plate of latok comes in at around 30 calories, making it one of the most diet-friendly things you can order in Sabah or Sarawak. The plain sea grapes themselves are practically nothing, around 13 calories per 100g of plain sea grapes with no dressing added. The nutrition table on this page shows 25 kcal per 100g because that blends in the weight of the dressing across the full 120g serving, so both figures are correct, just measuring different things. Plain with just a squeeze of lime? Closer to 15 calories. With sambal belacan and garnish, you're at roughly 30. These are honest estimates though, because hard nutrition data for latok specifically is thin.
realTalk: Latok is a type of seaweed, specifically Caulerpa lentillifera, also called sea grapes or green caviar. If you've never had it, picture tiny translucent green bubbles on thin stems that pop lightly when you bite them, fresh and briny like the sea. It's a Sabah and Brunei staple, served raw as a salad with chilli, lime, and sambal belacan. At around 30 calories per plate, it is genuinely one of the lowest-calorie foods you can eat in this part of the world. To be upfront though, the numbers here are ballpark estimates because robust lab data for latok is basically nonexistent. The raw seaweed is near-zero calories; everything on this page is our best approximation.

What actually moves the number is the dressing. Plain latok with just lime is around 15 calories for the whole plate. Add a typical sambal belacan dressing and some sliced chilli and tomato and you're at 30. Go heavier on the sambal, bigger diced onion, generous extra belacan, and the fuller salad version lands around 45. None of these numbers are going to stress your calorie budget, bah. The only real way to make latok a problem calorie-wise is pairing it with a massive plate of rice and three lauk. On its own, it's basically a free food.
lighter: Ask for the dressing on the side so you control how much sambal belacan goes on.
Squeeze fresh lime over it and skip the sambal entirely if you're going very low calorie, plain latok is about 15 calories.
Watch the diced tomato and onion garnish, they add almost nothing, but the sambal belacan can vary a lot in how oily the stall makes it.
Use latok as a side dish to replace a heavier vegetable order like kangkung in oyster sauce, you save 80 to 100 calories easily.
Order it first before your mains so you eat something filling and briny before the heavy stuff arrives.

faq.q: What exactly is latok and where do you get it?
faq.a: Latok is a type of seaweed (Caulerpa lentillifera) that looks like tiny green bubbles on thin stems, which is why it's also called sea grapes or green caviar. It's eaten raw, usually with chilli and lime or sambal belacan. You'll find it at seafood restaurants and hawker stalls in Sabah, Sarawak, and Brunei, it's not really a thing in peninsular Malaysia.

faq.q: Is latok good for weight loss?
faq.a: Honestly, yes. At 30 calories per plate it's about as low-calorie as a side dish gets. It's got a bit of fibre, a briny fresh flavour that feels satisfying, and the dressing is the only real variable. For anyone trying to eat at a calorie deficit without feeling miserable, ordering latok as a side is a solid move.

foods.name: Linopot
foods.metaDescription: Linopot is a Kadazan-Dusun rice parcel from Sabah. One plain parcel is about 300 cal. Here's what changes the number when you eat the full set.
foods.summary: A Kadazan-Dusun rice parcel from Sabah, pressed into a ball with hill or red rice, sometimes mixed with yam, and wrapped in fragrant wild leaf.
foods.answer: One plain linopot parcel (230g, rice and yam mix, no sides) comes in at around 300 calories. That's the traditional version with hill or red rice and some yam mixed in. If you're eating the modern white rice only version with no tuber, it's closer to 250 calories. Add a grilled fish set and you're looking at roughly 510 calories for the whole meal. Fair warning though: these numbers are ballpark estimates because linopot doesn't exactly have a mountain of lab data behind it, so treat them as a solid guide rather than gospel.
realTalk: Linopot is a Sabahan thing and if you haven't grown up in KK or the Kadazan-Dusun kampung circuit, you've probably never touched one. Picture this: cooked rice, often the nutty local hill rice or red/purple rice, sometimes mixed with a bit of yam or tapioca, then compressed into a tight ball and wrapped in doringin or tarap leaf. That leaf gives it a faint herbal aroma and it's traditionally eaten with grilled fish or meat. No oil in the rice itself, no coconut milk, nothing. So at 300 calories for a 230g parcel with the yam mixed in, it's honestly pretty clean as rice portions go. To be upfront about it though, the numbers here are a genuine estimate because hard nutritional data for linopot specifically is basically non-existent. So take 300 calories as a well-reasoned ballpark, not a lab result.

What actually moves the number is what you eat with it. The rice parcel alone, 250 to 300 calories depending on whether it's pure white rice or the traditional rice-plus-yam mix. The moment you add ikan bakar, a sambal, some ulam on the side, you're at 510 calories for the full set. That's still a pretty reasonable meal. The protein from a 120g grilled whole fish adds maybe 100 to 120 calories but bumps your protein up significantly, which matters if you're trying to stay full. The sambal is where you want to pay attention, because a heavy coconut-based sambal can add another 50 to 100 calories on top without you noticing. Go lighter on the sambal, load up on ulam, and the set meal stays well under 550 calories for a pretty satisfying feed.
lighter: Eat the traditional yam-mix version rather than a plain white rice parcel, the yam adds fiber and keeps you full longer for about the same calories.
Skip the coconut-heavy sambal or ask for it on the side and use it sparingly, that alone can save 50 to 80 calories.
Pair it with grilled fish rather than fatty meat like pork belly or rendang, the ikan bakar set stays around 510 calories total.
Load up on ulam and raw vegetables on the side, zero calories and they genuinely fill the gaps.
One parcel is the right serving size, the rice is compressed so it's denser than it looks. Two parcels pushes you to 500 to 600 calories on the rice alone before any protein.

faq.a: One plain linopot parcel (230g, traditional rice and yam mix) is about 300 calories. The white rice only version without yam is closer to 250 calories. A full linopot set with ikan bakar, sambal, and ulam comes to roughly 510 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is linopot?
faq.a: Linopot is a Kadazan-Dusun traditional food from Sabah. It's cooked rice, sometimes hill rice or red rice, pressed into a ball and wrapped tightly in doringin or tarap leaf. The leaf gives it a faint herbal smell and the parcel stays compact for eating on the go or at gatherings. It's usually eaten with grilled fish or meat.

faq.q: Is linopot a healthy choice for weight loss?
faq.a: It's one of the cleaner rice options out there because there's no added oil or coconut milk in the rice itself. At 250 to 300 calories per parcel, it's a reasonable carb portion. Pair it with grilled fish and ulam instead of heavy sambal and you've got a pretty decent meal under 550 calories. The yam version also has more fiber than plain white rice, which helps with fullness.

foods.name: Ambuyat
foods.serving: 1 serving ambuyat with basic cacah dip (per person)
foods.metaDescription: Ambuyat is around 245 calories per serving. The sago starch staple of Borneo is almost pure carb, dipped in sour cacah sauce.
foods.summary: Brunei and Sabah's iconic sago starch staple, twirled on bamboo forks and dipped in sour cacah sauce, simple in calories but serious in cultural weight.
foods.answer: A standard serving of ambuyat with basic cacah dip is roughly 245 calories for about 430g of food. That sounds like a lot of food for not many calories, and it is, because ambuyat is almost entirely water-swollen sago starch. The catch is that almost all of those 245 calories come from 54g of carbs, with barely 3g protein and 1g fat. On its own it keeps your stomach busy but does nothing for muscle. The full restaurant set with ikan goreng and stir-fried greens jumps to around 470 calories, which is a much more complete meal.
realTalk: Ambuyat is the national dish of Brunei and a proper staple in Sabah and Sarawak too. If you have never had it, imagine sago starch cooked into a thick, sticky, translucent gel, kind of like very dense wallpaper paste but weirdly satisfying. You twirl a big blob of it around a bamboo fork called chandas, dip it into a sour, spicy cacah sauce made from dried shrimp, belacan, chili and lime, and swallow the whole thing without chewing. Seriously, you do not chew ambuyat. At 245 calories a serving it sounds diet-friendly, but be honest with yourself: the plain ambuyat itself is just 210 calories of pure sago carbs with 3g protein. It will fill you up for maybe an hour before your body figures out there is nothing substantial in there. These numbers are a ballpark estimate by the way, hard nutritional data for ambuyat is basically non-existent, so treat the figures as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually changes the maths is what you eat alongside it. The plain ambuyat set at 245 calories is fine as a base, but nobody eats ambuyat alone for a full meal. Add one piece of ikan goreng, around 80g of fried fish, and that is roughly 180 calories extra. Add a plate of sayur tumis and you are looking at another 60 calories. The full set lands around 470 calories total, which is actually a solid, filling meal at a reasonable calorie count. The tempoyak cacah version adds about 40 calories from fermented durian fat and carbs and pushes you to 280 calories for the ambuyat portion alone. The real trap is not the ambuyat itself, it is ordering two servings because the first one felt light.
lighter: Order the full set with ikan goreng and sayur tumis instead of eating plain ambuyat alone. You get more protein and fibre, and the total meal at 470 calories is more satisfying than two rounds of plain ambuyat.
Stick to the basic cacah dip rather than tempoyak cacah. The tempoyak version adds around 40 extra calories from durian fat, and honestly the basic cacah hits different anyway.
Ask for extra cacah on the side and use it to slow yourself down. The tangy, spicy dip makes you more mindful of each bite and stops you from inhaling two portions back to back.
If you are at a restaurant, pair your ambuyat with a steamed or grilled fish rather than fried. You get the same protein with less added oil.
One portion of ambuyat is genuinely a lot of volume for 245 calories. Stick to one and let it settle before deciding you want more.

faq.a: A standard serving of ambuyat with basic cacah dip is around 245 calories per person (approximately 430g total). Plain ambuyat on its own is 210 calories, and the full restaurant set with ikan goreng and stir-fried greens comes to about 470 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is ambuyat and how do you eat it?
faq.a: Ambuyat is a thick, sticky, gel-like paste made from sago starch, essentially the staple carb of Brunei and parts of Sabah and Sarawak. You twirl it around a bamboo fork called chandas, dip it into a sour spicy sauce called cacah (made from dried shrimp, belacan, chili and lime), and swallow without chewing. It has a neutral flavour on its own so the cacah does most of the heavy lifting.

faq.q: Is ambuyat healthy or good for weight loss?
faq.a: It is low in fat and low in calories for the volume you eat, which is a plus. The problem is it is almost pure carbohydrate with barely any protein (3g per serving), so it will not keep you full for long on its own. For weight loss, order the full set with fish and vegetables so you actually get some protein in the meal. Treat the ambuyat as your carb portion rather than the whole meal.

foods.name: Kuih Penjaram (Pinjaram)
foods.metaDescription: One medium kuih penjaram at the pasar tamu is about 210 calories. Here's where those calories come from and how to eat it without the guilt.
foods.summary: A Sabah and Sarawak deep-fried rice-flour fritter sweetened with gula apong, shaped like a little UFO with a chewy centre and lacy crisp edges.
foods.answer: One medium kuih penjaram (the standard pasar tamu size, about 50g) comes in at roughly 210 calories. Most of that comes from the rice flour batter and palm sugar together at around 167 calories, with the frying oil adding another 43 calories on top. Be aware this is a ballpark estimate since solid nutrition data for penjaram specifically is basically non-existent, but 210 calories per medium piece is a reasonable working number.
realTalk: Penjaram (also spelled pinjaram or penyaram depending on who you ask) is a Sabah and Sarawak thing that a lot of peninsular Malaysians have never actually tried. Think of it like a fried fritter shaped like a UFO or a little hat, with a thick chewy middle and a thin lacy edge that goes properly crispy from the fryer. The batter is rice flour, plain flour, and gula apong, which is Bornean palm sugar with a deep caramel, almost smoky sweetness. It is genuinely good. At 210 calories per medium piece, it is not a disaster either, but those calories are basically all carbs and frying oil. The palm sugar alone contributes about 84 calories, and the oil absorbed during frying adds another 43. There is almost no protein here, which is why penjaram is a snack, not a meal. To be straight with you: these numbers are estimates. Hard data on penjaram calories is thin, so treat 210 as a reasonable ballpark rather than a lab-tested figure.

The maths changes quite a bit depending on where you buy it and what size you grab. The small ones sold three for RM1 at Sabah tamu are only around 130 calories each because they are roughly 30g finished weight, less batter, less oil. The big ones at places like Donggongon tamu can hit 290 calories at around 70g. If you are calorie counting, the size difference matters more than anything else here. The other variable is how much oil the individual fritter absorbs during frying, which depends on oil temperature and how long it sits in the wok. A hotter, faster fry absorbs less oil. You cannot really control that at a market stall, but knowing it helps you understand why two penjaram from different stalls can taste and feel quite different. If you want to enjoy a couple pieces at the tamu without it wrecking your day, just know two medium ones is about 420 calories lah, so factor that in before adding nasi lemak on top.
lighter: Go for the small tamu size (three for RM1 style) instead of the medium. You drop from 210 to 130 calories per piece, that is a real difference.
Eat it fresh and hot. A penjaram that has been sitting out re-absorbs some oil as it cools, so you get the lacy edge at its crispiest and the oil at its lowest right out of the wok.
Stop at two pieces. Two small ones is about 260 calories, which is a proper snack. Two large ones is close to 580 calories, which is basically a full meal.

If you are at the tamu, pair penjaram with something protein-based like a hard-boiled egg or a piece of grilled chicken rather than stacking up on more kuih. You will stay fuller and the calorie count stays manageable.
Skip the ones sitting in a covered container sweating. Go for the stall that is actively frying. Fresher means less oil absorption and honestly they just taste better.
