faq.a: A medium kuih penjaram at pasar tamu size (about 50g) is roughly 210 calories. The small tamu ones are around 130 calories each, and the large market versions can hit 290 calories. These are estimates since there is no official nutritional data for penjaram.

faq.q: What exactly is kuih penjaram?
faq.a: Penjaram is a deep-fried Bornean kuih made from a rice flour and palm sugar batter. It is shaped like a UFO or small hat, with a thick chewy centre and a thin lacy edge that crisps up in the fryer. The sweetness comes from gula apong, a Sabah palm sugar with a distinctly caramel, almost smoky flavour. You find it all over Sabah and Sarawak pasar tamu, sometimes spelled pinjaram or penyaram but it is all the same kuih.

faq.q: Is penjaram healthy?
faq.a: Honest answer: it is a deep-fried sugar fritter, so not exactly a health food. At 210 calories per medium piece with almost zero protein and 6g of fat, it is a snack that sits purely in carbs and frying oil. That said, two small pieces at around 260 calories total is a perfectly reasonable treat if you are calorie counting. Just do not eat five of them and call it a light snack.

foods.name: Kuih Cincin
foods.metaDescription: Kuih Cincin is about 120 calories per ring cookie. This Sabah deep-fried rice flour snack is dense, crunchy and dangerously easy to eat by the handful.
foods.summary: A hard, dark-brown ring cookie from Sabah, deep-fried from rice flour and palm sugar until it shatters like a cracker.
foods.answer: One piece of Kuih Cincin is roughly 120 calories. Each ring cookie weighs about 18g and packs 7g of fat and 12g of carbs, which is what you get when you double-fry something in oil. The number is a ballpark estimate since solid lab data for this traditional snack is thin, but it sits comfortably in the same territory as a small curry puff or a few pieces of Kuih Bangkit.
realTalk: Kuih Cincin is a traditional ring-shaped cookie from the Bajau and Brunei Malay communities in Sabah and Brunei. If you have never seen it before, imagine a small dark-brown ring that looks a bit like a miniature doughnut, except it is bone-dry, rock-hard and crunchy all the way through. It is made from rice flour and gula apong (palm sugar), which gives it that deep caramel flavour, and it is deep-fried twice in the traditional Sabah hawker version to get that shattering crunch. At 120 calories per piece, the main culprit is the frying oil, which accounts for about 34 of those calories on its own. It is not a diet food, and nobody is pretending it is. But because it is so dense and hard, you actually chew it slowly and tend to eat fewer pieces than you think. Fair warning though: these numbers are a genuine ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for Kuih Cincin is basically nonexistent, so treat the figures as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually moves the maths is how many you grab. One piece is 120 calories, which is manageable. Three pieces is 360 calories, which is already a medium-sized meal in cookie form. The double-fried Sabah hawker version clocks in slightly higher at around 125 calories per piece versus the softer single-fried Brunei-Malay version at about 110 calories, because more frying means more oil absorbed. If you are buying these from a stall or pasar malam, they almost always come in packs of 10 to 20 pieces, and that is where it gets dangerous. Nobody stops at two. If you portion yourself to five pieces, you are looking at 600 calories from snacks alone, which is a lot for something that does not fill you up the same way real food does. Eat them as an occasional treat, not a bag-a-day habit.
lighter: Stick to a hard limit of three pieces before you close the bag. At 120 calories each, three is 360 calories total, which is already a meaningful snack.
Go for the soft single-fried Brunei-Malay style if you can find it. It saves you about 15 calories per piece, and over a handful of pieces that actually adds up.
Pair a couple of pieces with plain black coffee or unsweetened tea instead of a sweetened drink. Teh tarik alongside adds another 100 to 150 calories on top.
Do not eat them standing at the stall. Sit down, put a fixed amount on a plate, and walk away from the pack. Out of sight really does help here.
If you are craving something crunchy and Malaysian that is lower calorie, a piece of Keropok Lekor or plain Ulam-Ulaman gives you crunch for fewer calories without the double-fried oil load.

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Cincin?
faq.a: One piece of Kuih Cincin is approximately 120 calories, based on a standard 18g ring cookie. The double-fried Sabah hawker version runs slightly higher at around 125 calories, while the softer Brunei-Malay style is closer to 110 calories.

faq.q: What is Kuih Cincin made of?
faq.a: Kuih Cincin is made primarily from rice flour and palm sugar (gula apong), shaped into rings and deep-fried until hard and dark brown. Some versions include a small amount of wheat flour. The double-frying is what gives it that distinctive crunch and also why the fat content is relatively high for a small cookie.

faq.q: Is Kuih Cincin suitable if I am trying to lose weight?
faq.a: It can fit into a calorie-controlled diet if you are strict about portions. At 120 calories per ring, a couple of pieces with your coffee is fine. The problem is portion creep because they come in big packs and are very easy to keep eating. Treat it as an occasional snack, count your pieces before you start, and it is manageable lah.

foods.name: Kelupis
foods.metaDescription: Kelupis is a Borneo glutinous rice snack wrapped in leaf and cooked with coconut milk. One piece is about 190 calories. Here's what changes the total.
foods.summary: Kelupis is a Sabah, Sarawak and Brunei snack of glutinous rice steamed in coconut milk and wrapped in nyirik leaf, eaten on its own or with serunding, curry or rendang.
foods.answer: One piece of kelupis (about 70g) comes in at roughly 190 calories, and almost all of that comes from the glutinous rice and the coconut milk it soaks up during cooking. It is compact and dense, so it does not feel like much in your hand, but the calories are real. Add serunding or rendang on the side and you are looking at 250 to 290 calories for the full plate.
realTalk: Kelupis is a traditional snack from Sabah, Sarawak and Brunei. Think of it as the Borneo cousin of ketupat or lemang: glutinous rice packed into a leaf parcel (usually nyirik or daun nyiru), cooked with coconut milk until it is dense and slightly sticky, then served with something rich on the side like serunding kelapa or rendang. If you have never had it, the texture is tighter and more compact than nasi lemak rice, almost like a firm rice cake. The 190 kcal per piece estimate is a ballpark because hard nutrition data for kelupis is genuinely thin. The main drivers are the coconut milk absorbed into the rice during cooking, which alone accounts for around 90 of those calories, and the glutinous rice base at about 85 kcal. The fat is where it sneaks up on you: 12g of fat from coconut milk in a 70g parcel is not nothing.

What really moves the number is what you eat it with. Plain kelupis at 190 kcal is fine as a snack. But pair it with 20g of serunding kelapa (dry-fried coconut floss) and you add roughly 60 kcal, landing at 250. Dip it into two or three tablespoons of thick rendang or curry gravy and that jumps to around 290 kcal. If you are watching your numbers, eat it plain or with a lighter sambal rather than the full serunding and gravy combo. Also worth knowing: portion discipline is tricky here because kelupis are small and you can easily eat three without thinking. At a makan event or pasar malam, stop at one or two and call it lah.
lighter: Eat it plain without the serunding or rendang to keep it at 190 kcal instead of 250 to 290.
Stop at one piece. They are small and it is easy to grab a second or third without realising you have added another 380 calories to the tally.
If you want something on the side, a light sambal or a broth-based dipping sauce is far better than thick coconut curry gravy.
Pair kelupis with a high-protein main like grilled fish or hinava instead of using it as a carb on top of another carb-heavy meal.
Treat it as a snack between meals, not a side dish added onto a full plate of rice and lauk.

faq.q: How many calories in Kelupis?
faq.a: One piece of kelupis (about 70g) is roughly 190 calories. That number climbs to around 250 with serunding kelapa on the side, or up to 290 if you are dipping it in rendang or thick curry.

faq.q: What exactly is kelupis?
faq.a: Kelupis is a traditional snack from Sabah, Sarawak and Brunei. Glutinous rice is mixed with coconut milk, wrapped tightly in nyirik or nyiru leaf, then steamed until firm and compact. It is similar in spirit to ketupat or lemang, just smaller and shaped by the leaf into a neat little parcel.

faq.q: Is kelupis healthy or just another carb bomb?
faq.a: It is not terrible, but it is not light either. The coconut milk gives it 12g of fat per piece, and the glutinous rice means it is a high-GI carb. As an occasional snack eaten plain it fits fine. The problem is portion creep at events where you grab three or four pieces without thinking, and each one is 190 kcal before any accompaniment.

foods.name: Asam Rebus
foods.metaDescription: Asam rebus is around 180 calories per serving, one of the lighter ways to eat fish in Malaysia. Clear tamarind broth, no frying, no thick gravy.
foods.summary: Asam rebus is a clear, sour tamarind-based fish dish, lighter than asam pedas because there is no thick sambal base, just a simple broth with belacan, aromatics and whole fish boiled until tender.
foods.answer: One serving of asam rebus, which is one medium ikan kembung with broth, comes in at around 180 calories. That covers 330g of food total, with 23g protein, 7g fat and only 4g carbs. It is one of the leaner ways you can eat fish in a Malaysian spread, mainly because there is no frying and no thick coconut gravy involved. The fish does the heavy lifting, the tamarind broth adds almost nothing to the calorie count.
realTalk: Asam rebus is basically fish boiled in a tangy tamarind broth with belacan, shallots, chili and a few aromatics. No oil, no thick base, no coconut milk. If you are not familiar with it, think of it as the cleaner, more sour cousin of asam pedas, the kind of thing your grandma makes when she wants something quick and not too heavy. At 180 calories for a full fish with broth, the numbers are genuinely good for a lauk, and that 23g of protein is doing real work. Fair warning though, these numbers are a ballpark estimate because detailed lab data for asam rebus is basically nonexistent. The figure is built from the fish flesh calories plus a very light broth, so treat it as a reasonable guide rather than a hard fact.

What actually changes the maths here is the fish size and whether anyone adds extra oil at the end, because some versions do get a small drizzle before serving. Swap ikan kembung for ikan merah and you are looking at roughly 190 calories, mainly because the fillet tends to be a bit bigger. Go with ayam kampung instead and that jumps to around 240 calories, though you get more protein from the larger meat portion, roughly 150g of chicken versus 100g of fish. The broth itself is basically free calories, around 20 calories for 200g, so drinking the kuah is fine. Where people quietly wreck this dish is by pouring it over a mountain of white rice without accounting for that extra 400 to 500 calories sitting underneath.
lighter: Stick to ikan kembung over ikan merah if you want the lower-calorie option, about 10 calories less per serving and the taste difference is minimal.
Skip any extra oil drizzle at the end, that step alone can add 40 to 60 calories for basically nothing.
Drink the broth freely, it is almost calorie-free and genuinely filling, great for slowing down how fast you eat the rice.
Watch your rice portion more than the fish itself. A standard rice plate at a nasi campur stall is 300g or more, that is where most of the meal's calories actually come from.
If you are doing this at home, load the broth with extra tomatoes, lady's fingers and chili, more volume with almost zero added calories.

faq.a: One serving of asam rebus, which is one medium fish with broth, is around 180 calories. That is based on a 330g serving with ikan kembung. The ikan merah version is about 190 calories and the ayam kampung version is around 240 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is asam rebus?
faq.a: Asam rebus is a sour fish or chicken dish cooked in a light tamarind broth with belacan, shallots, chili and aromatics. Unlike asam pedas, there is no thick fried sambal base, so the result is a clearer, thinner soup with a sharp tangy taste. Very common in Malay home cooking.

faq.q: Is asam rebus a good option if I am watching my calories?
faq.a: Yes, it is one of the better lauk choices out there. Low in carbs, solid on protein at 23g per serving, and no added oil in the cooking process. The main thing to watch is portion of rice you eat it with, not the dish itself.

foods.name: Ayam Goreng
foods.metaDescription: Ayam goreng comes in at around 390 calories per piece. Here is what drives that number and how to make it hurt less.
foods.summary: Malay-style fried chicken, marinated in turmeric and spices, coated in batter and deep fried skin-on until golden and crispy.
foods.answer: One piece of ayam goreng (thigh or drumstick, bone-in, around 160g) will cost you roughly 390 calories, with 28g protein, 12g carbs and 25g fat. That is a pretty decent protein hit, but the skin and the deep frying are doing a lot of heavy lifting on the fat side.
realTalk: Ayam goreng is basically Malay fried chicken. You marinate a piece of chicken in turmeric, garlic, lemongrass and whatever spices your mak or the nasi campur auntie likes, then you coat it and drop it in hot oil. The skin crisps up, the batter turns golden, and it smells like something you should definitely not be eating on a deficit. At 390 calories per piece, it is not exactly diet food, but it is also not crazy. The 25g of fat is the main issue, and most of that comes from two things: the skin (do not underestimate it) and the oil absorbed during frying. The batter adds another layer. To be straight with you, these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid lab data for Malaysian home-style ayam goreng is basically nonexistent. Different stalls, different batters, different oil temperatures, different drain times. Take the 390 as a reasonable middle ground, not gospel.

What actually moves the needle is the variant and the piece size. Ayam goreng kunyit (no thick batter, just a turmeric marinade) drops to around 280 calories because there is less coating to absorb oil. The full berempah version with that thick lemongrass-galangal-coriander batter climbs to about 420 calories. If you pull the skin off before eating, you are probably saving 40 to 60 calories right there. Two pieces at a nasi campur stall and you are looking at close to 800 calories before the rice even touches the plate. Pair it with kangkung or a plain sayur instead of another lauk, and the whole meal lands somewhere reasonable.
lighter: Go for ayam goreng kunyit over berempah. The thin turmeric marinade version saves you about 110 calories per piece just from less batter and less oil absorption.
Pull the skin off before you eat. Annoying, yes. But the skin is where a big chunk of the fat lives.
Pick breast over thigh if you have the option. Breast meat is leaner, so even with the same coating the base fat is lower.
At the nasi campur stall, treat the ayam goreng as your one lauk and fill the rest of the plate with veg. Do not stack it with rendang and sambal too.
Pat the chicken down with tissue after frying or after it comes off the stall tray. Even a bit of surface oil removal helps lah.

faq.a: One piece of ayam goreng (thigh or drumstick, bone-in, around 160g) is approximately 390 calories. The berempah version with thick batter is closer to 420 calories, while kunyit style without batter comes in around 280 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is ayam goreng?
faq.a: Ayam goreng is Malay fried chicken. The chicken is marinated in turmeric, garlic, lemongrass and spices, then either coated in spiced batter or left with just the marinade, and deep fried skin-on. You will find it at nasi campur stalls, mamak shops and basically every warung in the country.

faq.q: Is ayam goreng a good source of protein?
faq.a: One piece gives you 28g of protein, which is solid. The catch is the 25g of fat that comes with it, mostly from the skin and the oil absorbed during frying. If you are watching calories, kunyit style without thick batter is the smarter pick.

foods.name: Paru Goreng
foods.serving: 1 serving (2-3 pieces, side dish at nasi campur)
foods.metaDescription: Paru Goreng has 390 calories per serving (80g). Deep-fried spiced beef lung, high protein but the oil is doing heavy work. Full breakdown here.
foods.summary: Paru Goreng is deep-fried spiced beef lung, marinated in turmeric and coriander, then fried until crispy and chewy, a classic lauk you will spot at any nasi campur stall.
foods.answer: Two to three pieces of Paru Goreng, the standard side at a nasi campur stall, comes in at 390 calories for about 80g. That is 32g of protein and 29g of fat, with zero carbs. The beef lung itself is not the problem. It is the deep frying. That 80g serving absorbs roughly 16g of oil in the fryer, which alone accounts for 145 of those calories.
realTalk: Paru Goreng is beef lung, deep-fried with a spice marinade of turmeric, coriander, garlic and shallots. If you have not had it before, think of it as the chewy, crispy offal piece sitting in the tray next to the rendang at nasi campur. The texture is very different from muscle meat, slightly spongy inside and crunchy on the outside, and it soaks up oil like a sponge in the fryer. At 390 calories for a small 80g serving, it is one of the heavier lauk choices per gram, driven almost entirely by that absorbed frying oil (145 calories worth) rather than the lung itself (210 calories). The protein return is genuinely solid at 32g though, so if you are tracking macros it is not a terrible trade, just be honest about the portion.

The maths here are almost entirely about the frying. That 16g of absorbed oil is the swing factor. At a nasi campur stall you have zero control over how hot the oil is or how long the pieces sit in it, and cooler oil means even more absorption. If you take one piece instead of three you are looking at roughly 130 calories, which is a lot more manageable. Pairing it with lower-calorie lauk like steamed veg or a broth-based dish helps balance the plate. Swapping to ayam goreng gives you a similar fried-protein hit but around 280 calories for a comparable serving, so that is one way to shave 100 calories off your plate without feeling like you are eating a salad.
lighter: Take one piece, not three. One piece is roughly 130 calories and still gives you that taste hit with the rice.
If you get the choice, pick pieces that look drier and crispier rather than shiny and oil-soaked. Less visible oil means less absorbed oil.
Eat it with plain rice and a plate of sayur to dilute the overall calorie density of the meal instead of stacking multiple fried lauk.
Skip any extra sambal or kuah that gets drizzled on top at the stall, that adds calories fast and you often cannot see how much they are pouring.
Treat it as a flavour piece, not a protein main. One piece for the taste, then get your protein bulk from a grilled or steamed option on the same plate.

faq.q: How many calories in Paru Goreng?
faq.a: A standard serving of Paru Goreng, 2 to 3 pieces or about 80g, contains 390 calories, with 32g protein, 29g fat and 0g carbs.

faq.q: What exactly is Paru Goreng?
faq.a: Paru Goreng is deep-fried beef lung. The lung is marinated in turmeric, coriander, garlic and shallots, then deep-fried until the outside goes crispy. It is a common lauk at nasi campur stalls and has a chewy, dense texture unlike regular beef.

faq.q: Is Paru Goreng healthy?
faq.a: It has a decent protein count at 32g per serving, but the fat is high at 29g because beef lung absorbs a lot of frying oil. It is fine as an occasional lauk, but if you are in a calorie deficit it is worth keeping to one piece and pairing it with lower-calorie sides.

foods.name: Kerang Masak
foods.serving: 1 hawker serving (cockles in sambal or kicap sauce)
foods.metaDescription: Kerang masak is about 300 calories per hawker serving. Cockles are lean, but that sambal base is where calories pile up. Full breakdown here.
foods.summary: Cockles cooked in sambal or kicap sauce, a classic hawker lauk where the shellfish itself is surprisingly lean and the sauce does most of the calorie work.
foods.answer: A standard hawker serving of kerang masak comes in at around 300 calories for roughly 180g, with 20g protein, 16g carbs, and 17g fat. The cockles themselves are only about 105 calories. The other 200-odd calories come from the oil in the sambal base, the chili paste and aromatics, and the palm sugar. Order the kicap version and you drop to around 230 calories. These are ballpark estimates though, not lab results.
realTalk: Kerang masak is blood cockles cooked in either a spicy sambal or a soy sauce (kicap) gravy. The cockles themselves are genuinely lean, around 105 calories for 130g of shelled meat, with decent protein for a shellfish. The problem is the sambal. That chili paste base with belacan, shallots, palm sugar, and a generous pour of cooking oil adds roughly 200 calories on its own. So you are looking at about 300 calories for the whole thing, which is not bad as a lauk to go with rice, but you want to be honest with yourself about how much gravy you are scooping up. To be clear, these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid nutrition data for this specific dish is thin. Take the figures as a useful guide, not gospel.

What actually changes the maths here is the sauce version and how heavy the cook's hand is with oil. Go for kerang masak kicap instead of sambal and you save roughly 70 calories per serving, dropping to around 230. The sambal petai version adds stink beans and bumps it up to about 330. If you are at a nasi campur stall, use a slotted spoon to grab mostly cockles and leave some of the oil-heavy gravy behind. You can easily cut 50 to 80 calories that way. Kerang is also a solid protein choice at 20g per serving, so pairing it with plain rice and a vegetable is genuinely one of the smarter hawker plate combinations you can put together.
lighter: Order kerang masak kicap instead of sambal. Same cockles, about 70 fewer calories per serving.
At the nasi campur counter, use a slotted spoon and let the oily gravy drain off before it hits your plate.
Ask for less gravy, or eat the cockles and leave most of the sauce behind. The meat itself is lean.
Pair it with plain steamed rice and a simple vegetable like sayur manis to keep the whole plate under control.
Avoid the sambal petai version if you are counting, as the extra ingredients push it closer to 330 calories.

faq.q: How many calories in Kerang Masak?
faq.a: About 300 calories for a standard hawker serving of roughly 180g. The cockles themselves are only around 105 calories. The sambal base with oil, chili paste, and palm sugar accounts for most of the rest. The kicap version is lighter at around 230 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is kerang masak?
faq.a: Kerang is blood cockles, and masak just means cooked. You get small shelled cockles stir-fried in either a spicy sambal sauce (chili paste, belacan, shallots, palm sugar, oil) or a darker soy-based kicap sauce. It is a common lauk at nasi campur stalls across Malaysia.

faq.q: Is kerang masak a healthy choice for someone losing weight?
faq.a: The cockles themselves are a good lean protein at 20g per serving. The issue is the oil-heavy sambal base. It is a decent choice if you pick the kicap version and avoid drowning your plate in the gravy. Not the lowest calorie lauk out there, but not a disaster either.

foods.name: Lala Masak
foods.serving: 1 hawker plate (approx 400g shell-on clams, ~150g edible serving)
foods.metaDescription: Lala Masak has about 250 calories per hawker plate. Clam meat is lean but that stir-fry oil adds up fast. Here's the full calorie breakdown.
foods.summary: Lala Masak is stir-fried clams cooked with garlic, cili padi or ginger, oyster sauce and a generous pour of oil at your average hawker stall.
foods.answer: A standard hawker plate of Lala Masak comes in at around 250 calories for the edible portion, which is roughly 150g of clam meat and sauce from a 400g shell-on serving. The clam meat itself is actually quite lean at about 74 calories per 100g cooked, but the cooking oil alone accounts for around 136 calories, so the shells are doing you a favour by keeping portion sizes honest. Protein sits at 18g, which is decent for a seafood side dish.
realTalk: Lala are small saltwater clams and this dish is a Malaysian hawker staple. You order a plate, you get a heap of shells, you dig out the little nuggets of clam meat and you mop up the sauce with whatever carbs you ordered alongside. The clam meat itself is genuinely low calorie and high protein, very similar to other shellfish. The 250 calories here is a ballpark estimate, honestly, because reliable nutrition data for hawker-cooked lala is thin. Different stalls use wildly different amounts of oil and sauce, so treat this as a reasonable middle-ground guess rather than a precise number.

What actually swings the calories up or down is the oil. The hawker version uses around 1.2 tablespoons of oil in the wok, which contributes about 136 of those 250 calories. Kam Heong lala, which adds dried prawns, curry leaves and more sauce, runs closer to 300 calories. Sambal lala pushes to around 320 because sambal paste is oil-heavy by nature. The halia version with ginger and spring onion is the lightest at about 220 calories because the sauce is simpler and the oil tends to be more restrained. If you are eating lala as a side to white rice, the lala itself is not your problem. Watch the rice portion and whatever sauce you pour over it.
lighter: Order the masak halia version if available. The ginger and spring onion base is simpler, uses less oil, and saves you around 30 calories per plate.
Ask for kurang minyak if you can. Some stalls will actually listen. Even a small reduction in oil cuts 50 to 100 calories.
Skip soaking up the leftover sauce with bread or rice. The sauce sitting at the bottom of the plate carries a good chunk of that oil.
Pair lala with a steamed or boiled side rather than fried rice or noodles. The clam meat is lean enough that your overall meal stays reasonable.
Stick to one plate as a shared side rather than eating a full plate solo. At 250 calories it is fine, but lala is meant to be shared at the table anyway.

faq.q: How many calories in Lala Masak?
faq.a: A hawker plate of Lala Masak is around 250 calories for the edible portion (roughly 150g of clam meat and sauce from a 400g shell-on plate). The clam meat is only about 74 calories per 100g cooked; the cooking oil is what pushes it up to 250.

faq.q: What exactly is Lala Masak?
faq.a: Lala is a type of small saltwater clam common at Malaysian seafood stalls. Masak just means cooked. You get a plate of clams stir-fried with garlic, oyster sauce, soy sauce and usually either cili padi or ginger. You crack them open at the table and eat the little piece of clam meat inside.

faq.q: Is Lala Masak a good choice if I am trying to lose weight?
faq.a: The clam meat itself is great: high protein, low fat, low calorie. The issue is the stir-fry oil used at the hawker stall. If you can go for the masak halia version or ask for less oil, it sits around 220 calories and 18g protein, which is a solid side dish. Just do not drown your rice in the leftover sauce.

foods.name: Ikan Goreng
foods.serving: 1 piece (medium, e.g. kembung, tilapia slice, or cencaru)
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Goreng has around 230 calories per medium piece. Good protein, but that frying oil adds up fast. Here is what you need to know.
foods.summary: Ikan Goreng is your everyday Malaysian fried fish, rubbed with turmeric and a little flour then deep-fried until the skin goes crisp and golden.
foods.answer: One medium piece of ikan goreng, around 140g, comes in at roughly 230 calories with 25g protein and 12g fat. The fish itself is lean, so the calories mostly come from frying oil absorbed into the skin and that thin flour coating. If you are grabbing kembung from a nasi campur stall, expect around 180 calories for the smaller whole fish. Go for a big siakap fillet fried with thick batter and you are looking at 350 calories or more.
realTalk: Ikan goreng is one of those dishes that sounds healthy because, well, it is fish. And honestly it is not bad. The fish flesh itself is lean protein, whether you are eating kembung (Indian mackerel), tilapia, or cencaru. The problem is the frying. About 80 of those 230 calories come purely from oil absorbed during frying, and that number is a ballpark estimate because solid nutrition data for Malaysian hawker-style fried fish is thin. Different fish sizes, oil temperatures, and how long it sits in the pan all change things. Treat 230 as a reasonable middle-ground guess, not gospel.

What really moves the calorie count is the fish size and what is stuffed into it. A small kembung goreng runs about 180 calories. A standard tilapia slice is around 230. Cencaru sumbat sambal, where they stuff a spiced chili-herb paste inside the whole fish, jumps to around 290 calories because of that filling. A big siakap goreng tepung with thick batter coating hits 350 calories, because more batter means way more oil absorbed. If you are trying to keep things tighter, stick to smaller fish or request it without the thick flour batter, and eat the flesh while leaving the skin (where most of the oil lives) on the plate. Pair it with rice and kangkung rather than lauk that come with heavy gravy, and you have a solid high-protein meal without doing too much damage.
lighter: Choose kembung or cencaru over big battered fillets like siakap goreng tepung. You save 100-170 calories just by picking the smaller fish.
Skip the thick flour batter. A light turmeric dusting absorbs far less oil than a proper coating.
Eat the flesh and leave the crispy skin. Most of the absorbed frying oil is concentrated in the skin.
Drain it on a paper towel or newspaper before eating, the hawker way actually does reduce surface oil a bit.
Pair with steamed dishes like ikan stim or sayur campur instead of another oil-heavy lauk, so the whole plate stays reasonable.

faq.q: How many calories in Ikan Goreng?
faq.a: A medium piece of ikan goreng, around 140g, is approximately 230 calories. A small kembung goreng is around 180 calories, while a large battered fillet like siakap goreng tepung can hit 350 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is Ikan Goreng?
faq.a: Ikan goreng just means fried fish in Malay. At a nasi campur or nasi kandar stall you will usually see whole small fish like kembung or cencaru, or cut slices of tilapia, rubbed with turmeric and sometimes a little flour, then deep-fried until crisp. It is one of the most common side dishes in Malaysian everyday cooking.

faq.q: Is Ikan Goreng healthy for weight loss?
faq.a: It is decent, especially compared to other lauk. You get 25g of protein per piece, which is solid. The catch is 12g of fat, mostly from frying oil. If you stick to smaller fish without thick batter, it is one of the better protein options at a nasi campur stall. Just watch what else you pile on the plate.

foods.name: Ikan Stim
foods.serving: 1 whole fish (siakap or ikan merah, mid-size), as served at restaurant or kopitiam
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Stim is around 310 calories for a whole siakap or ikan merah. High protein, low fat, and one of the smartest orders at any kopitiam.
foods.summary: Ikan Stim is a whole fish, usually siakap or ikan merah, steamed and dressed with a light sauce, served at Chinese kopitiams and Malay restaurants across Malaysia. The most common preparation you will find is a Thai-influenced lime and chili style, though Chinese ginger steam versions are just as popular.
foods.answer: A whole ikan stim at a typical kopitiam or restaurant comes to around 310 calories for a mid-size siakap or ikan merah (about 280g as served). The standard hawker version uses fish sauce, lime juice, chili, lemongrass, and a touch of palm sugar, which is the Thai-style limau preparation you see at most kopitiams and seafood stalls. You are getting 45g of protein out of that, which is genuinely impressive for a dish that tastes this good. The fat is only 8g and carbs are 6g, so this is about as lean as a restaurant lauk gets.
realTalk: Ikan stim is steamed whole fish, typically siakap (barramundi) or ikan merah (red snapper), covered in a light sauce and finished with aromatics like ginger, chili, garlic, and coriander. It is a staple at Chinese kopitiams and plenty of Malay restaurants. At roughly 310 calories for the whole fish, about 216 of those calories come from the fish flesh itself. The sauce adds around 66 calories, mostly from the sesame oil and a bit of palm sugar. The aromatics are basically calorie noise. So honestly, the fish is just a really good deal, protein per calorie is one of the best you will find anywhere on a Malaysian menu. Fair warning though: these numbers are a ballpark estimate. Reliable lab data for steamed fish as cooked in Malaysian hawker settings is thin, and sauce quantities vary a lot between cooks.

What actually moves the number is the sauce. A heavier hand with sesame oil or more palm sugar can push the sauce component up by 30 to 50 calories without you noticing. The Thai-style stim limau version stays around 310 calories because the lime and fish sauce base is fairly light. The ginger steam version (stim halia) comes in a bit lower at 280 calories because it skips the sugar and heavier aromatics. If someone adds coconut milk to the sauce, which does happen in some Malay-style preparations, you are looking at 390 calories instead. Also worth noting: the edible flesh on a mid-size fish is roughly 200g out of the 280g total served. If you order a bigger fish, scale the numbers up accordingly.
lighter: Ask for the sauce on the side or request less of it, the sauce adds 66 calories and that is easy to halve just by not pouring the whole thing over.
Go for stim halia over the Thai-style version if you want to trim about 30 calories without sacrificing flavour.
Skip the white rice and pair it with sayur manis or a plain vegetable dish instead, the fish alone is filling enough with 45g of protein.
Do not eat the skin if you are being strict, most of the fat in steamed fish sits in and around the skin layer.
Order siakap over ikan merah if you have a choice, siakap flesh tends to be slightly leaner by default.

faq.a: A whole ikan stim (siakap or ikan merah, mid-size) as served at a kopitiam or restaurant is around 310 calories, with 45g protein, 8g fat, and 6g carbs for roughly 280g total.

faq.q: What exactly is ikan stim?
faq.a: It is a whole fish, usually siakap (barramundi) or ikan merah (red snapper), that is steamed and then poured over with a hot sauce. The most common version is Thai-influenced, using fish sauce, lime juice, chili, lemongrass, and palm sugar. You also get a Chinese kopitiam style that uses soy, sesame oil, ginger, and scallion instead. Both are standard sights at Malaysian kopitiams and seafood restaurants.

faq.q: Is ikan stim a good choice if you are trying to lose weight?
faq.a: Bro, it is probably one of the best things on any Malaysian menu. 310 calories, 45g of protein, and it is genuinely filling. The only thing to watch is the sauce, which adds about 66 calories. Compare that to something like rendang or masak lemak and it is not even close.

foods.name: Sup Daging
foods.metaDescription: Sup Daging comes in around 400 kcal for a standard hawker bowl. Clear spiced beef soup, tender chunks, and it goes up fast if you add roti for dipping.
foods.summary: Sup Daging is a clear, warmly spiced Malaysian beef soup, usually served with tender beef shank or short rib chunks and eaten with bread for dipping.
foods.answer: A standard hawker bowl of Sup Daging is around 400 calories for roughly 510g of soup, beef, and veg. Most of that comes from the beef itself (about 300 kcal for 150g of shank or short rib), with the spiced broth adding another 60 kcal and the potato and carrot rounding out the rest. On its own it is actually a pretty reasonable meal, but add two pieces of roti for dipping and you are looking at closer to 580 kcal total.
realTalk: Sup Daging is a clear spiced beef soup you find at Malay hawker stalls and warung, usually ordered alongside roti canai or a crusty French loaf. The broth is light and fragrant, flavoured with things like star anise, cinnamon, and cloves, but do not let "clear soup" fool you into thinking it is low calorie automatically. At 400 kcal a bowl, it is solidly in the middle range, and that is because beef shank and short rib are fatty cuts by nature. The rendered fat from the meat bleeds into the broth, and bone marrow versions (Sup Berempah) push it to 460 kcal. Fair warning though: these numbers are genuine ballpark estimates. Hard lab data for Malaysian hawker soups is thin, so take them as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually swings the number is the cut of beef and how much fat ends up in your bowl. Lean cuts like topside instead of shank can shave off 80 to 100 kcal without you noticing much. The broth itself at around 60 kcal per 300ml is not the villain, but stalls that skim less fat off the top will give you a noticeably richer, higher-calorie soup. Potato and carrot add about 45 kcal from 60g, which is fine. The real jump comes from the roti. Two pieces of roti canai or French loaf adds roughly 180 kcal and takes you to 580 kcal total. If you are watching calories, eat the soup on its own first. You might not even want the bread after that.
lighter: Order it without bread, or ask for just one piece of roti instead of two. That one swap saves around 90 to 180 kcal right there.
Ask for leaner cuts if you can. Topside or silverside instead of short rib means less fat rendered into the broth.
Skip the bone marrow version if calories matter. Marrow adds 60 to 80 kcal to an already decent bowl.
Drink the broth but leave some of the oilier layer at the bottom. Sounds fussy but the last third of a fatty soup has more calories than the first two thirds.
This soup is high in protein at 38g per bowl, so it keeps you full. Eat it slowly and you probably do not need rice or bread on the side.

faq.q: How many calories in Sup Daging?
faq.a: A standard hawker bowl of Sup Daging is around 400 calories for roughly 510g with beef chunks, spiced broth, potato, and carrot. The lean version without potato comes in closer to 300 kcal, and the berempah version with marrow can reach 460 kcal. Add roti for dipping and the total goes up to about 580 kcal.

faq.q: What is Sup Daging exactly?
faq.a: It is a Malaysian clear beef soup, spiced with aromatics like star anise, cloves, and cinnamon. The beef is usually shank or short rib, slow-cooked until tender. You get a clean, warmly spiced broth with soft beef chunks, sometimes potato and carrot, and it is almost always eaten with bread for dipping.

faq.q: Is Sup Daging a healthy choice for someone trying to lose weight?
faq.a: It is one of the better hawker options, bah. You get 38g of protein in a 400 kcal bowl, which is a solid ratio. The broth keeps you full, it does not come with rice by default, and you control whether you add bread. Main thing to watch is the cut of beef and how fatty the broth is. Skip the roti or have just one piece, and it is a genuinely good diet meal.

foods.name: Sup Ikan
foods.serving: 1 bowl (clear sup ikan, fish pieces + tofu + veg + broth, no rice or noodles)
foods.metaDescription: Sup Ikan has about 290 calories per bowl, clear broth style. One of the leanest soups at any hawker stall. Calories and macros breakdown here.
foods.summary: Sup ikan is a clear Malaysian fish soup, usually ikan jenahak or kembung with tofu, tomatoes, and cabbage in a ginger-lemongrass broth, served at Malay hawker stalls and kopitiams.
foods.answer: A standard bowl of clear sup ikan comes in at around 290 calories for roughly 640g of food, with 34g of protein, 10g of fat, and only 4g of carbs. That's the version with fish pieces, soft tofu, veg, and broth but no noodles or rice. Add bihun and you're at 420 calories. Add a plate of white rice and you're at 580. The base bowl on its own is one of the leaner things you can order at a hawker stall.
realTalk: Sup ikan is basically fish cooked in a clear, mildly spiced broth with aromatics like ginger and lemongrass, soft tofu, tomatoes, and whatever greens the stall has. It's a regular fixture at Malay hawker stalls and nasi campur places, and it's genuinely one of the lightest hot dishes you'll find. At 290 calories with 34g of protein, the clear version is almost unfairly good for a dieter. The fish does most of the heavy lifting here, 150g of cooked ikan jenahak or kembung sitting at 188 calories. The broth itself? Only 20 calories. Fair warning though: these are ballpark estimates. Hard calorie data on Malaysian hawker soups is thin, and the fish portion, oil used, and broth concentration will vary stall to stall.

What actually moves the numbers is what you order with it and how much oil the cook adds to the broth. The clear soup version keeps fat low at 10g, but an asam pedas-style sour fish soup pushes you to 350 calories from the tamarind, chilli paste, and extra oil used in the base. Throw in a bowl of bihun, that's an extra 130 calories bringing you to 420 total. Order it with rice and you're at 580 for the full meal. If you want to stay at the 290 base, eat it plain, ask for less oil if you can, and go heavy on the fish and tofu rather than padding it with carbs.
lighter: Order clear sup ikan without bihun or rice, you save 130 to 290 calories right there.
Ask the stallholder to go light on oil in the broth. Most will oblige if you ask nicely.
Pile on the tofu and veg rather than asking for extra fish if cost is a concern, the tofu adds protein for very few calories.
Skip the asam pedas version if you're counting. The tamarind and chilli paste base adds oil that bumps you from 290 to 350.
Eat the soup first before the rice. You'll feel fuller faster and naturally eat less rice.

variants.name: Asam pedas-style sour fish soup
variants.note: Tamarind, dried chillies, and more oil push calories up. Usually served as a lauk with rice rather than a standalone bowl.

variants.name: Sup ikan dengan nasi (with white rice)
variants.note: Add 200g cooked white rice (~260 kcal). Full meal as typically eaten for lunch.

faq.q: How many calories in Sup Ikan?
faq.a: A standard bowl of clear sup ikan with fish, tofu, veg, and broth (no rice or noodles) is around 290 calories. Add bihun and it goes to 420. With a plate of white rice, you're looking at 580 calories for the full meal.

faq.q: What exactly is sup ikan?
faq.a: Sup ikan is a clear fish soup common at Malay hawker stalls and kopitiams. Usually ikan jenahak or kembung cooked in a light broth with ginger, lemongrass, soft tofu, tomatoes, and cabbage. Simple, clean, and genuinely filling for the calories.

faq.q: Is sup ikan actually healthy?
faq.a: Pretty much yes, for a hawker dish. 34g of protein and only 290 calories in a 640g bowl is a solid ratio. Low carbs, moderate fat, very filling. The main thing to watch is how much oil goes into the broth, and what you order alongside it.

foods.name: Sup Sayur
foods.metaDescription: Sup sayur is about 60 calories per bowl. Clear vegetable soup with cabbage, carrot and tomato. Probably the most diet-friendly thing on any Malaysian menu.
foods.summary: Sup sayur bening is a clear mixed vegetable soup, usually cabbage, carrot and tomato simmered in a light garlic broth, and it is genuinely one of the lowest-calorie things you can order in Malaysia.
foods.answer: One bowl of sup sayur (about 320g) comes in at roughly 60 calories. That is it. Two grams of protein, 10g carbs, 1g fat. The vegetables themselves are almost free calorie-wise; the broth adds maybe 15 calories and there is a tiny bit of oil used in the base. If you are tracking and you need something warm and filling to pad out a meal without blowing your budget, this is pretty much the answer lah.
realTalk: Sup sayur bening is as simple as it sounds: clear broth, aromatics like garlic and onion, then cabbage, carrot and tomato. No coconut milk, no heavy rempah. The 60 calories for a full 320g bowl is genuinely that low because vegetables are mostly water and fibre. The 15-calorie broth and about 8 calories from the minimal oil in the base are actually doing more numerical heavy lifting than the vegetables themselves. To be honest, these numbers are a ballpark estimate because solid lab data for this dish is thin. Kedai to kedai will vary, and some hawkers are heavier-handed with oil than others, but 60 to 80 calories is a reasonable range for the plain version.

What actually moves the maths here is what gets added. Stay plain and you are at 60 calories. Throw in 60g of soft tofu and you are at 100. Ask for chicken and you are up to about 120. Add 30g of cooked vermicelli and you are at about 95, which now makes it a light noodle soup instead. The oil in the base is already minimal at 1g and 8 calories, but if you are at a stall that fries the aromatics more generously, you could creep toward 80 or 90 calories before any protein is added. Order it plain with rice on the side and you have basically used your soup allocation for nothing.
lighter: Order it bening, meaning plain, no protein added. That keeps it at 60 calories instead of 100 to 120.
If you want protein, ask for tofu instead of chicken. Sixty grams of soft tofu adds about 40 calories and keeps it light.
Avoid the version at places that fry the aromatics heavily. The base oil is supposed to be minimal. If the broth looks a bit greasy, that is where your extra calories are hiding.
Eat it with steamed rice rather than ordering the vermicelli version. Thirty grams of cooked vermicelli adds about 35 calories, and the volume difference is not that meaningful.
Use it to bulk out a meal: pair a bowl of sup sayur with a smaller portion of rice and one lauk. You get the volume and warmth without spending many calories on the soup itself.

variants.note: Add 60g soft tofu; common in kedai kopi

variants.note: Add 30g cooked vermicelli (cooked weight, mostly water); turns it into a light noodle soup

faq.q: How many calories in Sup Sayur?
faq.a: About 60 calories per bowl (320g), for the plain bening version with cabbage, carrot and tomato in clear broth. Add tofu and it goes to roughly 100, add chicken and it is about 120.

faq.q: What exactly is sup sayur?
faq.a: It is a clear Malaysian vegetable soup, usually with cabbage, carrot and tomato simmered in a light garlic and onion broth. No coconut milk, no curry paste. You find it at Malay kedai makan as a side to rice, and it is one of the mildest things on the menu.

faq.q: Is sup sayur actually good for weight loss?
faq.a: Bro, 60 calories for a full bowl of warm soup, yes. It is hard to find something this filling for this few calories. The fibre from the vegetables helps too. The only risk is if you order it with protein added or from a stall that is heavy on the oil, which can push it toward 90 to 120 calories.

foods.name: Bubur Jagung
foods.metaDescription: Bubur Jagung has about 360 calories per bowl. Sweet corn porridge in coconut milk sounds innocent but the santan adds up fast. Here is the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Bubur Jagung is a warm sweet corn porridge cooked in coconut milk with sago pearls and sugar, a common dessert at pasar malam stalls and kopitiams across Malaysia.
foods.answer: A standard hawker bowl of Bubur Jagung (280g) has about 360 calories. The corn itself is not the issue, only 70 calories worth. The real story is the 80g of full-fat coconut milk at 185 calories and another 97 calories from sugar, whether white sugar or gula Melaka. Add the sago pearls and you are already at 360 before you even pick up the spoon.
realTalk: Bubur Jagung is basically sweet corn swimming in santan and sugar. It is a warm dessert porridge, very common at pasar malam and kopitiam dessert stalls, and it looks totally harmless in the bowl. But 360 calories for a dessert portion is not nothing. To be upfront, the numbers here are a ballpark estimate because solid lab data for Malaysian hawker bubur jagung is thin. What we know for certain is that the fat comes almost entirely from the coconut milk (17g fat, mostly saturated) and the carbs come from corn, sago, and sugar stacked together. If you are someone trying to lose weight and you finish your nasi lemak and then bowl this down as an afterthought, that is an extra meal worth of calories you probably did not account for.

The version you get matters a lot. A stall using diluted or low-fat coconut milk drops the whole thing to around 220 calories. A generous pasar malam bowl with extra santan and gula Melaka can push past 450 calories. If the stall adds cubed sweet potato (ubi keledek), that is another 40 to 50 calories on top. The sago pearls themselves are pretty innocent at only 30 calories for 30g. Portion size is the other lever since most stalls just ladle freely, and a generous pour can easily be 320g to 340g instead of the standard 280g.
lighter: Ask the stall if they do a lighter version with diluted or low-fat santan. Saves roughly 100 to 140 calories right there.
Skip the add-ons. No sweet potato, no extra sago, no second scoop of gula Melaka drizzle on top.
Treat it as your dessert only, not a side dish on top of a full meal. At 360 calories it is a meaningful chunk of your day.
Split a bowl with someone. Pasar malam portions are generous and half a bowl still satisfies the craving.
Go earlier in the evening when the santan is less concentrated. The longer it sits on the burner, the more the water evaporates and the richer it gets.

faq.q: How many calories in Bubur Jagung?
faq.a: A standard hawker bowl of Bubur Jagung (280g) has about 360 calories. The coconut milk alone contributes 185 of those calories, with sugar adding another 97.

faq.q: What exactly is Bubur Jagung?
faq.a: It is a warm Malaysian dessert porridge made from sweet corn kernels cooked in full-fat coconut milk with white sugar or gula Melaka and sago pearls. You will find it at pasar malam stalls and kopitiam dessert corners, usually served warm in a bowl.

faq.q: Is Bubur Jagung healthy?
faq.a: The corn and sago themselves are fine. The issue is the full-fat santan and sugar, which push the calorie count to 360 per bowl with 17g of fat. It is not a diet food but having it occasionally as a proper dessert rather than an everyday snack is perfectly reasonable.

foods.name: Pulut
foods.serving: 1 serving, plain pulut with santan (steamed glutinous rice cooked in coconut milk)
foods.metaDescription: Plain pulut with santan is about 250 calories per 160g serving. Add sambal ikan bilis and you're at 310. Here's what you're actually eating.
foods.summary: Pulut is steamed glutinous rice cooked in coconut milk, dense and sticky, served plain or topped with sambal ikan bilis, sweet grated coconut, or as part of festive spreads.
foods.answer: Plain pulut with santan comes in at around 250 calories for a 160g serving, with 42g carbs and 7g fat. Most of those calories come from the glutinous rice itself (116 kcal) plus the coconut milk absorbed during steaming and resting (129 kcal total across cooking and pressing). Add sambal ikan bilis on top and you're looking at 310 calories. Go for the pulut inti with sweet grated coconut topping and it jumps to 370. It's a decent breakfast snack on its own, but the portions at the pasar pagi are usually bigger than you think.
realTalk: Pulut is glutinous rice steamed with coconut milk until it's dense, sticky, and slightly rich. It's a staple at Malay breakfast stalls, pasar pagi, and big occasions like weddings and Hari Raya. Plain pulut with santan sits at around 250 calories per 160g serving, which sounds reasonable until you realise it's almost entirely carbs with very little protein (just 4g). The coconut milk adds a decent chunk of fat, 7g, and that's before any topping. These numbers are a ballpark estimate since hard nutritional data for traditional kuih like pulut is genuinely thin. Treat it as a close approximation, not a lab result.

What really moves the calories is the topping. Plain pulut is 250 kcal. Add 40g of sambal ikan bilis and you're at 310 kcal, the oil and fried anchovies doing the heavy lifting. Go for pulut inti, that sweet grated coconut cooked with gula melaka, and it climbs to 370 kcal, with the sugar and coconut fat adding 100 to 120 kcal on top. Portion size is the other big variable. A hawker scoop can easily be 200g or more, which pushes even plain pulut past 300 kcal before you add anything. If you're tracking, weigh it or at least be honest about how much you took.
lighter: Go for plain pulut with sambal on the side rather than piled on top, so you control how much sambal you actually use.
Skip the pulut inti if you're watching calories. That sweet coconut topping adds 100 to 120 kcal and zero protein.
Take a smaller scoop. A 100g portion of plain pulut is around 155 kcal, which is a much easier number to fit into your day.
Pair it with a boiled egg or some ikan bilis on the side instead of embedded in oily sambal. You get protein without as much extra fat.
Eat it as breakfast rather than a mid-morning snack on top of actual breakfast. Pulut is dense enough to be a proper meal if you portion it right.

variants.name: Pulut kuning (turmeric coconut glutinous rice, plain)
variants.note: Similar to plain pulut; turmeric adds no significant calories. Often served at Malay weddings and Hari Raya, ~160g piece.

variants.name: Pulut sambal (with sambal ikan bilis)
variants.note: Add ~40g sambal ikan bilis on top; anchovy sambal contributes ~60-70 kcal from oil and fried anchovies. Most common hawker breakfast variant.

variants.name: Pulut inti (sweet grated coconut topping)
variants.note: Add ~40g kelapa parut (grated coconut) cooked with gula melaka; the sweet coconut topping adds ~100-120 kcal from sugar and coconut fat. Popular Nyonya kuih variant.

components.name: Coconut milk (santan) absorbed during steaming and resting

faq.q: How many calories in Pulut?
faq.a: Plain pulut with santan is around 250 calories per 160g serving. With sambal ikan bilis it goes up to about 310 calories, and with sweet grated coconut topping (pulut inti) it reaches around 370 calories.

faq.q: What is pulut exactly?
faq.a: Pulut is glutinous rice, a stickier, denser variety of rice, steamed with coconut milk and pandan. It's not regular rice. The texture is chewy and compact, and it's served as a snack or breakfast staple, either plain or with toppings like sambal ikan bilis or sweet grated coconut.

faq.q: Is pulut fattening?
faq.a: It's calorie-dense for the size, mostly from carbs and a bit of fat from the coconut milk. At 250 calories for a 160g serving with very little protein, it won't keep you full for long. As an occasional breakfast or snack it's fine. The issue is when you eat a big scoop plus a sweet topping and don't account for it.

foods.name: Ketupat
foods.metaDescription: Ketupat (compressed rice cake) has about 145 calories per piece. Raya staple, pure carbs, and the rendang next to it is doing most of the damage.
foods.summary: Ketupat is compressed rice boiled inside a woven palm-leaf pouch, eaten at Raya alongside rendang or kuah kacang, and it is basically a dense little brick of carbs.
foods.answer: One piece of ketupat nasi (about 110g) comes in at roughly 145 calories, almost entirely from carbs (32g), with basically zero fat. The ketupat itself is not the problem at all. It is just rice, boiled in a leaf. The rendang, the kuah kacang, the sambal that comes with it, that is where your calorie count quietly explodes.
realTalk: Ketupat nasi is honestly one of the more innocent things on the Raya table at 145 calories a piece. If you have never had it, picture plain jasmine rice that has been compressed into a firm cube by boiling it inside a woven coconut-leaf pouch. Chewy, dense, mild on its own. The calorie numbers here are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data on traditional ketupat is thin, so treat 145 as a reasonable guide rather than a lab-verified figure. The real trap is the glutinous version, ketupat palas, which is cooked with coconut milk inside a palas leaf and comes in at around 210 calories per triangle despite being smaller than a ketupat nasi. Santan does that to things.

What actually wrecks your Raya calories is everything around the ketupat. A serving of rendang alone adds 200 to 300 calories. A ladle of kuah kacang can pile on another 150 to 200 calories depending on how thick it is. If you eat two pieces of ketupat nasi (290 calories) with a proper serving of rendang and kuah kacang, you are already looking at 600 to 700 calories before you touch the serunding or the kuih. The fix is not skipping the ketupat. It is controlling the sauces. One piece with a modest scoop of rendang and lots of acar or raw ulam on the side keeps the meal enjoyable without going totally overboard.
lighter: Stick to ketupat nasi over ketupat palas. That one swap saves you about 65 calories per piece and cuts most of the saturated fat.
Go easy on the kuah kacang. It tastes light but one generous ladle can be 150 to 200 calories of peanut and santan. Use it as a dip, not a flood.
Load your plate with acar and raw ulam first. They fill space, add crunch, and cost almost nothing calorie-wise.
Treat rendang as a condiment. Two or three pieces of meat is plenty. You do not need to drown the ketupat in it.
Eat one piece at a time and wait a bit before going for seconds. Ketupat is dense and it takes a moment for your stomach to register how full you actually are.

variants.name: Ketupat nasi (plain white rice, ~110g piece)
variants.note: Standard compressed jasmine rice boiled in woven coconut leaf; pure carbs, essentially no fat

variants.name: Ketupat palas (glutinous rice + santan, ~80g triangle)
variants.note: Glutinous rice cooked with coconut milk in palas leaf; denser, richer, notably higher in fat and calories despite smaller size

faq.q: How many calories in Ketupat?
faq.a: One piece of ketupat nasi (about 110g) is roughly 145 calories, nearly all of it carbs. The glutinous version, ketupat palas, is around 210 calories per smaller triangle because it is made with coconut milk.

faq.q: What exactly is ketupat?
faq.a: It is compressed rice cooked inside a woven pouch made from young coconut or palm leaves. The weave tightens as the rice expands during boiling, which gives ketupat its firm, dense texture. It is a Raya classic eaten with rendang, kuah kacang, or sambal.

faq.q: Is ketupat fattening?
faq.a: The ketupat itself is pretty lean, just compressed rice with no added fat. The issue is always the accompaniments. Rendang, kuah kacang, and sambal are all high in calories, so the full Raya spread adds up fast. If you are watching your intake, control the sauces and keep your ketupat to one or two pieces.

foods.name: Ketupat Sotong
foods.serving: 1 medium squid stuffed with glutinous rice in coconut gravy
foods.metaDescription: Ketupat Sotong has around 590 calories per piece. Squid stuffed with pulut rice in sweet santan gravy, a Terengganu classic that hits harder than it looks.
foods.summary: Ketupat Sotong is a Terengganu and Kelantan specialty where whole squid is stuffed with glutinous rice then simmered low and slow in a sweet, rich coconut milk gravy.
foods.answer: One medium ketupat sotong comes in at around 590 calories, with 80g of carbs, 21g of protein, and 19g of fat. That is for a single stuffed squid piece sitting in its coconut gravy, roughly 310g total. Not a light dish by any stretch, but the squid itself is actually lean protein doing honest work. The calories are being driven by the pulut stuffing and the santan gravy around it.
realTalk: Ketupat sotong is one of those east coast dishes that most Malaysians from KL or the west have never actually tried. Picture a whole squid body, cleaned and packed tight with raw glutinous rice, then sealed and braised in coconut milk sweetened with gula melaka until the pulut cooks inside the squid and absorbs all that gravy. The result is dense, sticky, sweet, and honestly very good. But at 590 calories for one piece, it earns its place on the higher end of the calorie list. The pulut stuffing alone accounts for about 240 calories, the thick santan gravy adds another 178, and the palm sugar in that same gravy throws in 80 more. The squid itself is only 92 calories. So you are really paying for the rice and the coconut sauce, not the seafood. Fair warning though: these numbers are a genuine ballpark estimate. Hard nutrition data for ketupat sotong is almost nonexistent, and portion sizes vary a lot between home cooking and pasar malam stalls, so treat this as a rough guide rather than a precise count.

What actually moves the maths here is gravy portion and squid size. A large squid stuffed more generously could easily push past 700 calories, while a smaller piece from a pasar ramadan stall might land closer to 450 to 500. If you are eating this at a kenduri or during Raya and someone ladles extra gravy on your plate, that 55g of coconut milk sauce in our estimate can quickly become 90 to 100g, adding another 100 calories right there. There is no real way to make a lighter version at a stall since you eat what you are served. If you are cooking at home, using light coconut milk (santan pekat campur air) instead of full-fat santan can bring the gravy calories down by roughly 40 to 50 calories per serving, and going easier on the gula melaka saves another 20 to 30. The squid is not the problem at all, bro. It is the stuff around it.
lighter: Ask for less gravy when possible, because that thick santan is where the bulk of the fat calories live. Even dropping from 55g to 30g of gravy saves around 80 calories.
Eat it without rice on the side. The pulut inside the squid is already your carb load for this meal, adding a plate of nasi on top pushes you well past 900 calories.
If cooking at home, swap full-fat santan for a diluted version, one part thick coconut milk to one part water. Same flavour profile, noticeably lighter gravy.
Pair it with ulam-ulaman or raw vegetables on the side rather than another heavy lauk. You get volume and fibre without adding significant calories.
One piece is genuinely a full meal. This is not a side dish, it is a main. Treat it that way and you will not feel the need to keep reaching for more.

components.name: Palm sugar / gula melaka in gravy

faq.q: How many calories in Ketupat Sotong?
faq.a: One medium ketupat sotong with coconut gravy is around 590 calories. That covers the squid body at 92 cal, the glutinous rice stuffing at 240 cal, the thick santan gravy at 178 cal, and the palm sugar in the gravy at 80 cal, for a total of roughly 310g of food.

faq.q: What exactly is Ketupat Sotong?
faq.a: It is a traditional dish from Terengganu and Kelantan where a whole squid is stuffed with raw glutinous rice, then simmered in sweetened coconut milk until the rice cooks inside the squid body. The result is a sticky, dense, slightly sweet dish usually eaten during Raya or at east coast pasar malam stalls.

faq.q: Is Ketupat Sotong healthy?
faq.a: The squid itself is lean and decent in protein at 21g per serving, which is fine. The problem is the glutinous rice and the sweet coconut gravy pushing the carbs to 80g and the overall calories to 590 for one piece. It is not something you want to eat daily if you are watching your intake, but as an occasional Raya dish it is absolutely worth it.

foods.name: Lemang
foods.metaDescription: Lemang has about 290 calories for 2 slices (180g). Glutinous rice roasted in bamboo with coconut milk, best known as the Raya staple eaten with rendang.
foods.summary: Lemang is glutinous rice cooked with coconut milk inside bamboo lined with banana leaf, roasted over open fire until fragrant and sticky, eaten almost exclusively at Raya alongside rendang or serunding.
foods.answer: Two slices of lemang (about 180g, a normal Raya serving) comes in at roughly 290 calories, with 45g carbs, 12g fat, and only 4g protein. That 12g of fat is all from the santan soaked up during roasting, which is what makes lemang taste so good and also why it is not exactly a diet food. On its own it is not catastrophic, but nobody eats lemang on its own, kan.
realTalk: Lemang is basically glutinous rice that has been sitting in coconut milk inside a bamboo tube over a fire, so the santan gets fully absorbed into every grain. The result is dense, sticky, slightly fatty rice that is genuinely delicious. At 290 calories for 2 slices, the rice itself is not outrageous, but the carb count is high (glutinous rice hits harder than regular rice gram for gram) and there is almost no protein to speak of. If you are tracking, note that these numbers are a ballpark estimate as there is very little hard nutritional data published for lemang specifically, and fat absorption from coconut milk varies depending on how long it is roasted and the ratio used.

The number that actually matters is what you put next to it. Two slices of plain lemang at 290 cal is fine. Add 2 tablespoons of serunding kelapa and you are at 380. Add a full piece of beef rendang and you are at 490 calories in one plate. The rendang is worth it calorie-wise because it adds real protein, but the serunding is basically just fat and coconut with very little upside. Portion is everything here: one slice of lemang (roughly 90g) cuts you to about 145 calories, which leaves way more room for rendang.
lighter: Stick to one slice instead of two. You get the flavour hit at half the carbs, and honestly one slice with rendang is already a solid plate.
Go for rendang over serunding as your pairing. Rendang adds about 200 calories but also real protein. Serunding adds 90 calories of mostly fat with almost no protein.
Balance the plate with a pile of ulam, raw vegetables, or at least some cucumber on the side to slow down the carb spike from the glutinous rice.
Skip the nasi and just let the lemang be your carb for that meal. Do not double up on white rice and lemang at the same Raya spread.
If you are making it at home, reducing the coconut milk ratio by a third cuts fat absorption meaningfully without killing the texture completely.

variants.note: Just the glutinous rice cylinder, 2 slices, no rendang or serunding

variants.name: Lemang with serunding kelapa
variants.note: Add ~2 tbsp dry coconut serunding (~90 cal); common pairing at Raya

variants.name: Lemang with beef rendang (1 piece)
variants.note: Add 1 piece beef rendang (~200 cal); the classic full Raya combo

faq.q: How many calories in Lemang?
faq.a: Two slices of lemang (180g, a typical Raya serving) is approximately 290 calories, with 45g carbs, 12g fat, and 4g protein. These are estimates as published data for lemang is limited.

faq.q: What exactly is lemang?
faq.a: Lemang is glutinous rice cooked with coconut milk inside bamboo tubes lined with banana leaf, then roasted over an open fire. It is a traditional Malay dish eaten mainly during Hari Raya, almost always paired with beef rendang or dry coconut serunding.

faq.q: Is lemang healthy for someone trying to lose weight?
faq.a: Not the easiest choice, bro. It is high in simple carbs from glutinous rice and has decent fat from coconut milk, with almost no protein. It is a once-a-year Raya food, so enjoy it, but keep the portion to one or two slices and make sure your protein for that meal comes from the rendang, not a second helping of lemang.

foods.name: Masak Kicap
foods.metaDescription: Masak kicap comes in around 300 calories for a hawker chicken piece with gravy. Not a light dish, but not the worst either. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Masak kicap is protein braised in sweet dark soy sauce with onion and chili, the kind of dish that looks simple but sneaks in more calories than you'd expect from that dark, glossy gravy.
foods.answer: A standard hawker serving of ayam masak kicap, one bone-in chicken piece with gravy, comes to about 300 calories. You're getting 25g protein, 14g carbs, and 15g fat for that 200g portion. Not bad on the protein front, but roughly 65 of those calories come purely from the kicap manis gravy, and about 35 from absorbed cooking oil. So yeah, the chicken itself is doing honest work, it's the sauce and frying that push the number up.
realTalk: Masak kicap is basically protein, chicken, fish, egg, or beef, fried first then braised in kicap manis (sweet dark soy sauce) with some aromatics. The dish is popular across Malay warung and nasi campur stalls nationwide. It tastes way more indulgent than 300 calories sounds, because kicap manis is genuinely sugary, that gravy alone adds 65 calories to your plate. The cooking oil adds around 35 calories from what actually gets absorbed during frying and braising, since most of the oil stays in the pan. Worth flagging honestly: these numbers are a ballpark estimate since detailed lab data for masak kicap is thin, different stalls use wildly different amounts of oil and gravy, so treat this as a guide rather than gospel.

What actually moves the number is how heavy-handed the cook is with oil and how much gravy you spoon onto your rice. A portion with generous gravy poured over can easily add 20 to 30 extra calories compared to eating the piece dry. Swapping to ikan kembung masak kicap drops you to around 220 calories, or go for telur masak kicap at about 210 calories if you want the lowest option. Daging (beef) masak kicap runs higher at around 320 calories because beef adds more fat. If you're eating this at a nasi campur stall, watch the rice portion more than the lauk itself, 200g of white rice is already 260 calories before any lauk lands on your plate.
lighter: Ask for less gravy, or eat the chicken piece without soaking the rice in the sauce. That dark kicap gravy is 65 calories for 45g, and most stalls pour it generously.
Pick ikan kembung or telur over chicken if it's available. Telur masak kicap is around 210 calories, and ikan kembung sits at about 220 calories.
Skip the second piece. Seems obvious but bro, at a nasi campur stall it's tempting. One piece is already a solid protein hit at 25g.
Pair it with sayur campur or kangkung rather than extra rice to keep the overall meal calories manageable.
If you're cooking at home, reduce the kicap manis by half and use low-sodium soy sauce to stretch the flavour without dumping in as much sugar.

variants.name: Ayam kampung masak kicap (free-range chicken)
variants.note: Leaner bird, less subcutaneous fat than broiler; similar gravy; slightly lower calories

variants.name: Ayam masak kicap standard (broiler/regular chicken)
variants.note: Most common hawker version; bone-in thigh or drumstick with generous kicap gravy

variants.note: Beef chuck or shank braised in kicap; higher fat from beef; MOH estimate 140 kcal/100g meat, add gravy and oil

faq.q: How many calories in Masak Kicap?
faq.a: A standard hawker serving of masak kicap, one bone-in chicken piece with gravy at around 200g total, comes to about 300 calories. That breaks down as 25g protein, 14g carbs, and 15g fat. The gravy and absorbed cooking oil account for about 100 of those calories combined.

faq.q: What exactly is masak kicap?
faq.a: Masak kicap means cooked in soy sauce, specifically kicap manis which is the thick, sweet dark soy sauce common in Malaysian cooking. The protein gets fried first, then braised in a sauce made with kicap manis, dark soy, oyster sauce, onion, and chili. It's a staple at Malay nasi campur and warung stalls.

faq.q: Is masak kicap a healthy choice for someone trying to lose weight?
faq.a: It's decent but not great. The protein content is solid at 25g per serving, which helps with satiety. The problem is the kicap manis adds sugar and the frying adds oil, so the calories come in higher than plain grilled chicken. It's a reasonable nasi campur pick as long as you control your rice portion and don't drown everything in extra gravy.

foods.name: Masak Merah
foods.serving: 1 piece bone-in chicken with sauce (ayam masak merah, no rice)
foods.metaDescription: Ayam masak merah has about 340 calories per piece with sauce. The fried chicken plus sweet tomato-chili gravy adds up fast, here is the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Masak merah is chicken (or fish, prawns, or beef) fried then simmered in a sweet, slightly spicy tomato and chili sauce, a fixture at kenduri spreads and everyday warung alike.
foods.answer: One bone-in piece of ayam masak merah with sauce comes in at around 340 calories for roughly 220g. That breaks down to 27g protein, 14g carbs, and 20g fat. The fried chicken itself accounts for most of it at 200 calories, but the sauce piles on another 140 or so from oil, ketchup, and sugar combined. Not a light lauk by any stretch, but not outrageous either if you are only having one piece.
realTalk: Masak merah is one of those dishes that sounds healthier than it is because it looks saucy and tomatoey, not greasy. But that sauce has two calorie traps: cooking oil and sweet tomato ketchup. The fried chicken underneath adds another layer of fat from the pre-frying step before everything gets simmered together. At 340 calories for one bone-in piece, it is decent protein for the calorie cost (27g), but you are also getting 20g fat. Worth noting these numbers are a ballpark estimate since hard nutrition data for this dish is thin, and every mak cik's recipe is a bit different in how much oil and sugar goes in.

What really moves the number is two things: the protein you pick and how generous the sauce is. Swap chicken for udang masak merah and you drop to around 220 calories for a similar serving because prawns carry almost no fat. Ikan merah sits in the middle at about 260 calories. Go the other way with daging lembu and you are looking at 380 calories because beef cubes are fattier. For the chicken version, kenduri or catering style preparation can hit 430 calories from extra oil and sometimes santan thrown in. The sauce itself is only 45 calories, but the oil share per serving adds 55 calories on its own, so ladles of extra gravy over your rice are not free.
lighter: Go for udang or ikan merah instead of chicken and you save 80 to 120 calories per serving without touching the sauce at all.
Ask for less gravy, or scrape some off before eating. The oil in the sauce is where a big chunk of calories hide.
If you are cooking at home, cut the oil in the sauce by half and skip the ketchup, using fresh tomatoes instead. You can trim 50 to 80 calories per serving that way.
One piece only, lah. The chicken itself is already 200 calories before the sauce. Two pieces with rice and you are well past 800 calories for just that lauk and carb.
Pair it with plain steamed rice rather than nasi minyak or nasi tomato. Those festive rices add another 100 to 150 calories on top and they are usually served together at kenduri.

faq.q: How many calories in Masak Merah?
faq.a: A standard serving of ayam masak merah, one bone-in chicken piece with sauce and no rice, is around 340 calories. The fried chicken contributes about 200 of those, with the oil and sweet tomato sauce making up the rest.

faq.q: What exactly is masak merah?
faq.a: Masak merah literally means 'cooked red'. It is a Malaysian dish where protein (most commonly chicken, but also red snapper, prawns, or beef) is first fried, then simmered in a sauce made from blended chili paste, tomatoes, tomato ketchup, and spices. It is a staple at kenduri (feasts) and everyday warung, and it sits somewhere between a curry and a sambal in terms of heat level.

faq.q: Is masak merah a good choice if I am watching my calories?
faq.a: It is okay but not the lightest option. At 340 calories per chicken piece you get solid protein (27g), which is decent value. The issue is the 20g fat from the fried chicken and oil-heavy sauce. If you want a lower-calorie version of the same dish, order udang masak merah instead, prawns drop the count to around 220 calories for a similar portion.

foods.name: Sayur Campur
foods.metaDescription: Sayur Campur has about 130 calories per side portion at the nasi campur stall. The vegetables are fine, it's the wok oil you need to watch.
foods.summary: Sayur Campur is a simple stir-fried mix of kampung vegetables like cabbage, carrot and long beans, often with tofu, cooked with wok oil and oyster sauce.
foods.answer: A typical 160g side serving of Sayur Campur at a nasi campur or kopitiam stall comes in at around 130 calories. The vegetables themselves are basically free calories, but the cooking oil from the wok adds up fast, contributing about 80 of those 130 calories on its own. Add tofu and a bit of oyster sauce and you get a pretty decent side that still won't kill your day.
realTalk: Sayur Campur is one of those nasi campur sides that looks virtuous and mostly is, bah. It's just mixed stir-fried vegetables, usually cabbage, carrot and long beans, sometimes with a few cubes of firm tofu thrown in. The 130-calorie number is our best ballpark estimate, honestly, because there's not much hard data out there for hawker-cooked veg dishes and every uncle at every wok runs it differently. What we do know is that the vegetables themselves clock in at only about 34 calories for 100g. The real calorie driver here is the wok oil, around 80 calories from just 9g of cooking oil. So yes, it's a vegetable dish, but it's not a zero-calorie situation.

What changes the maths quite a bit is how heavy-handed the cook is with the oil. A health-conscious stall with minimal oil can bring this down to around 80 calories for the same portion size. The oyster sauce version sits at the standard 130. If they crack an egg through it (the telur campur version), add roughly 50 calories and you're at about 175. And if you get the santan version, basically a lodeh-style coconut milk base, that jumps to around 220 calories. Portion-wise, if you're piling this onto a rice plate, a second scoop adds another 130 or so to your count, which is still pretty manageable compared to the rendang sitting next to it.
lighter: Ask the aunty for 'sikit minyak' (less oil) and mean it. The difference between a heavy-handed wok and a light one is the difference between 80 and 130 calories for the same plate.
Skip the santan version if you see it. That lodeh-style coconut milk base pushes calories from 130 up to around 220 per portion.
Go plain without tofu if you want the lightest version, around 80 calories. The tofu is fine nutritionally but adds volume to the calorie count.
Treat sayur campur as your buffer dish at nasi campur. Pile this up instead of reaching for a second scoop of rice or an extra piece of fried chicken.
If you're making it at home, a non-stick pan with one teaspoon of oil instead of a wok full cuts the oil calories by more than half.
