variants.note: Smaller, thinner crepe-style with mashed banana folded in; banana adds ~20 kcal but pieces are usually smaller and use less coconut

variants.name: Lempeng kelapa plain (no sambal)
variants.note: Standard medium pancake with grated coconut, eaten with white sugar or kaya

variants.name: Lempeng kelapa with sambal
variants.note: Add ~20 kcal for a tablespoon of sambal accompaniment

variants.name: Lempeng jagung (corn)
variants.note: Corn kernels added to batter; slightly more carbs and a touch more sugar than plain kelapa

variants.name: Lempeng berlauk (with filling/topping)
variants.note: Served with heavier lauk like rendang or curry chicken; accompaniment adds 40-70 kcal depending on portion

faq.q: How many calories in Lempeng?
faq.a: One medium lempeng is about 155 calories. The banana version (lempeng pisang) is lighter at around 130 calories, while the corn version (lempeng jagung) is slightly higher at 180 calories. Add a heavy lauk topping and it can reach 220 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is lempeng?
faq.a: Lempeng is a traditional Malay pancake made from flour, fresh grated coconut, and a little water, cooked flat on a griddle with oil. It is a common kampung breakfast or teatime snack, usually eaten with white sugar, kaya, or sambal on the side.

faq.q: Is lempeng a healthy snack?
faq.a: It is decent for a snack at 155 calories per piece, not amazing but not terrible either. The main thing to watch is the oil used on the griddle and what you eat it with. Plain with minimal accompaniment it fits fine into a calorie-controlled day. Just do not eat three of them.

foods.name: Kuih Putu
foods.metaDescription: Kuih Putu is about 230 calories for 2 pieces. Steamed rice flour, gula melaka centre, coconut outside. Here is what you are actually eating.
foods.summary: Kuih Putu is a traditional steamed kuih made from rice flour, filled with melted gula melaka palm sugar, and rolled in grated coconut, sold fresh off the steamer at pasar malam and morning markets across Malaysia.
foods.answer: Two pieces of Kuih Putu (about 60g) comes in at roughly 230 calories, with 42g carbs, 5g fat, and barely any protein to speak of. The gula melaka filling is doing the most work here, contributing around 77 calories on its own. This is a ballpark estimate, not a lab result, so treat it as a solid guide rather than gospel.
realTalk: Kuih Putu is one of those snacks that feels innocent because it is small and steamed, not fried. If you have never had it, picture a soft cylinder or disc of steamed rice flour with a molten palm sugar centre and grated coconut coating the outside. 230 calories for two pieces is not bad for a kuih, but the catch is that nobody really stops at two. Grab four and you are already at 460 calories from something you barely noticed eating. The gula melaka is the main calorie driver at around 77 kcal per serving, and the coconut adds another 46. Fair to note: calorie data for traditional kuih is thin, so this is a genuine estimate based on the known components, not a precise lab figure.

What actually changes the count is how generous the vendor is with filling and coconut. A stall that loads up the gula melaka and piles on extra coconut can easily push a serving to 270 calories or more. Putu piring, the bigger disc-shaped version, runs around 260 calories because the mold holds more dough and filling. If you are eating this as a snack, two pieces is fine. The problem is buying a whole bag of six or eight at the pasar malam and finishing them on the drive home. That is 700 plus calories gone before dinner, and your brain did not even register it as a meal.
lighter: Stick to two pieces, not the whole packet. It sounds obvious but this is genuinely where most people go wrong with kuih.
Go for putu bambu over putu piring if you have a choice. The bamboo tube version is smaller and more consistent at around 230 calories versus 260 for the disc.
Skip the extra coconut topping if the vendor asks. That generous handful adds 20 to 40 calories and you honestly will not miss it.

Eat it as a standalone snack with plain water or teh o kosong, not paired with other kuih. It is easy to collect three or four different kuih at the market and suddenly you have had a full meal in finger food form.
Eat it fresh off the steamer when it is piping hot. You slow down naturally and actually taste it, instead of powering through a cold bag of them.

variants.name: Putu piring (disc-shaped, larger)
variants.note: Larger disc mold holds slightly more dough and filling; heavier gula melaka centre

variants.name: Putu bambu (bamboo tube, standard)
variants.note: Standard hawker version; compact cylindrical shape, consistent size

variants.name: Extra coconut topping
variants.note: Generous extra grated coconut added on top adds roughly 20-40 kcal to any variant

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Putu?
faq.a: About 230 calories for 2 pieces (60g), which is the standard hawker serving. This covers the rice flour shell, gula melaka filling, and grated coconut coating. It is an estimate since lab data for traditional kuih is limited, but it is a solid ballpark.

faq.q: What exactly is Kuih Putu?
faq.a: It is a Malaysian steamed kuih made from rice flour dough, shaped into cylinders (putu bambu) or discs (putu piring), with a centre of gula melaka palm sugar that melts when steamed. The outside is coated in grated coconut. It is sold fresh and hot, typically at morning markets and pasar malam.

faq.q: Is Kuih Putu healthy?
faq.a: It is not a health food, but it is also not deep-fried, so it is better than a lot of snacks. The problem is it is almost entirely simple carbs and sugar with almost no protein. Two pieces is a reasonable treat. A whole bag of six is basically dessert pretending to be a snack.

foods.name: Kuih Bom
foods.metaDescription: Kuih Bom packs around 210 calories per piece. That sesame-coated deep-fried dough ball is tastier than it looks on paper, but the calories add up fast.
foods.summary: Kuih Bom is a deep-fried glutinous rice dough ball coated in sesame seeds and filled with sweet gula melaka grated coconut, a classic Malaysian kuih that is dangerously easy to eat more than one of.
foods.answer: One Kuih Bom is around 210 calories for a 55g piece. That comes from the glutinous rice dough mixed with coconut milk (100 cal), the sweet gula melaka coconut filling (60 cal), sesame seed coating (20 cal), and the frying oil the dough soaks up (30 cal). It is a small ball but it is not a light snack. Worth knowing before you grab three off the kuih tray.
realTalk: Kuih Bom is that round, golden, sesame-coated ball you see at kuih stalls and pasar malam. The dough is glutinous rice flour mixed with coconut milk, deep fried until puffed up, with a soft sweet coconut filling inside. At 210 calories per piece, it is not catastrophic if you eat one. The problem is nobody eats one. The calories come from three places: carbs from the glutinous flour, fat from the coconut milk in the dough plus the frying oil absorbed, and sugar from the gula melaka filling. Fair warning: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because detailed lab data for kuih bom specifically is thin, so treat it as a reasonable guide rather than a precise count.

What changes the number most is how much oil the dough absorbs during frying. Freshly fried pieces that have been properly drained will be on the lower end. Ones sitting in a tray soaked in oil, or fried at too low a temperature, absorb more fat and could push past 230 calories easily. The filling matters too: the chocolate variant in modern kuih shops runs about 230 calories versus the classic coconut version at 210. The sweet potato dough version (keledek) drops to around 185 calories because less glutinous flour is used. Two pieces of the classic version is already 420 calories, which is a full meal's worth of calories for some people. One is fine as a snack. Two is a decision you should make consciously lah.
lighter: Stop at one. Seriously. One piece is a proper snack at 210 calories. Two pieces is 420 calories and at that point you could have had a real meal.
Look for the sweet potato dough version if you see it. At around 185 calories it saves you 25 calories per piece and the texture is actually pretty good.
Eat it fresh off the fryer rather than from a tray that has been sitting. Fresh ones have had less time to absorb excess oil.
Pair it with plain water or unsweetened tea, not teh tarik or sirap. Adding a 150-calorie drink to a 210-calorie kuih turns a snack into a 360-calorie side quest.

Skip the chocolate filling variant. The extra sugar and fat in the chocolate version pushes it to around 230 calories for the same size piece, which is not worth it when the coconut filling is honestly better anyway.

variants.name: Sweet potato dough (keledek) version
variants.note: Dough made with mashed sweet potato replacing some glutinous flour; lower fat, slightly lower calories

variants.name: Standard glutinous rice dough with grated coconut filling
variants.note: Classic version; sesame-coated, deep fried, filled with gula melaka and grated coconut

variants.name: Chocolate filling variant
variants.note: Chocolate filling adds extra sugar and fat versus coconut filling; sold in some modern kuih shops

components.name: Sweet grated coconut filling (gula melaka + coconut)

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Bom?
faq.a: One Kuih Bom is around 210 calories for a standard 55g piece. This covers the glutinous rice dough, sweet coconut filling, sesame coating, and absorbed frying oil.

faq.q: What exactly is Kuih Bom?
faq.a: It is a Malaysian deep-fried kuih made from glutinous rice flour dough mixed with coconut milk, rolled in sesame seeds, then fried until it puffs up. Inside is a sweet filling of grated coconut cooked with gula melaka. Some modern versions use chocolate filling instead. You will find it at kuih stalls, pasar malam, and traditional bakeries.

faq.q: Is Kuih Bom healthy?
faq.a: It is a deep-fried sweet snack, so no, it is not something you eat for nutrition. At 210 calories per piece with 9g of fat and 30g of carbs, it is a treat. One piece occasionally is fine. The issue is portion control because they are small and easy to eat several at a time without noticing.

foods.name: Kuih Siput
foods.metaDescription: Kuih siput has about 120 calories per small handful (25g). These crunchy fried Raya snacks are easy to demolish by the bowl, so let's talk numbers.
foods.summary: Kuih siput is a crunchy, savoury fried snack shaped like a snail shell, made from spiced flour dough and popular during Raya as a cookie you grab by the handful.
foods.answer: One small handful of kuih siput, about 6 to 8 pieces or 25g, comes in at roughly 120 calories, with 13g carbs, 6g fat, and 2g protein. The calories are mostly coming from the fried dough itself. It is not a heavy snack per piece, but that is the whole problem lah, because nobody stops at one handful.
realTalk: Kuih siput is that classic Raya cookie you find in every rumah terbuka, sitting in a big toples next to the muruku and the cornflake cookies. The name means snail in Malay because of the coiled shape. It is deep fried spiced dough, so the calorie drivers are pretty straightforward: flour base giving you the carbs, and absorbed frying oil pushing the fat up. At 120 calories for 25g, it sounds manageable until you realise a proper makan session at a Raya open house means you are mindlessly grabbing these while talking and laughing. Easy to put away 100 to 150g without noticing, which is 480 to 720 calories from snacks alone. Fair warning: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because there is not much hard data on kuih siput specifically, and every recipe is a bit different in how much butter and oil goes in.

What actually changes the count is the recipe and how long they are left to drain. More butter in the dough means more calories before it even hits the oil. Poorly drained pieces can carry noticeably more absorbed fat, easily pushing a 25g serving from 120 to 140 or 150 calories. The spice blend itself, usually curry powder or cumin and sesame, adds almost nothing calorie-wise. If you are trying to manage your intake at a Raya gathering, portion it out upfront: put 6 to 8 pieces on your plate and then step away from the toples. Do not eat standing next to the container or you will lose count entirely.
lighter: Portion it out before you eat. Six to eight pieces on a plate and that is your serving. Do not snack straight from the jar.
Alternate kuih siput with zero or low calorie options at the table, like plain air and conversation, so you are not reaching out of boredom.
If you are making them at home, try baking instead of frying. You cut out the absorbed oil which is 36 calories of the 120 right there.
Drain fried kuih siput on paper towels properly before storing. Better draining means less residual oil in each piece.
Be honest about the context. If you are going to three open houses in a day, this is where the calories pile up, not from one bowl but from three.

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Siput?
faq.a: About 120 calories per small handful of 6 to 8 pieces, which is around 25g. That works out to roughly 480 calories per 100g.

faq.q: What exactly is kuih siput?
faq.a: It is a crunchy deep fried savoury snack made from spiced dough, shaped like a snail shell. It is especially popular during Raya as a festive cookie and you will find it in almost every Malaysian home during the celebration.

faq.q: Is kuih siput considered a healthy snack?
faq.a: Not really, bro. It is deep fried dough, so it is pretty calorie dense for its size. The main issue is that it is so easy to overeat. In small controlled portions it is fine as an occasional treat, but mindlessly snacking on it at open houses will add up fast.

foods.name: Kuih Ros (Kuih Loyang)
foods.metaDescription: Kuih Ros has about 75 calories for 2 pieces (20g), but nobody eats just 2. Here's the real calorie count and what to watch out for.
foods.summary: Kuih Ros, also called Kuih Loyang, is a deep-fried crispy snack made by dipping a brass mould into coconut-egg batter and frying it until it pops off in a thin, honeycomb-shaped shell.
foods.answer: Two pieces of Kuih Ros (about 20g) comes in at 75 calories, with 5g fat, 7g carbs, and 1g protein. On paper that sounds harmless. The problem is the serving size. Two pieces is about the weight of a 50 sen coin. At a Raya open house you're looking at 10 to 20 pieces without even noticing, which puts you at 375 to 750 calories from a snack you didn't really plan to eat.
realTalk: Kuih Ros is one of those festive snacks that looks delicate and tiny so your brain tells you it's basically calorie-free. It's not. Each piece is mostly deep-fried batter, so the fat content is doing most of the work here. The batter itself is rice flour, a bit of corn starch, sugar, coconut milk, and egg, all dipped in hot oil until a thin crispy shell forms. Pretty light per piece at 75 calories for 2 pieces, sure, but the density of oil absorbed relative to the size is what gets you. Worth flagging that these numbers are a ballpark estimate since there's almost no hard lab data on home-fried kuih, so treat the figures as a reasonable guide rather than gospel.

What actually moves the number is how many you eat and how much oil the batter soaks up, and both of those vary a lot. Thinner batter means less mass but also potentially more surface area for oil absorption. A plate of 10 pieces is roughly 375 calories and you can clear that in under 5 minutes while talking lah. If you're at a makan table, put a small handful on your plate and walk away from the serving tray. Pair it with plain water or teh-o kosong rather than syrup drinks. The kuih itself has very little protein, so don't fool yourself into thinking it's a snack that keeps you full. It won't.
lighter: Count before you eat. Put 4 to 6 pieces on your plate (150 to 225 calories) and go sit somewhere away from the tray.
Eat it slowly. The crunch is the whole point and rushing means you lose track of how many you've had.
Balance it with something with protein, a hard-boiled egg or some satay nearby so you don't just snack on pure carbs and fat.
Skip the condensed milk dip if it's being served. That adds another 30 to 50 calories per dip and most people dip multiple times.
Drink a full glass of water first. It won't change the calories but it genuinely slows you down.

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Ros (Kuih Loyang)?
faq.a: Two pieces of Kuih Ros (20g) has about 75 calories, with 5g fat, 7g carbs, and 1g protein. These are estimate figures since hard data on home-fried kuih is thin, but it's a reasonable ballpark.

faq.q: What exactly is Kuih Ros?
faq.a: It's a traditional Malaysian deep-fried snack made by heating a decorative brass mould in oil, dipping it into a thin batter of rice flour, coconut milk, egg, and sugar, then lowering it back into the hot oil until the batter sets and releases as a crispy shell. The rose or honeycomb shape comes from the mould. It's common at Hari Raya and festive gatherings.

faq.q: Is Kuih Ros a healthy snack?
faq.a: Not really, bro. It's deep-fried, has no meaningful protein, and the portion sizes at actual events are way beyond 2 pieces. It's a festive treat, enjoy it as one. If you're tracking calories, count your pieces before you eat rather than trying to remember afterwards.

foods.name: Tepung Pelita
foods.metaDescription: Tepung Pelita has about 105 calories per cup. The santan top layer is doing most of the damage. Here's the full breakdown for this Ramadan bazaar kuih.
foods.summary: Tepung Pelita is a two-layer steamed kuih, green pandan bottom and salted coconut milk on top, served in a small banana-leaf cup and basically a Ramadan bazaar staple.
foods.answer: One cup of Tepung Pelita is around 105 calories. That's for a 75g piece, the standard small banana-leaf cup size you get at the bazaar. It sounds low until you realise nobody eats just one.
realTalk: Tepung Pelita is one of those kuih that looks innocent because it's small and it comes in a cute little banana-leaf cup. Two layers, green pandan jelly at the bottom and a silky salted coconut milk (santan) layer on top, steamed and served slightly chilled. At 105 calories per cup, it's not a disaster on its own. But that 6g of fat is almost entirely from santan, which makes up the whole top layer. The pandan layer is basically just rice flour, sugar, water and pandan juice so it barely clocks in. The sugar across both layers adds another 31 calories. Fair warning: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard calorie data for traditional kuih like this is genuinely thin. Treat it as a rough guide, not a lab result.

The real maths problem is that tepung pelita is very easy to eat three or four of in one shot at the bazaar. Four pieces is 420 calories, which is getting close to a proper meal. The santan ratio in the top layer is where different stalls diverge a lot. Thick, rich santan versus a thinner mix can shift the fat content by 2 to 3 grams per piece, which is maybe 20 to 25 extra calories each. If you want to keep it lighter, just set a hard limit of two pieces and move on. Pair it with something savoury instead of stacking it with other sweet kuih.
lighter: Cap yourself at two pieces. At 105 calories each, two is 210 calories, which is a reasonable sweet snack. Four or five liao, you've eaten a full meal in kuih form.
Look for stalls where the santan layer looks thinner and less glossy. Thick, jiggly santan on top means more fat. The flatter-looking ones are usually lighter.
Eat it as your dessert after a low-calorie meal, not on top of an already heavy bazaar spread.
Avoid the versions sold alongside heavy syrup or extra coconut drizzle. Plain is already enough.
If you're making it at home, use light coconut milk for the top layer. You drop maybe 1 to 2g of fat per piece without killing the flavour.

faq.q: How many calories in Tepung Pelita?
faq.a: One piece of Tepung Pelita (75g, one small banana-leaf cup) has about 105 calories, with 1g protein, 15g carbs and 6g fat. The santan top layer accounts for most of the calories.

faq.q: What exactly is Tepung Pelita?
faq.a: It's a traditional Malay kuih made of two layers steamed in a small banana-leaf cup. The bottom layer is green from pandan juice and made with rice flour, and the top layer is a salted coconut milk (santan) jelly. You eat it together and the sweet-salty combo is the whole point. It's especially common at Ramadan bazaars.

faq.q: Is Tepung Pelita healthy?
faq.a: One piece at 105 calories is fine. The issue is portion control because these things are tiny and you tend to grab a few at once. The fat is all from coconut milk so it's saturated fat, and the carbs come from rice flour and sugar. It's a treat, not a health food, but one or two pieces won't wreck your day.

foods.name: Amplang
foods.metaDescription: Amplang is a Sabah fish cracker made from mackerel and sago flour. One handful (25g) is around 135 calories, and yes, half the damage is frying oil.
foods.summary: Amplang is a puffy, deep-fried fish cracker from Sabah, made with mackerel or shrimp mixed into a sago flour dough and fried until light and crunchy.
foods.answer: One small handful of amplang, about 25g, comes in at around 135 calories. That's 14g carbs, 8g fat, and 2g protein. Not a disaster for a snack, but the catch is that 25g disappears in about 30 seconds flat, and most people eat two or three handfuls without thinking twice.
realTalk: Amplang is one of those Sabahan snacks that sounds innocent because it has fish in it, but bro, the fish is almost a side note. The real calorie driver here is the sago starch base and the frying oil absorbed during cooking. Out of 135 calories per 25g handful, roughly 65 of them are straight from oil. The fish content is only about 5g per serving, giving you a measly 15 calories of actual protein. If you see it being sold at Kota Kinabalu airport or a pasar malam stall, it's genuinely delicious and worth trying, especially the ikan tenggiri (Spanish mackerel) version. Just be honest with yourself about the portion. These numbers are a ballpark estimate by the way, because proper lab data for amplang is thin and most packages round off or differ by brand.

What actually moves the maths is how much you eat in one sitting. A small 25g handful is 135 calories but a typical 100g snacking session (which is easy to hit while watching TV) is around 540 calories, roughly the same as a full plate of nasi goreng. The udang (shrimp) variant runs slightly higher at about 140 calories per 25g. There is no real lower-calorie way to prepare amplang since the deep frying is baked into the product itself. Your best move is to portion it out before you start eating, put the bag away, and pair it with something filling like a cup of black coffee or tea rather than snacking from an open packet.
lighter: Pour a measured 25g into a bowl and seal the bag immediately. You will eat less without thinking about it.
Buy the smaller travel packs instead of the big souvenir bags. Built-in portion control without any willpower needed.
Pair it with plain kopi-o or teh-o so you have something in your hand between crackers and slow down the pace.
If you want the fish flavour with less oil, otak-otak or ikan bakar gives you actual fish protein and far fewer calories per 100g.
Treat it as a once-in-a-while thing when you are actually at the pasar or airport, not a pantry staple to graze on daily.

faq.q: How many calories in Amplang?
faq.a: One small handful of amplang, around 25g, is approximately 135 calories. Scale that up and 100g is about 540 calories, most of it coming from the sago starch base and absorbed frying oil.

faq.q: What exactly is amplang?
faq.a: Amplang is a deep-fried fish cracker from Sabah, East Malaysia. It is made by mixing ground fish (usually ikan tenggiri, which is Spanish mackerel, or shrimp) with sago or tapioca flour and seasonings, then deep frying until puffy and crunchy. You will commonly find it sold at Sabah airports and pasar malam stalls as a regional snack or souvenir.

faq.q: Is amplang a healthy snack?
faq.a: It is not a terrible snack in small amounts but it is not a healthy one either. The fish content per serving is low, around 5g, so the protein benefit is minimal. Most of the calories come from starch and frying oil. For the same calorie spend you could eat a hard-boiled egg and feel fuller for longer.

foods.name: Kuih Kapit (Love Letters)
foods.metaDescription: Kuih Kapit (Love Letters) has about 120 calories per 3 pieces (25g). The danger is nobody stops at 3. Here is the full calorie breakdown.
foods.summary: Kuih Kapit is a thin, crispy folded wafer made from egg, coconut milk and sugar, pressed in a hot iron mould and eaten by the stack during Chinese New Year and beyond.
foods.answer: 3 pieces of Kuih Kapit (about 25g) comes in at roughly 120 calories, with 18g carbs, 4g fat and 2g protein. Fair warning though, these numbers are a ballpark estimate since detailed lab data for this snack is pretty thin. What is not a ballpark is how fast you go through half a tin without realising it.
realTalk: Kuih Kapit, also called Love Letters or kuih sepit, is that thin crispy folded wafer your aunty makes in bulk for Chinese New Year using a special hinged iron mould pressed over a flame. The batter is simple: rice flour, egg, coconut milk and sugar. Each piece is light, maybe 8g, and at 40 calories a wafer it sounds harmless. The problem is nobody eats just 3. You sit in front of the tin while watching TV and suddenly you have eaten 15 pieces, which is 600 calories of snack you barely registered. The calories come mainly from the carbs (flour and sugar) plus the fat from coconut milk. It is genuinely delicious and there is nothing wrong with it, just know what you are working with.

The maths change fast with quantity. Stick to 3 pieces (25g, 120 calories) as an actual conscious serving rather than a background snack and it is totally fine as a treat. The sesame seed variant nudges up to about 135 calories for the same 3 pieces because of the added fat from the seeds. If you are making these at home, the coconut milk is the biggest lever: swapping thick coconut milk for a lighter version can shave 10 to 15 calories per serving without killing the texture. The honest answer on all these numbers though is treat them as a reasonable estimate, not gospel, because hard nutritional data for traditional kuih like this is scarce and recipes vary quite a bit between households and commercial makers.
lighter: Portion it out before you sit down. Put 3 to 5 pieces in a small bowl and put the tin away. Eating straight from the tin is how you accidentally finish 300 calories.
If you are making it at home, use a slightly thinner batter and less sugar. You can cut sugar by 20% and most people cannot tell the difference once the wafer is crispy.
Pair it with unsweetened tea or plain coffee so you are not doubling up on sugar from the drink side.
Go for plain original over pandan or sesame variants. The difference is small but plain keeps you at 120 calories per 3 pieces instead of the 135 calories for sesame.
Treat it as a proper dessert moment, not background snacking. Eat it slowly, actually taste it. You will eat fewer pieces and enjoy it more.

faq.q: How many calories in Kuih Kapit (Love Letters)?
faq.a: About 120 calories per 3 pieces (25g). That works out to roughly 40 calories per individual wafer. These are estimates as hard nutritional data for traditional kuih is limited, but this is a reasonable ballpark for the standard egg, coconut milk and sugar batter.

faq.q: What exactly is Kuih Kapit?
faq.a: Kuih Kapit is a thin, crispy wafer made by pressing a batter of rice flour, egg, coconut milk and sugar between a hot hinged iron mould. The result is a delicate folded or rolled wafer. It is a Chinese New Year staple in Malaysia and Singapore, though you can find it year-round in snack shops. Also known as kuih sepit or Love Letters.

faq.q: Is Kuih Kapit healthy?
faq.a: It is a sugary, starchy snack so it is not something you build meals around, but a few pieces as a treat is perfectly fine. The issue is it is very easy to mindlessly eat a lot of them because each piece feels so light. If you are tracking calories, count your pieces before you start eating, not after.

foods.name: Keropok Keping
foods.serving: 1 small bag / hawker plate (~50g crackers + sweet chili dip)
foods.metaDescription: Keropok keping runs about 260 calories per small bag with sweet chili dip. Light per piece but the oil adds up fast. Here's the honest breakdown.
foods.summary: Keropok keping are flat, crispy fish crackers, sliced thin from a log of fish paste and tapioca, sun-dried, then deep fried to a satisfying snap and served with sweet chili sauce.
foods.answer: A small bag or hawker plate of keropok keping, around 50g of crackers with the sweet chili dip, comes to about 260 calories. That breaks down as 5g protein, 34g carbs, and 10g fat. Each individual piece is light as air, but the tapioca base and the oil it absorbs during frying add up quickly once you get through a whole bag.
realTalk: Keropok keping are the flat, shatteringly crispy cousin of keropok lekor. If you haven't had them, picture thin wafers made from fish paste and tapioca starch, sliced from a log shape, dried in the sun, then deep fried until they puff up and go translucent. Popular all along the Terengganu and Kelantan coast but honestly sold everywhere in Malaysia now. At 260 calories for a small bag with dip, they're not a disaster, but almost all of those calories come from starch and frying oil, not from anything useful. The fish content is real but modest, so you get 5g of protein and that's about it. Fair warning: these numbers are a ballpark estimate. Hard nutritional data for keropok keping specifically is thin, and oil absorption varies a lot depending on frying temperature and how thick the keping are cut.

What really shifts the maths is portion size and how much you dip. The sweet chili sauce on its own is only about 30 calories for 15g, which is fine, but people don't stop at 15g. Double the dip and you're adding another 30 calories easily. The bigger issue is the crackers themselves: 40g of fried cracker base brings 145 calories, plus another 85 calories estimated just from absorbed oil. If you buy the 100g bag instead of the 50g bag you're already past 500 calories before you notice. Eating them alongside a meal rather than as the whole meal helps keep things in check, and sharing a bag at the table is the sensible play.
lighter: Share a bag. Seriously, a 50g portion shared between two people is 130 calories each and you still get the full experience.
Go easy on the sweet chili dip. One quick dip per piece, not a full soak. The sauce is sugar and every extra spoonful counts.
Don't make it a standalone snack if you're hungry. Pair a small portion with something higher in protein so you actually feel satisfied.
Buy the smaller bags at the hawker stall rather than the big takeaway packs. Out of sight, out of stomach.
If you make them at home, baking or air frying the dried keping instead of deep frying can cut the oil-absorbed calories significantly, though the texture will be a bit different.

faq.q: How many calories in Keropok Keping?
faq.a: A small bag or hawker serving of keropok keping, around 50g of crackers with sweet chili dip, is approximately 260 calories. That's 5g protein, 34g carbs, and 10g fat. Note that this is an estimate as hard data for this specific snack is limited.

faq.q: What exactly is keropok keping?
faq.a: Keropok keping are flat fish crackers made from a mixture of fish paste and tapioca starch. The dough is formed into a log, sliced thin, sun-dried, and then deep fried until crispy and puffy. They're a Terengganu staple but you'll find them all over Malaysia served with sweet chili sauce.

faq.q: Is keropok keping healthy?
faq.a: It's a deep fried tapioca snack, so no, it's not a health food. The protein is low at 5g and most of the calories come from starch and frying oil. That said, a small serving at 260 calories is manageable if you're not eating it on top of a full meal. The issue is portion control since the light, airy texture makes it very easy to eat way more than you planned.

foods.name: Umai
foods.metaDescription: Umai is Sarawak's raw fish salad and one serving is only about 200 calories. High protein, almost no carbs. Seriously good diet food.
foods.summary: Umai is a Sarawak Melanau dish of thin-sliced raw fish tossed in lime juice, shallots, chili and salt, eaten cold and fresh.
foods.answer: One hawker serving of umai (about 160g) comes in at around 200 calories, with 25g protein and only 6g carbs. The bulk of those calories is from the raw fish itself, mostly ikan tenggiri (Spanish mackerel). The condiments, lime, shallots, chili, barely register. As raw fish dishes go, this is genuinely one of the leanest things you can order.
realTalk: Umai is basically Sarawak's version of ceviche, bro. Melanau people have been eating raw fish this way for generations: thin slices of fresh tenggiri or terubok, dressed with calamansi, sliced shallots, chili, and salt. No cooking, no oil, no coconut milk. At 200 calories for a full serving, it is one of the rare hawker dishes where you can eat the whole plate and not regret it later. The 25g of protein is solid too, roughly the same as a medium chicken breast. Fair warning though, these numbers are a genuine ballpark estimate because there is almost no hard nutritional data published for umai specifically, so take the figures as a useful guide rather than gospel.

What actually moves the calorie count is the fish you pick. Tenggiri lands at about 200 calories a serving, which is your standard order. Swap to umai terubok (the shad-family fish, fattier and oilier) and you jump to around 260 calories for the same portion size. Go the other way with umai udang (prawns) and you drop all the way down to about 115 calories since prawns are much leaner than any fish. The condiments change almost nothing. One thing to watch: some stalls add a splash of chili oil or mix in a tiny bit of sugar to balance the acidity, which can quietly add 30 to 50 calories. Ask if you want to keep it clean.
lighter: Order umai udang instead of the fish version and you cut down to about 115 calories, same dish, same experience.
Eat it as a main, not a side, since at 200 calories and 25g protein it holds up fine on its own without needing rice.
Skip any version that comes with a coconut milk dressing or sweet sauce on the side, those add calories fast.
Ask the stall to go easy on any added chili oil or sugar syrup if they use it to balance the lime.
Choose tenggiri over terubok if you want the leaner fish option, terubok is the fattier fish and runs about 60 calories higher per serving.

faq.q: How many calories in Umai?
faq.a: A standard hawker serving of umai (about 160g) is around 200 calories with 25g protein and 6g carbs. Umai udang is much lower at about 115 calories, while umai terubok is higher at around 260 calories due to the fattier fish.

faq.q: What exactly is umai and where does it come from?
faq.a: Umai is a raw fish salad from Sarawak, traditionally made by the Melanau coastal community. Fresh fish is sliced thin and mixed with calamansi lime juice, sliced shallots, chili and salt. The acid from the lime cures the fish slightly, similar to ceviche. No cooking involved.

faq.q: Is umai actually healthy or is there a catch?
faq.a: Honestly, for a hawker dish it is as clean as it gets. High protein, low carbs, no added fat, no frying. The main thing to be aware of is that you are eating raw fish, so freshness matters a lot. At a legit stall that sources their fish daily, it is fine. The calorie count is also a ballpark estimate since data for this dish is limited.

foods.name: Manok Pansoh
foods.serving: 1 serving (mixed bone-in chicken pieces with broth and aromatics)
foods.metaDescription: Manok Pansoh: ~210 cal per serving, 32g protein, barely any fat. Sarawak bamboo chicken cooked over fire, no oil. One of the cleanest lauk you can eat.
foods.summary: Manok Pansoh is a Sarawak Iban and Bidayuh chicken dish cooked inside a sealed bamboo tube over an open fire with lemongrass, ginger, garlic, torch ginger flower and cassava leaves, producing a fragrant, brothy result with almost no added oil.
foods.answer: One serving of Manok Pansoh (about 280g of bone-in chicken pieces, broth and aromatics) comes in at roughly 210 calories, with 32g protein, 7g carbs and 5g fat. That 5g of fat is mostly from the chicken itself, not from any oil added during cooking, because the bamboo seals everything in and the chicken essentially steams in its own juices. For a proper lauk, those are genuinely good numbers.
realTalk: Okay so first, let me put you on to this dish if you haven't had it before. Manok Pansoh is a traditional Iban and Bidayuh dish from Sarawak where chicken gets packed into a fresh bamboo tube with lemongrass, ginger, galangal, shallots, garlic, bungai kantan (torch ginger flower) and cassava leaves (pucuk ubi), then the whole thing goes over a fire until it's cooked. No wok, no oil, no frying. The bamboo keeps everything moist and adds a faint smoky, grassy aroma that you cannot replicate any other way. At 210 calories for a 280g serving, most of that comes from the 140g of bone-in chicken (175 cal). The broth is basically free at 20 cal, the pucuk ubi adds 12 cal and the aromatics are 5 cal. It's genuinely one of the leanest ways to eat chicken you'll find in any Malaysian cuisine. Fair warning though: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for traditional Borneo dishes is thin, so treat 210 as an honest best guess rather than a lab-verified figure.

What actually moves the number is the chicken cut. If you're getting a version with a lot of thigh or drumstick versus mostly breast, the fat can creep up a bit, maybe 230 to 250 calories per serving instead of 210. The broth is not really an issue calorie-wise unless someone has added coconut milk to it, which is not traditional but does happen at certain restaurants, and that can push it closer to 280 to 320 calories. Portion size matters too: the standard festival or warung serving is roughly 280g but if you're getting a generous plate with extra broth, you might be looking at 350g, which would put you around 260 calories. The good news is there's basically no way to make this dish high-calorie accidentally if you're eating it in its traditional form, no oil, no coconut milk, bone-in skinless chicken, lots of aromatics and cassava leaves.
lighter: Ask for breast-heavy pieces if you can. Bone-in breast in pansoh style will keep you closer to 180 to 190 calories per serving versus thigh-heavy cuts.
Skip the skin if there is any left on. Some versions include a bit of skin for flavour during cooking; pull it off before eating and you shave off maybe 20 to 30 calories.
Drink the broth, skip extra rice if you're watching carbs. The broth is essentially 20 calories and packed with aromatics, so it fills you up without doing damage.

At a restaurant, ask if coconut milk was added. Traditional pansoh has none. Coconut milk in the broth is the one thing that turns this from a diet-friendly dish into something you need to account for properly.
Pair it with ulam-ulaman or paku pakis on the side instead of extra rice. You get volume, fibre and more micronutrients without adding many calories.

faq.q: How many calories in Manok Pansoh?
faq.a: A standard serving of Manok Pansoh (about 280g, bone-in chicken with broth and aromatics) has around 210 calories, with 32g protein, 7g carbs and 5g fat. These are estimates because solid nutritional data for this traditional Sarawak dish is hard to find, but 210 is a reasonable ballpark.

faq.q: What exactly is Manok Pansoh and is it healthy?
faq.a: Manok Pansoh is a traditional Iban and Bidayuh dish from Sarawak where chicken is cooked inside a bamboo tube over fire with lemongrass, ginger, garlic, torch ginger flower and cassava leaves. Because there's no added oil and the chicken steams in its own juices, it's genuinely one of the healthiest ways to eat chicken in Malaysian cooking. High protein, low fat, no deep frying involved.

faq.q: How does Manok Pansoh compare calorie-wise to other chicken dishes?
faq.a: Manok Pansoh at 210 calories per serving is on the lower end for a chicken lauk. Ayam goreng (fried chicken) can be 280 to 350 calories for a similar weight. Kari ayam with coconut milk gravy easily hits 300 to 400 calories per serving. Pansoh's no-oil bamboo cooking method genuinely keeps the calorie count low compared to most other ways Malaysians cook chicken.

foods.name: Midin
foods.metaDescription: Midin stir-fried belacan style is about 140 calories a plate. This Sarawak jungle fern is one of the lightest veg dishes you can order at a kopitiam.
foods.summary: Midin is a wild jungle fern from Sarawak, stir-fried fast over high heat with belacan, garlic and chilli until just-tender and a little crunchy at the tips.
foods.answer: A plate of midin masak belacan at a Sarawak hawker or kopitiam comes in at about 140 calories for roughly 160g. The fern itself is barely 44 calories, and the cooking oil contributes the bulk of the total at around 88 calories for 1 tbsp. Protein is modest at 5g, carbs 8g, fat 10g. As veg dishes go, this is genuinely one of the lighter things you can order.
realTalk: Okay first, if you have never heard of midin, let me put you on to it. It is a wild jungle fern that grows in Sarawak, and it is only really available there and at certain specialty restaurants in KL. The hawker throws it in a screaming-hot wok with belacan, garlic, chilli and a splash of oil, and it comes out with this satisfying crunch at the curly tips. At around 140 calories a plate, it is legitimately a low-calorie dish and something you can eat a lot of without wrecking your deficit. Fair warning though: the numbers here are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for midin is almost nonexistent. We are working from the components, not a lab test, so treat it as a rough guide.

What actually drives the calorie count is the oil. The cooking oil contributes roughly 88 of those 140 calories; the fern itself is barely anything. A hawker who is heavy-handed with the oil could easily push you from 140 to 180 or 200 calories for the same plate. If you are eating masak lemak style with coconut milk, that version runs about 380 calories because the santan contributes an extra 250 to 300 kcal on its own. The garlic-only version (masak bawang putih) saves you a little, coming in around 120 calories. If you are ordering this at a warung, ask for less oil (kurang minyak) and stick to the belacan or garlic versions rather than the lemak.
lighter: Order masak bawang putih instead of belacan style to shave off about 20 calories, or ask for kurang minyak whichever version you get.
Avoid midin masak lemak unless you have the calories to spare, the coconut milk alone adds 250 to 300 kcal and takes the dish to around 380 calories.
Pair it with a plain protein like steamed fish or grilled chicken rather than a saucy lauk, so your overall meal stays light.
If you are cooking at home, cutting back to 2 tsp of oil instead of 1 tbsp saves you around 30 calories and the texture difference is barely noticeable.
Use it as a high-volume filler alongside your rice, the bulk helps you feel full without adding much to your calorie count.

faq.q: How many calories in Midin?
faq.a: A standard plate of midin masak belacan from a Sarawak hawker or kopitiam is about 140 calories for 160g. The garlic-only version is slightly lighter at around 120 calories, and the masak lemak (coconut milk) version jumps to roughly 380 calories.

faq.q: What exactly is midin and where can I find it?
faq.a: Midin is a wild jungle fern native to Sarawak, Borneo. It is harvested from the rainforest and stir-fried with belacan, garlic or coconut milk. You will find it at almost every kopitiam and hawker centre in Kuching and Sibu, but it is hard to find outside Sarawak unless a restaurant specifically sources it.

faq.q: Is midin actually healthy or is it just another oily veg dish?
faq.a: The fern itself is very low calorie, around 44 calories for a cooked portion. It is the cooking oil that takes the total to 140 calories. Compare that to kangkung belacan which runs roughly similar numbers depending on oil. As long as it is not cooked masak lemak style, midin is a genuinely light and filling vegetable to add to your meal.

foods.name: Paku Pakis
foods.metaDescription: Paku pakis goreng belacan is about 180 calories per plate. One of the better veg orders you can make, honestly. Here is the full breakdown.
foods.summary: Pucuk paku fern shoots stir-fried with belacan or sambal, a classic veg dish across Sabah, Sarawak and the East Coast that punches way above its weight on flavour.
foods.answer: A standard plate of paku pakis goreng belacan comes in at around 180 calories for 170g. That gets you 9g protein, 14g carbs and 9g fat. Not bad at all for something that tastes that good with rice. The fern shoots themselves are barely 44 calories for 130g cooked, so the oil doing the stir-frying is where most of the calories come from. The protein figure of 9g is on the higher end for a veg dish, but hawker-style goreng belacan typically includes dried shrimp paste and sometimes ikan bilis, which bump up the protein compared to plain blanched ferns.
realTalk: Paku pakis is stir-fried fiddlehead fern shoots, called pucuk paku, and if you have never tried it, think of it like kangkung's wilder Bornean cousin. Slightly more tender, earthy, with that classic belacan smell that will make the whole table hungry. At 180 calories a plate it is genuinely one of the smarter veg dishes you can order at a warung. The fern shoots themselves only clock in at 44 calories for 130g, which is almost embarrassingly low. Worth noting though, these numbers assume a hawker goreng belacan that includes shrimp paste with some dried shrimp content. Plain blanched paku pakis without belacan will have noticeably less protein. Take the figures as a solid guide, not a lab result.

What actually moves the maths is the oil and whether santan gets involved. A hawker stall goreng will use roughly 1.5 tbsp of oil (14g, about 90 calories) and that alone accounts for half the plate total. Go kerabu style, blanched with lime and belacan and no frying, and the whole thing drops to around 90 calories. Order masak lemak and coconut milk pushes it up to 260 calories, and if there are prawns or ikan bilis in there too you are looking at 310 calories. Portion size matters too, warung plates vary, so if they pile it on generously add another 20 to 30 calories to whatever version you order.
lighter: Order it kerabu style if the stall offers it, blanched and tossed with lime and belacan, cuts the calories roughly in half to around 90 calories.
Skip the masak lemak version when you are watching your numbers, coconut milk adds 80 to 130 extra calories compared to the goreng belacan version.
Eat it with plain white rice rather than nasi goreng so you are not doubling up on oil at the same meal.
Ask the stall to go easy on the oil if you are ordering at a sit-down place, some will actually do it if you ask nicely.
Use it to bulk out your plate volume without adding many calories, paku pakis is genuinely filling for how low-cal it is.

faq.q: How many calories in Paku Pakis?
faq.a: A standard plate of paku pakis goreng belacan is around 180 calories for 170g. The kerabu salad version drops to about 90 calories, while masak lemak with santan climbs to 260 to 310 calories depending on what protein is added.

faq.q: What exactly is paku pakis?
faq.a: Paku pakis refers to fiddlehead fern shoots, called pucuk paku, that are stir-fried with belacan (shrimp paste), sambal or cooked in coconut milk gravy. It is a staple veg dish in Sabah, Sarawak and parts of the East Coast peninsula, and pretty much everyone who tries it becomes a fan.

faq.q: Is paku pakis a healthy choice when eating out?
faq.a: Honestly, yes, it is one of the better veg orders you can make. The fern shoots themselves are very low calorie, and the protein adds up when hawker-style belacan with dried shrimp content is in the mix. The main thing to watch is whether it is fried in a lot of oil or cooked in santan, both of which push the calories up considerably. Goreng belacan style at 180 calories is a solid call.

foods.name: Butod
foods.metaDescription: Butod (sago grub) has about 20 calories per grilled grub. Sabah's most talked-about snack, raw or fried. Here's what you're actually eating.
foods.summary: Butod is the sago grub harvested from rotting sago palms in Sabah, eaten raw and wriggling as a delicacy or grilled and skewered at markets for the slightly less adventurous crowd.
foods.answer: One grilled butod grub comes in at around 20 calories for roughly 7g. Raw it's about 15 calories, deep-fried closer to 25. The calorie count is genuinely low per grub, but fair warning: these numbers are estimates because hard nutritional data on sago grubs is basically non-existent. The fat content is what drives most of the calories, not protein or carbs.
realTalk: Butod is a Sabah thing. If you've never heard of it, it's a fat white grub that lives inside rotting sago palm trunks, and yes, people eat it alive. Locals, especially from Kadazan-Dusun and other indigenous communities, have eaten it for generations. Tourists try it on a dare. The grub has a coconut-y, creamy taste raw, and goes crispy and nutty when grilled or fried. Calorie-wise, 20 calories per grilled grub sounds almost too good to be true. And honestly, be straight with you, these are ballpark estimates because there's very little lab data on butod specifically. What we know is the macros are mostly fat with a bit of protein and basically zero carbs.

In practice, nobody sits down and eats one butod. At a market stall they come skewered in batches of 5 to 10. Ten grilled grubs puts you at around 200 calories, which is still pretty reasonable. Where it gets spicier is deep-fried, where each grub picks up a bit of oil and hits 25 calories each, so ten grubs is closer to 250 calories. The serving size is really what drives the maths here, not the cooking method. If you're eating it as a novelty snack at a Sabah night market, you're probably not having more than 5 to 10 grubs total, which is 100 to 200 calories. Honestly for a snack, that's not bad lah.
lighter: Stick to grilled over deep-fried. You save about 5 calories per grub, which adds up to 25 to 50 calories across a typical serving of 5 to 10.
Eat it raw if you can handle it. At 15 calories per grub it's the lowest calorie option and also how it's traditionally eaten.
Cap yourself at 5 grubs as a tasting experience rather than a full snack. That's only 100 calories grilled.
Skip any dipping sauces they might serve alongside. A sweet chili sauce can add 30 to 50 calories before you notice.
Don't add it on top of a full meal. Treat it as the snack it is, not a side dish to nasi goreng.

variants.name: Raw (live)
variants.note: Eaten wriggling or fresh-chilled; full moisture retained, slightly lower effective calories per grub

variants.note: Most common hawker preparation; crispy outside, juicy inside; fat renders slightly, moisture lost

faq.q: How many calories in Butod?
faq.a: One grilled butod grub is approximately 20 calories. Raw it's around 15 calories and deep-fried about 25 calories. These are estimates as formal nutritional data for sago grubs is limited.

faq.q: What exactly is butod and is it safe to eat?
faq.a: Butod is the larva of the Rhynchophorus ferrugineus beetle, harvested from sago palm trunks. It has been eaten in Sabah for generations and is perfectly safe. The raw version is eaten fresh and wriggling; grilled and fried versions are widely sold at Sabah markets and cultural festivals.

faq.q: Is butod actually a good protein source?
faq.a: Each grub only has about 1g of protein, so a serving of 10 grubs gives you maybe 10g of protein total. It's not a high-volume protein source by any stretch, but insects in general do have reasonably complete amino acid profiles. Think of it as a novelty snack, not a protein strategy.

foods.name: Ikan Empurau
foods.serving: 1 restaurant serving (steamed whole, shared from 1.5-2kg fish, individual portion)
foods.metaDescription: Ikan Empurau, the legendary Sarawak river fish, comes in at roughly 530 calories per restaurant portion. Here's what you're actually eating.
foods.summary: Ikan Empurau is a prized wild river fish from Sarawak, usually steamed simply with ginger and soy to let its naturally rich, fat-marbled flesh do all the talking.
foods.answer: One restaurant portion of Ikan Empurau (about 350g, your share of a 1.5 to 2kg steamed whole fish) comes in at roughly 530 calories, with 65g protein and 25g fat. That fat is the whole point of this fish. Its diet of wild buah engkabang fruit gives the flesh an almost buttery quality you won't get from farmed fish, and that richness is where most of the calories live. The ginger, soy, and aromatics add almost nothing calorie-wise. It's the fish itself doing the heavy lifting.
realTalk: Empurau is basically the wagyu of freshwater fish. It's expensive (think hundreds of ringgit per kilo at a restaurant), it's caught wild in Sarawak's rivers, and it's eaten simply steamed so nothing masks the natural fat. That fat is what gives it the flavour and that's also what drives the 530 calories per serving. At 65g protein and 25g fat, this is a high-protein, moderate-fat meal with almost zero carbs. For a weight loss meal it's actually not bad in terms of macros, assuming you skip the white rice and eat just the fish. Heads up though: these numbers are a genuine ballpark estimate. Hard nutritional data on Empurau is basically non-existent, so treat 530 cal as a reasonable guess rather than a lab result.

What actually changes the maths here is the sesame oil drizzle and any extra soy-based sauces the kitchen adds. That 5g sesame oil accounts for about 40 calories on its own, and some restaurants are heavy-handed with it. Ask them to go light. The bigger variable is portion size, because sharing a whole fish at a table means your 300g of edible flesh can swing 50 to 80 calories either way depending on who takes the thick belly cuts versus the thinner tail sections. Belly meat = more fat = more calories. If you're watching closely, take the tail and leave the belly to the person who's not counting lah.
lighter: Take the tail cuts over the belly cuts. The belly has the most fat and accounts for the biggest calorie variance.
Ask the kitchen to go easy on the sesame oil drizzle. That 5g adds 40 calories and if they pour generously it can double.
Skip the white rice entirely and eat the fish with just the ginger and spring onion. You're already at 530 cal from the protein alone, no need to add another 200 to 300.
Don't mop up the plate juices with extra rice. The soy and oil pooled at the bottom of the steaming plate are flavourful but calories you don't need.
Order just one plate of fish to share and load up on stir-fried vegetables like sayur manis or midin on the side instead of a second starch.

faq.q: How many calories in Ikan Empurau?
faq.a: One restaurant portion of steamed Ikan Empurau (around 350g, your individual share of a whole fish) is roughly 530 calories, with 65g protein, 25g fat, and only 3g carbs. Note that this is a best-estimate figure as reliable nutritional data for this fish is very limited.

faq.q: What is Ikan Empurau and why is it so expensive?
faq.a: Empurau is a wild-caught river fish found in Sarawak, Borneo. It's expensive because it can only be caught wild (it doesn't survive in farms), grows slowly, and its unique diet of wild forest fruits gives the flesh a buttery, rich flavour unlike any other freshwater fish. Prices at Sarawak restaurants often run into hundreds of ringgit per kilo, making it a special occasion order.

faq.q: Is Ikan Empurau a healthy choice for someone losing weight?
faq.a: Honestly, not bad. The macros are solid: 65g protein, low carbs, and the fat is natural fish fat rather than added cooking oil. The issue is cost more than calories. If you're eating it at a restaurant, skip the rice and pair with vegetables and you've got a high-protein, reasonable-calorie meal. Just watch the sesame oil drizzle and any extra sauces the kitchen adds.

foods.name: Kek Lapis Sarawak
foods.metaDescription: Kek Lapis Sarawak packs 200 calories per slice (45g) from butter, eggs and condensed milk. Gorgeous to look at, brutal on the calorie count.
foods.summary: Sarawak's famous layered cake, built slice by painstaking slice from butter, eggs, condensed milk and sugar, and wildly calorie dense for its size.
foods.answer: One slice of Kek Lapis Sarawak (about 45g) comes in at 200 calories, with 12g fat, 20g carbs and 3g protein. That's roughly 4-5 calories per gram, which puts it right up there with the densest cakes you'll find. The portion looks small on the plate but the numbers are not small at all.
realTalk: Kek Lapis Sarawak is a Sarawakian layered cake where each coloured band is baked separately, one layer at a time, until you get this stunning striped brick of butter, eggs, condensed milk and sugar. It's a big deal back home, gifted during Hari Raya and Gawai, sold by the loaf at Kuching airport for serious money. The problem is it's extremely dense. Butter alone accounts for about 129 of those 200 calories per slice, and that's before you get to the sugar and condensed milk. Honestly the numbers here are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for Kek Lapis is thin, and recipes vary enormously between home bakers and commercial producers. But 200 calories per 45g slice is a reasonable middle ground for the original plain version.

The variant matters a lot. Plain or pandan sits around 200 to 205 calories per slice, which is already not nothing. Cheese filling jumps to 250, and durian filling pushes to 270 calories per slice because durian pulp carries its own fat and sugar load. A typical gift box loaf weighs 600g to 800g and gets sliced into 13 to 18 pieces. If you eat three slices, you're looking at 600 calories just from cake. The only real way to manage this one is portion size: eat one slice, put the box away, and don't stand next to it. There's no low-cal swap here, it's a celebration food.
lighter: Stick to one slice and treat it like a proper dessert, not a casual snack you keep nibbling from. One slice is 200 calories, three slices is 600.
Choose original or pandan over cheese or durian variants. That's a difference of 50 to 70 calories per slice, which adds up fast if you're having a few.
Eat it after a protein-heavy meal so you're already fairly full. It's much easier to stop at one slice when you're not hungry.
If you're at a Gawai or Raya spread, pace yourself: have one slice of Kek Lapis and skip the other kuih on the table rather than sampling everything.
Don't pair it with teh tarik or Milo Ais on top. Those drinks add another 100 to 150 calories before you've even thought about it.

variants.note: Pandan paste adds negligible calories; essentially same calorie density as original

variants.note: Cocoa powder layers add modest extra calories; slightly denser than plain

variants.note: Gula apong replaces white sugar; slightly more calorific due to natural sugar concentration

variants.name: Durian

faq.q: How many calories in Kek Lapis Sarawak?
faq.a: One standard slice of Kek Lapis Sarawak (45g) is about 200 calories. The number shifts depending on the variant: plain or pandan sits around 200 to 205, cheese filling bumps it to 250, and durian filling goes up to 270 calories per slice.

faq.q: What actually is Kek Lapis Sarawak?
faq.a: It's a layered cake from Sarawak where each coloured band is baked individually, layer by layer, until you get a dense striped loaf. The batter is loaded with butter, whole eggs, condensed milk and sugar, which is why it's so rich. It's a prestige gift item, especially during Gawai and Hari Raya, and a serious point of Sarawakian pride.

faq.q: Is Kek Lapis Sarawak healthy?
faq.a: Straightforwardly, no. It's a celebration cake built almost entirely on butter, eggs and sugar. At 200 calories for a 45g slice with 12g fat, it's calorie dense without offering much protein or fibre in return. That's not a reason to never eat it, it's just not an everyday snack if you're watching your intake.

foods.name: Khau Yuk
foods.serving: 1 serving (3-4 slices pork belly with mui choy and gravy)
foods.metaDescription: Khau Yuk (Hakka braised pork belly) has around 490 calories per serving. Most of it is fat from the pork belly. Here is what you are actually eating.
foods.summary: Khau Yuk is a Hakka braised pork belly dish, slow-cooked with preserved mustard greens (mui choy) or fermented bean curd until the fat is meltingly soft.
foods.answer: A standard serving of Khau Yuk, which is 3 to 4 slices of braised pork belly with mui choy and gravy (about 220g total), comes in at around 490 calories. That is 16g protein, 8g carbs, and a hefty 41g of fat. This is Hakka braised pork belly, slow-cooked until the skin and fat layers go completely soft, and those numbers do not lie about where the calories are coming from.
realTalk: Khau Yuk is a Hakka dish you will find at kopitiams and Chinese restaurants across Malaysia, especially in communities with strong Hakka roots. The dish is pork belly braised low and slow with either mui choy (preserved mustard greens) or nam yue (red fermented bean curd), sometimes with fried taro layered in between. The result is pork belly so soft the fat practically dissolves when you eat it. That melt-in-your-mouth texture is exactly why 100g of the pork belly alone clocks in at 395 calories. The mui choy adds almost nothing calorie-wise at just 18 calories per 60g, but the braising sauce and absorbed oil contribute another 77 calories. So 490 calories for a serving is a reasonable ballpark, though be honest: this is a genuine estimate. Hard nutritional data for home-style Hakka dishes like this is thin, and fat content can swing quite a bit depending on how thick the belly slices are and how generously the cook ladles on the gravy.

The biggest variable here is portion size and how much gravy you take. Khau Yuk is not a lean protein situation, full stop. If you are counting calories, the practical move is to eat one or two slices instead of three or four, which cuts you from 490 calories down to roughly 250 to 300 calories. Skip the extra ladle of braising sauce too, that alone saves you maybe 30 to 40 calories per tablespoon of oil-rich gravy. The taro version (wu tau kau yuk) jumps to around 640 calories because deep-fried taro absorbs a lot of oil, so if you are watching numbers, stick to the mui choy version. Pair it with plain steamed rice rather than claypot or fried rice to keep the overall meal from blowing out your deficit for the day.
lighter: Take two slices instead of three or four. That alone brings you from 490 calories down to roughly 250 calories.
Ask for less gravy or leave the pooled oil at the bottom of the dish. The braising oil is where a chunk of the fat calories hide.
Go for the mui choy version over the taro version. Wu tau kau yuk is about 640 calories because of the fried taro, so the mustard greens version saves you roughly 150 calories per serving.
Eat it with plain steamed rice, not fried rice. Khau Yuk on white rice is already a full meal without adding another 400 calories from the rice side.
Balance the plate with a simple stir-fried vegetable like kangkung or kailan to pad the volume without adding much to your calorie count.

variants.name: Mui choy (preserved mustard greens) version
variants.note: Most common in Malaysian kopitiams and Hakka restaurants; mustard greens add negligible calories

variants.name: Nam yue (red fermented bean curd) version without taro
variants.note: Richer sauce from fermented bean curd adds slightly more fat and sodium

variants.name: Wu tau kau yuk (with fried taro)
variants.note: Deep-fried taro slices interleaved with pork belly add ~120-150 kcal from starch and absorbed frying oil

faq.q: How many calories in Khau Yuk?
faq.a: A standard serving of Khau Yuk (3 to 4 slices pork belly with mui choy and gravy, about 220g) is around 490 calories, with 16g protein, 8g carbs, and 41g fat. Note that this is a ballpark estimate as detailed nutrition data for this dish is not widely available.

faq.q: What exactly is Khau Yuk?
faq.a: Khau Yuk is a Hakka braised pork belly dish. The pork belly is slow-braised with either mui choy (preserved mustard greens) or nam yue (red fermented bean curd) until the fat layers go completely soft. It is a non-halal dish and one of the classic comfort foods in Malaysian Chinese cooking.

faq.q: Is Khau Yuk healthy?
faq.a: Honestly, no, not if you are trying to lose weight. At 490 calories for a small serving and 41g of fat, it is one of the higher-calorie lauk options out there. It is not something to eat every day if you are in a deficit. That said, a couple of slices alongside vegetables and plain rice is manageable as an occasional meal, just keep your portion honest.

foods.name: Abacus Seeds
foods.metaDescription: Abacus Seeds clock in at around 520 calories per plate. Here's what's actually in that chewy Hakka yam-dough dish and whether it fits your goals.
foods.summary: A Hakka stir-fried dish of chewy yam-tapioca dough beads tossed with minced pork, dried shrimp, mushroom and black fungus, popular in Hakka communities across Malaysia.
foods.answer: One plate of Abacus Seeds (around 320g) comes in at roughly 520 calories, with 22g protein, 65g carbs and 18g fat. The yam-tapioca dough beads carry most of the carb load, while the minced pork and cooking oil push the fat and protein up. Fair warning, these numbers are a ballpark estimate since hard nutritional data for this dish is basically nonexistent, but 500-plus calories for a full plate is a reasonable working figure.
realTalk: Abacus Seeds (算盘子, suan pan zi) is a Hakka dish you'll find at Hakka restaurants and some heritage kopitiam spots across Malaysia, especially in KL, Bentong and parts of Sabah. If you've never had it, the dough beads are made from yam and tapioca starch, then hand-rolled into little round shapes that look like abacus beads, boiled and stir-fried with minced pork, dried shrimp, shiitake mushrooms and black fungus. The texture is QQ and slightly sticky, think a chewier version of mochi but savory. At 520 calories a plate it's not a diet food, but it's also not a disaster. The yam dough beads alone account for 290 of those calories, and the minced pork adds another 145. To be straight with you though, this is a medium-confidence estimate because proper lab-tested nutrition data for Abacus Seeds is basically nonexistent. Take the number as a useful guide, not gospel.

What actually moves the number is how heavy-handed the wok is with oil and how big the portion is. A generous cook who doubles the oil can easily add 80 to 100 extra calories without you noticing. Portion size is the other big lever: a smaller serve of 200g instead of 320g would drop you closer to 325 calories. The minced pork contributes real protein but also fat, so if you could swap in lean chicken mince you'd save maybe 30 to 40 calories. Ask for less oil if you're ordering at a restaurant, most places will accommodate. The dried shrimp and mushrooms are practically free at only 40 calories for 30g, so don't stress about those.
lighter: Ask for less oil at the wok. This dish traditionally uses a fair bit and even cutting it by half saves you around 40 to 60 calories.
Eat a smaller portion. 200g instead of 320g puts you around 325 calories and honestly still feels satisfying because the dough is dense and chewy.
Pair it with a clear soup or a plate of stir-fried sayur manis instead of ordering extra rice or another fried item.
Skip any extra sauce or gravy that some places pour over. That stuff adds calories fast and you can't easily account for it.
Share a plate between two people and bulk up with a simple vegetable dish on the side. You still get to enjoy the flavour without eating the full 520 calories yourself.

faq.q: How many calories in Abacus Seeds?
faq.a: One plate of Abacus Seeds (roughly 320g) is around 520 calories. That breaks down to about 22g protein, 65g carbs and 18g fat. This is a solid estimate but hard to pin down precisely since the dish doesn't have much published nutritional data.

faq.q: What exactly are Abacus Seeds?
faq.a: Abacus Seeds are a Hakka dish made from yam and tapioca starch dough that's hand-shaped into little bead-like rounds, boiled until chewy, then stir-fried with minced pork, dried shrimp, mushrooms and black fungus. They taste savory and slightly earthy from the yam, with a QQ chewy bite. It's not pork-free, so non-halal.

faq.q: Is Abacus Seeds healthy?
faq.a: It's a balanced enough meal with decent protein from the pork and reasonable carbs from the yam dough, but 520 calories a plate means it's not a light option. The bigger issue is the oil used in stir-frying, which you can't always control. If you're counting calories, treat it as a proper meal rather than a snack, and maybe skip the sugary drink that usually comes with it.

foods.name: Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken)
foods.serving: 1 serving (2-3 bone-in chicken pieces with wine sauce)
foods.metaDescription: Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken) has around 530 calories per serving. The sesame oil is what pushes the number up. Here's the full breakdown.
foods.summary: A Foochow-Sarawak classic from Sibu where chicken is braised in red glutinous rice wine and sesame oil, traditionally served during confinement but honestly too good to wait that long.
foods.answer: One serving of Ayam Masak Arak, which is 2 to 3 bone-in pieces with the wine sauce, comes in at around 530 calories, with 30g protein, 6g carbs, and 35g fat. The dish is lower carb than you'd expect but the fat is real because sesame oil alone contributes about 180 calories per serving. These are honest estimates since detailed nutritional data for this dish is sparse, so treat it as a ballpark rather than a precise lab result.
realTalk: Ayam Masak Arak is a Foochow confinement dish from Sibu, Sarawak. If you're not from that community, you may have only seen it at Sarawakian kopitiam or at a friend's mum's place after she gave birth. It's chicken braised in ang chao, which is red glutinous rice wine, cooked down with sesame oil and ginger until the sauce is fragrant and slightly sticky. At 530 calories for a solid serving, it's not a diet dish. The two big calorie drivers are the sesame oil, about 180 calories from just 1.5 tablespoons, and the chicken thigh and drumstick fat. On the protein side, 30g is decent. Worth flagging: these numbers are a ballpark estimate because hard nutritional data for this dish basically doesn't exist, so there's genuine uncertainty of maybe plus or minus 60 to 80 calories per serving.

What actually moves the number is mostly the oil. A soup-style version with more wine broth and less sesame oil drops the count to around 380 calories for the chicken and broth alone. The rich confinement version with extra sesame oil and wine can hit 680 calories for the same portion size. If you're eating it at home or at a kopitiam, ask for less oil in the braising if you can. Choosing breast over thigh would cut maybe 40 to 60 calories from the chicken portion. The ang chao wine and dregs themselves only add about 75 calories from the 70g in a standard serving, so the wine isn't the villain here.
lighter: Ask for the soup-style version with more wine broth and less sesame oil. That alone can bring it down to around 380 calories.
Skip the mee sua noodles if they come on the side. They add calories fast and you probably don't need them if you're already eating rice.
If you're cooking at home, cut the sesame oil to 1 tablespoon instead of 1.5. You still get the flavour but lose about 60 calories from the dish.
Use chicken breast instead of thigh and drumstick. Less flavour, yes, but if you're counting calories the swap saves you 40 to 60 calories per serving.
Eat it with plain steamed rice and a pile of sayur manis or other low-calorie veg on the side. The dish pairs well with greens and you'll stay full without needing a second helping.

faq.q: How many calories in Ayam Masak Arak (Rice Wine Chicken)?
faq.a: Around 530 calories per serving of 2 to 3 bone-in chicken pieces with wine sauce, roughly 300g total. That's 30g protein, 6g carbs, and 35g fat. The sesame oil is the main calorie driver at about 180 calories on its own.

faq.q: What is Ayam Masak Arak exactly?
faq.a: It's a Foochow Chinese dish from Sibu, Sarawak where chicken is braised in ang chao (red glutinous rice wine) with sesame oil and ginger. It's traditionally a confinement dish eaten after childbirth but you'll also find it at Sarawakian kopitiam. The sauce has a slightly sweet, winey, deeply aromatic flavour from the wine dregs and sesame oil cooked together.

faq.q: Is Ayam Masak Arak a healthy dish?
faq.a: It depends what you mean by healthy. The protein is solid at 30g, the carbs are low at 6g, and ginger has its merits. But 35g fat and 530 calories for a side dish means it adds up fast if you're not careful with portions. The soup-style version at around 380 calories is a lighter option if you're watching your intake.

foods.name: Butter Prawns
foods.serving: 1 restaurant portion (6-8 medium-large prawns, shell-on, with egg floss)
foods.metaDescription: Butter Prawns clock around 580 calories per restaurant portion. The butter and egg floss add up fast. Full breakdown inside.
foods.summary: Shell-on prawns deep-fried then wok-tossed in a rich butter, curry leaf and egg-floss sauce, which is as good as it sounds and as calorie-heavy as you'd expect.
foods.answer: A restaurant portion of Butter Prawns (6-8 medium-large shell-on prawns with egg floss) comes in at around 580 calories, with 28g protein, 14g carbs and 44g fat. The prawns themselves are not the problem; it's the butter, the deep-frying oil and those crispy egg-yolk strands that stack the numbers fast. Note that this is a ballpark estimate because reliable lab data for this dish is thin, so treat it as a realistic guide rather than gospel.
realTalk: Butter Prawns is one of those dishes where the main ingredient is genuinely good for you and then the cooking method absolutely wrecks the macro profile. You get prawns, which are lean and high-protein, but they go into a deep fryer first, then get tossed in a wok with a generous amount of butter, evaporated milk, curry leaves, and egg-yolk floss fried in more butter. The egg floss alone contributes around 115 calories. The butter base adds another 130 calories. So out of 580 total calories, roughly 390 come from fat sources. If you've never had this dish, picture crispy golden prawns coated in a fragrant, slightly creamy sauce with delicate egg strands that melt on your tongue. It's genuinely one of the better things Malaysian Chinese cuisine has produced. Worth eating. Just not every day, lah.

The version you order matters a lot. A home-cooked pan-fried version with the same butter and egg floss but without deep-frying sits around 280 calories, basically half the restaurant number, because you skip the absorbed frying oil. The salted egg version pushes up to 640 calories because salted egg yolks replace or supplement the egg floss and those yolks are very fat-dense. Portion size is another big variable. A restaurant order is typically shared between two or three people alongside rice and vegetables, so your actual intake might be 180-200 calories per person if you split it properly. The calorie estimates here are best guesses since standardised data for this dish is genuinely hard to find, so treat the numbers as a solid ballpark rather than exact figures.
lighter: Share it properly. Split one restaurant portion between two people and you're looking at roughly 290 calories each, which is perfectly manageable.
Order the pan-fried version when you can, or ask at hawker stalls. Skipping the deep-fry step cuts about 80 calories straight away.
Eat it with plain steamed rice, not fried rice. The dish already has enough fat going on, you don't need more from the rice.
Go easy on the sauce at the bottom of the plate. A lot of the butter and oil pools there. You can leave it and lose maybe 50-80 calories.
Skip the salted egg upgrade. The regular egg floss version saves you around 60 calories per portion and honestly tastes just as good.
